come, not as we would have it, but as the Great Architect of the Universe has
decreed, and we, the brethren of the Craft, can now only in the agony of· our
spirit and in the distress of our llrief exclaim "farewell ! "

The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :BRETHREN 01!' THE GRAND LODGE:-

In compliance with the Constitution of the Grand Lodge, it now becomes
my duty to submit to you an account of my official acts during the past
Masonic year, and to ma.ke such recommendations as may seem to be for the
best interests of .this Grand Jurisdiction. For the forty-sixth time have the
representatives of our several Lodges assembled in Annual Communication.
Mindful of our dependence on God, His blessings have been invoked upon us
and upon our deliberations. We are now ready to proceed with our annual
business.
It is with unfeigned satisfaction that I am able to congratulai;e you upon
the prosperity of the Craft within our jurisdiction during the year just closed,
and that peace and harmony everywhere prevail.
There have been 2,522 degrees conferred and we have made a net gain
in membership of 391.
While we rejoice in our prosperity, we are called upon to mourn. The
gavel has sounded in the Heavens, and two of our loved and honored Past
Grand Masters have been summoned to tba.t blillaful Lodge on high, where
our Supreme Grand Master forever presides.

It is my sad duty to report to the Grand Lodge, at this time, the ~ea.th .of
a beloved brother, who for four years occupied the Grand East of this JUnsdiction :..:__
Joe:N MILLS BROWNE, the illustrious Mason, citizen and soldier, has
crossed the river and is forever at rest.
Brother BROWNE first appeared in Grand.Lodge, as a member, at the
twenty-second Annual Communication, in 1871. He was a surgeon in the
United States Navy, stationed at Mare Island Navy Yard, and a member of
Naval Lodge, No. 87 ; he was elected Master of Naval Lodge at the annual
election of 1870, and represented hie Lodge in this Grand Lodge at the
ensuing session. Gifted with a pleasing addreBB,· and a mannner tha.t created
a. desire on the pa.rt of his audience to be convinced, hie position was assured.
Brother BROWNE a.t once took part in the endeavor to procure an amendment
to our Constitution, authorizing the Grand Master to. grant dispeI18ations to
Lodges to receive and act upon petitions of persons en~aged in the naval a~d
military service of the United States, who had not resided twelv~ months Ill
the Sta.te a.nd six months in the jurisdiction of the Lodge, as reqmred by that
instrument. The favorable impreBBion created upon the members of the
Grand Lodge by Brother .BROWNE in the advocacy of his nmendment led to
his election as Junior Grand ·warden at the same ses~ion. He was continually in the service of the Grand Lodge from that time until the conclusion of
his four years of service as Grand Master in 1879.
.
Brother BROWNE never lost his interest in Masonry, but to the day of his
death was active in the promulgation of its sublime philosophy. The life of
our brother was devoted to his country's service, Upon his retirement at the
age of 62, he was credited in the department a.rchi.ves with forty-one ~ear:'
continuous service as surgeon in the navy of the Un\ted Stat~s. As an lilCI·
dent of th~t service, Brother BROWNE was the surgeon of the United States
Ship " Kearsarge " in her world-renowned contest with the " Alaba.ma" off
the coast of France on the twelth da.y of June, 1864, which comba.t is so
gra.phically narrated by him in a. pa.per published in the Century War
Records.
Joe:N MILLS BROWNE wa.s born in Hinsdale, New Hampshire, May 10th,
1831. He was graduated with distinguished honor in his chosen profeBBi~n of
medicine before he attained his majority, and wa.s, at the age of 21, appomted
a surgeon in the navy of the United States, in which position he serv~ continuously until his retirement at the age of 62 years. He was hold'.ng the
office of Medical Director when his merits were still further recogm.zed by
President Cleveland by his appointment as ''Surgeon General," to which
position he was reappointed by President Harrison four years la.tar. .
.
Brother BROWNE was retired with the rank of Commodore, the highest m
the medical department of the United States Navy.
·
With such qualificatioil8 as he poBBessed, it is not strange that he was genera.Uy beloved by all who knew him, nor remarkable that we should honor
and revere his memory, and endeavor to follow his exa.mple in his attachment
and loyal service to Freemasonry as exemplified in the Grand Lodge of California.

1895.J

Grand Lodge of Ualij<Yrnia.

Our Past Grand Master has not been with us for several years, and yet so
true is it that a man's good deeds. live after him that his eminent service has
remained with us, and needs but this reminder to revive in the memories of
his brethren of California the loyal service of a master workman.
The saddest duty which, as Grand Master, I have been called upon to
perform, was to call a special meeting of the Grand Lodge on September 7th
last, for the purpose of laying to rest, with appropriate ceremonies, the
remains of our lamented brother, Past Grand Master WILLIAM CALDWELL
BELCHER. The day was propitious, and was emblema.tical of the calmness
and sunshine in the life of this beloved patriarch in Masonry. He passed to
his reward on the morning of September 1st, 1895. The gra.nd old jurist had
"filed his last brief," and entered the Sanctum Sanctorum, to offer up his
devotions throughout eternity. He was more generally known, perhaps,
than any other Mason in California ; and on the following day the daily preBB
carried the saddening message to every city and village in the State. Whereever he was known he wa.s respected and loved-respected for the spotless
character he bore, and loved for his gentleneBS, fidelity and broad humanity.
Time is not wasted in the studying of the various phases of a good man's.
character. In addition to the interest taken in the achievement of succeBB,
there is the fostering influence of noble example.
For thirty-five years he was a conspicuous figure in the Grand Lodge of
California. During all the years of his Ma.sonic life, he gave it patient, faithful and untiring service ; it was, in every sense, a labor of love-an individ·
ual interest a.nd solicitude for Masonry.
·
For three years he wa.s Grand Master, and for twenty-eight years Chair·
ma.n of the Committee on Jurisprudence. In this capacity he did his best
and most successful work. To be convinced of this, you have but to take the
annual reports and see the evidence of his superior skill. He was the most
thoughtful a.nd coil8iderate man for the feelings of others tha.t I have ever
known. Whenever he ma.de a ruling on a. point of Masonic law, those who
may have differed with him well knew that he had but one grand object
in view, that of promoting the best interests of the Order he loved ; and
when he found occasion to differ with a Grand Master upon some decieion, he
has been known, time and again, to seek a private interview, that he might
expla.in the reason of the adverse opinion he entertained. The kind and
paternal interest he ma.nifested on such occasions was most touching. The
tender rega.rd for the opinion of his fellow members on ·the committee of
which he wa.s so long chairma.n w~ likewise remarkable. While all were ever
ready to defer to his wisdom, his experience a.nd his superior judgment, he
never seemed conscious of it, and wa.s never too much hurried to patiently
consider ~nd give due weight to the suggestions of his confrP.res. No one
was more polite and courteous in debate, always yielding to his opponent as
much as he asked for himself; and though, after due deliberation, his views
and principles were unchangeable, he never misrepresented nor wronged those
who differed with him,
Born with a capacity for development of the best qualities of mind and
heart, Bro. BELCHER was a specimen product of nature. Inherent worth was

14

Proce,edings of the

[Oct. 8,

his birthright ; culture and refinement were the outgrowth of aelf-effort and
the environments of t~e age in which he lived. His aim and ambition was to
be useful, accomplish good and render a lasting service to humanity. Not an
ambition which dwarfs the affections and prostitutes the soul to worldly
clamor, but an ambition to daily apply the golden rule of life. This was h'.s ·
constant and sturdy purpoee, and was pursued unfalteringly to the end. His
modesty amounted to diffidence ; he scorned sensationalism and shrank from

The following letter was received from P<L8Mena Lodge:" An appeal has been made to our Lodge for pecuniary aid by an aged
woman who claims that her husband was a Mason; that he died forty years
ago in the State of Iowa, and that he was a d.i mitted Mason seven years pre·
ceding his death. This arced lady comes to the coast with a grandson, who is
a victim of that dread disease consumption, expecting to be supported by
Pasadena Lodge. Any suggestions you may be pleased to offer us for our
guidance regarding the validity of drawing on the already depleted treasury
of our Lodge will be thankfully received.
Answer. Pasadena Lodge is under no Masonic obligation to extend to the
applicant any of the rights, privileges or charities of the Order. Under our
Masonic law her husband was certainly not entitled thereto, and I can see
no good reason why it should be different in the case of his widow.
The following case was referred to me by the Master of Athena Lodge,
No. 228:At the annual election for officers· votes were cast by members who were in
arrears for dnes, the votes were canvassed and the officers declared elected.
Prior to the next stated meeting a brother insists that the Master declare the
election illegal.
I decided that the election must stand. While it is true that under the
provisions of Section 2, Article IX of the Uniform Code of By-Lawe of
Lodges, delinquents should not be permitted to vote, in this case delinquents
having been permitted to do so would not, in my opinion, justify the Master
in declaring the election illegal.
A member of Woodland Lodge, No. 156, writes as follows:·•Previous to voting the Master announced that brethren in arrears for dues
were not entitled to vote. The~ were .twenty-six vo~ cast and only twentytwo brethren present who had paid theu dues. In view of these facts was it
a legal election ? And has the Lodge a right to install the officers so elected ? "

As in the case of .Athens Lodge, I decided the election to be legal and that
the officers should be installed.
The Master of .Athens Lodge, No. 228, proposed the following questions:lst. Some weeks a.go the infant son of the Secretary of the Lodge died.
The father was without means; I, as Master of the Lodge, advanced the sum
of fifty dollars to defray the funeral expenses, My claim against the Lodge
was demurred to on the ground that the Secretary had no claim upon the
Lodge, and that the money_ should be ~ega.rded as a loan, to be repaid at some
future time. I consider. this unmasomc, for never was there a case of greater
need.
2d. Our Trustees have, it ~ppears, made loans of considerable sums to
certain irrespor,sible parties, entaili~g a loss to the Lodge of several hundred
dollars. Are these Trustees responsible, and to what extent?
The case presented in the first instance, is one altogether proper for the
consideration of the Lodge. If its Secretary, or any other member, under
the circumstances stated, was unable to meet the necessary expenses of burying his child, it was the duty of the Lodge to help him, and, so we may say,
it was the duty of every member of the Lodge to see that he did receive the
requisite ·assistance, And it certainly would be proper, if the Master made
the advance on the part of the Lodge, because it was not then convenient to
call his Lodge together to act upon the case, or, if it has a Uommittee on
Charity, to call that committee together, that the Lodge should repay the
sum to him. If, however, the advance made was as a loan, then, as a matter
of course, the Lodge would be under no obligation to repay the amount. .
As to the second, Trustees are appointed for the purpose of making investments, and if they exercise their best judgment in making
loans, and act in good faith, they incur no liability as guarantors or otherwise,
and would not be responsible in case the parties to whom the loans were
made, for any reason, were unable 1Jo pay. If they made the loans to parties
whom they knew to be irresponsible at the Mme, they acted in bad faith,
dealing with trust funds as they would not have dealt with their own. The
law requires of Trustees that they shall act in good faith and exercise their
best judgment. That is all.
Question. Can the Tyler of a Lodge (he being a member in good standing) debate and vote on questions before the Lodge ?
Answer. Yes. The Tyler should lie granted this privilep;e if he so desires, a.nd the Master should relieve him of bis duties for the purpose.
A person received the three degrees in Masonry in the Ea.stern states some
twenty yea.rs ago, and shortly afterward removed from the jurisdiction of his
Lodge, and was suspended for non-payment of dues. About fifteen years ago
he came to California and ha.s ever since resided here. After leaving the East
he changed his name. I was asked if a Lodge could receive a petition signed
by the new name and confer on him the three degrees. I answered, No. He
must place himself in standing, by eithn paying his dues, or by having the
same remitted by his Lodge, and secure a. dimit therefrom; then make application for membership in the manner provided in our Constitution.
Question. When charges are preferred against the Secretary of a Lodge,
who should notify the members of the special meeting called to elect Commissioners ?

Answer. The Secretary should issue the notices, and act in his official
capacity until the Commissioners are elected; then he should be temporarily
suspended from office, and a Secretary pro tem. appointed to discharge the
duties of the office to the conclusion of the trial. The Secretary is not supposed to know against whom 'the charges are preferred.

Answer. No.
A brother had for a number of years remained suspended for non-payment
of dues. He became sick, and thinking his life fast drawing . to a close, expressed a desire to be restored by his Lodge, that he might die a Mason in
good standing. This re.q uest was made known to his Lodge at the next
stated meeting thereof, when a brother moved that the delinquent's dues be
remitted, and the motion was carried without opposition. Prior to the next
stated meeting I was asked if, at that meeting, the vote by which the dues
were remitted could be reconsidei;ed. I answered, No.
In another case, the question as to a reconsideration of the action of the
Lodge was referred to me as follows :A brother was suspended for non-payment of dues at the stated meeting
in December, 1894, the Lodge having refused to grant him further time. At
the stated meeting in January, 1895, a brother, who felt aggrieved at the
action of the Lodge, made the following statement in open Lodge : "That he
had seen the Grand Master, and had talked the matter over with him, and
that the Grand Master would very likely order us to rescind our action, or he
would take our charter."
Upon this statement being made, a member made a motion to rescind the
action of the Lodge, and to remit the dues of the brother to January lst,
1895, stating "that if we had to reinstate the brother, we had better do it
voluntarily than to be ordered to do so by the Grand Master, or lose our
charter."
The mbtion was carried and the brother ~as reinstated. Soon thereafter
the Master of the Lodge called on me, and stated that by reason of such action
the harmony of the Lodge had been disturbed, and asked my advice as to the
best way to proceed, with a view of restoring harmony. I assured him that
the statement made by the brother as coming from me was incorrect; "that
the suspension of the brother was a matter with which the Lodge had a per·
feet right to deal, and I did not think I had any right to interfere." The
Master then asked : " Can our Lodge reconsider the vote by which the
brother's dues were remitted?" I answered: Your Lodge having acted in
the matter under a misrepresentation of facts, its action may be reconsidered.
Question. Can a Lodge set apart; for social purposes, money received for
rent of their hall ?
Answer. No. Such funds are part of the revenue of the Lodge, and a
sum not exceed~g five per cent of the total revenue for the preceding Masonic year can be used for such purposes.

PKNSACOLA, FLORIDA, May 20th, 1895.
At a meeting of Escambia Lodge, No. 15, F. & .A. M., held May 20th,
1895, a committ.ee was appointed to draft resolutions expressive of the feeling
of this Lodge in the case of WALTER Wu.cox, to be communicated to the
Grand Master of California, and through him to the Masonic bodies of the
State.
The following resolution was reported and adopted : -

Be it ReRol~, That while Masonry is founded on, and its cardinal pnnc1ples are, Faith, Hope and Charity, its teachings, traditions and practice,
protection of the widow, care of the destitute orphans, relief of the distreBBed,
and brotl:terly love exercised in its broadest and fullest meanin~, - the Christian charity followed to complete consummation in this instance is admirable
in its devotion to the tenets of Masonry, and is worthy of the emulation of
all Masons, in all lands. The care and guardianship of one's own blood is a
binding tie-a God imposed obligation.
When the friendless, helpless orphan is carefully brought to man's estate,
fully equipped for the battle of life by those bound only by the Mystic Tie, it
is of the truest and purest Christian charity. Escambia Lodge sends greetingd
to the Masons of the Golden State for this charity, so pure, so true, extended
to one of Florida's sons.

On .August 3d I visit-ed La Fayette Lodge, No. 126, at Sebastopol, with the
Inspector of.the Sixteenth District. The thit"d degree was conferred in a very
correct and impressive manner by the officers of the Lodge.
On .August 9th I visited Callayomi Lodge, No. 282, at Middletown. The
Master of the Lodge was prevented from being" present by reason of sickness.
Past Master JAMES PARRISH presided, and the third degree was conferred in a
very creditable manner.
On .Angust 17th I visited San Benito Lodge, No. 211, at Hollister, in com·
pany with the Inspector of the Twenty-eighth District. The manner in
which the third degree was conferred was an evidence that the officers of this
Lodge are interested in the work. There was a large attendance of the
brethren at this meeting, and from an inspection of the register -I found that
the attendance at their meetings was larger in proport;ion to membership than
any other Lodge visited.
On .August 31st I visited Pajaro Lodge, No. llO, at Watsonville. On this
visit I again l;lad the pleasqre of the company of the Inspector of the Twenty.
eighth District. · The third degree' was conferred in a very impressive manne_r.
Tqe attendance was large and much interest manifested.
, On September 14th, in company with the Grand Lecturer and the Inspector

of the District, I visited Abell Lodge, No. 146, at Ukiah. There was a large

On September 16th I visited Hartl.ey Lodge, No. 199, at Lakeport. The
Grand Lecturer and the Inspector of the Fifteenth Dietrict were with me on
this visit. The third degree was conferred in a very impressive manner by
the officers of the Lodge. There was a very large attendance, every Lodge in
the District being well represented. A large delegation of brethren from
Abell Lodge at' Ukiah paid a fraternal visit on this occasion, and I am convinced that much good resulted from the meeting.
On September 21st I visited Oroville Lodge, No. 103, at Oroville. The Inspector had called a District meeting, and all the Lodges comprising the
Eleventh District were well represented. The third degree was conferr'ld in
a very impressive manner by the officers of the Lodge, and a very pleasant
and profitable evening was spent with the brethren of Butte county. The
Grand Lecturer and the Inspector of the District were with me on this visit.
On September 25th, in comp:i.ny with a number of brethren of Live Oalc ·
Lodge, I visited Arcturu.9 Lodge, No. 180, at Petaluma.. The Inspector had
made this the occasion for a District meeting, and there was a large attend·
ance from the various Lodges. The third degree was conferred on two candi·
dates, the Worshipful Master and officers of the Lodge doing the work in one
case and the Inspector of the District and members of Live Oak Lodge in the
other. In both cases the work was performed in a perfect and impressive
manner.
. At each and all of these meetings I have invariably been received in the
most fraternal spirit by the brethren, and the many courtesies extended me
by the officers and members of the various Lodges are remPmbered with
much pleas"Q.re, and I feel justified in saying that much good will result therefrom. A sumptuous repast concluded ea.ch meeting, and an hour or more of
social intercours!l wa.s profitably passed with the brethren, and in every instance save one it was my pleasure to congratulate them on the absence of
wine at the.banquet table. Temperance is one of our cardinal virtues, and
every Mason should practice it at all times, and more especially in the Lodgeroom or its environments. I have endeavored to impress this upon the minds
of my brethren, aud hope that the advice I have given may result in good.
On September 22d, I paid a fraternal visit to our venerable Past Grand
Master, JOHN .AJiHBY Turr, at Madison, Yolo county. Bro. T UTT ie now in
his eighty-second year. He was our second Grand Master, and is now one
of the few living representatives who participated in the organization of this
Grand Lodge. He is comfortably situated, and occupies most of his time in
reading. He informed me that the ca.res of this world sat lightly upon him
and that his wants are fully supplied, for which he expressed his gratitude to
thia Grand Lodge, I would recommend that "the appropriation for our venerable brother be continued.
The affairs of our Home for widows and orphans have not, I regret to say,
progressed with that .rapidity I could have wished ; but progress has been

made, the details of which will be submitted for your consideration by the
President of the Board.
To the various Grand Officers who have been called upon from time to time to
assist me in the discharge of my duties, and who have so promptly responded
to the call, I tender my grateful acknowledgments. Especial thanks are due
from me, and are cheerfully tendered to our Very Worshipful Grand Secretary, whose advice, so often sought, and so freely given, has been of great
assistance to me, and has materially lightened the responsibilities placed upon
me. His courtesies will always be kindly remembered. I am deeply indebted
to the Worshipful Grand Lecturer for the never ceasing attention to the impor•
tant duties of his office.
It is due to the Southern Pacific Company and its officers in authority that ·
recognition and record · should be made of the voluntary assistance which has
been rendered me in the discharge of charitable Masonic duties. In every
case where transportation in this State has been asked for distressed and
worthy persons, entitled to Masonic care and assistance, it has been cheerfully furnished without charge; and for these repeated ancl continued favors
the Southern Pacific Company is entitled to this mention, and to the thanks
of this Grand Body.
Brethren, I return to you my thanks for the high honor you have con·
ferred upon me, and assure you that the remembr!!.nce of your favors will
ever remain fresh in my memory. May that God in whom we place our trust,
guide us in the future as in the past, and may the principles which we profess be the rule of our action in future life, thus preparing us for admission
into that Celestial Lodge, where we shall fore\fer be free from labor and dwell
'
in harmony throughout the endlesa ages of eternity.

By reference to pages 542 and 556 of the Proceedings of last year, it will be seen
that on the twenty-sixth day of June, 1893, the Grand Master arrested the charter
of St. Mark's Lodge, No. 85, and the Grand Secretary was directed to take the usual
measures for closing up its affairs. In accordance with that direction Bro. JuLTo
AMBROSE GESSLER, Past Master of Drytown Lodge, No. 174, was appointed to act
as aR"ent of the Grand Lodge in the settlement of its affairs; and it is pleasing to
note that all the business connected therewith has been transacted in a manner
most praiseworthy and satisfactory. 'l'he final settlement shows a balance due
to the Grand Lodge, after payment of all the liabilities of the Lodge, of $36.85,
which amount hae been received and will be found accounted for in the financial
portion of this report which follows. 1So the affairs of that extinct 'Lodj!'e may
be considered as finally ·settlej. The correspondence and accounts relative to this
settlement are herewith submitted.
The numbers of the chartered Lodges which are and have been borne upon our
register, have reached to three hundred and twenty-two. Of these thirty-five have
voluntarily surrendered their charters; seven have become extinct by the rev90ation of those instruments; two, established in Oregon, assisted in the formation
of and became subordinate to the Grand Lodge of that State; eight, instituted
in Nevada, transferred their allegiance to the Grand Lodge there established by
themselves ; three withdrew to form the Grand Lodge of Arizona ; and eighteen
have consolidated into nine : making in all sixty-four vacancies upon our roll.
Thus there are now in existence within this juriodiction two hundred and fiftyeight chartered Lodges, which, with the three acting under dispensation, make a
total number of two hundred and sixty-one, with a membership of seventeen thousand four hundred and thirty-one, being a net j!'ain for the year of three Lodges
and three hundred and ninety-one members.
At the last Annual Communication, Grand Master ORME recommended that
the charter of Fall River lodge, No. 270, be revoked. The Committee on Charters, to whom that portion of the Gr1md Master's Address was referred, reported as
follows:In the matter of Fall River T,odge, No. 270, located at Glenburn, in the county
of Shasta, your committee ask that the recommendation oi the Grand Master be
not concurred in, but that their charter remain in force until the first day of June,
1895, by which time the brethren of Fall River Lodge promise that their Lodge
shall be in good working order.
No returns for the year ending July 31st, 1895, have been received from that
Lodge, nor has its Grand Lodj!'e dues been paid. The following letter from its
Secretary, received at this office on the twenty-sixth. day of August last, is submitted:Goorge Johnson, (Jioand Secretary :

· 1JEAR tlrn AND BROTHER.-! beg leave to inform you that it is not within my
power to send the dues of this Lodge to the Grand Lodge. I have done all I can
do to obtain the money, but have failed. We have not held a meeting for over a
year and a half ; in fact therA are not enough members, that will attend, to hold
a meeting. I think it is the sense of the Lodge to surrender its charter.
Fraternally yours,
WILLIAM C. SILVESTER, Secretmry.

respective Lodges-all which have been placed in the hands of the Chairman of the
Committee on Grievances-are as follows: from-

to redo~ those dues : two, being from J.odges Nos: 262 and 266, proposed to increase

Notice of the approval of the Grand Master has been given to the Lodges, their
action in all these cases having apparently been in consonance with the la.w upon
that subject. But information in regard to the last named fact has, in many
instances, been obtained only after repeated letters from the undersigned, which
would have been trnnecessary had the Secretaries, in the first instance, properly pre·
sented the application for approval. The law requires that an amendment shall be
proposed at a stated meeting of a Lodge; shall, at a subsequent stated meeting, be
adopted by a vote of at least two-thirds of the members then present; and shall then
be transmitted to the Grand Master for hie approval. It le probably true, that in
most, perhaps in all, cases the nction of the Lodge ha.q been exactly in accordance
with the law; bot the Secretary, in many instances, simply sends information, in
brief, that a certain amendment has been adopted, without stating, in terms, as he
should, for the proper information of the Grand Master, that it has been 8.llopted in
the manner which the law prescribes. That fdct, then, has to be ascertained by an
otherwise unnecessary further correspondence between the undersigned and the
8eoretary; and the snbject is presented here in the hope that some of the Becretanes
will note this published suggestion.
Proposed amendments to the by-laws, relative to the reduction of duee of
members, from Lodges Nos. 81, 161, 2U and 264, were disapproved by the Grand
Master for the reason that the rate of dues proposed was thought to be too low for
the Lodges to maintain a healthy and useful exiRtence.
The approval or disapproval of the Grand MRSterobeing but temporary, the
foregoing amendmAnts, as required by our lawS, have been placed in the hands of
the Chairma11 of the Committee on By.Laws of Lodges, and will be submitted to
the Grand Lodge for final action, as havA the books of by-laws of the three Lodges
now working under dispensation.

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :To the M. '. W. ·. Grand Lodge of California:In conformity with usage, I hereby present to this Grand Lodge & report
of my movements, observations and work during the past year, together with
certain recommendations for the consideration of this Grand Body, looking to
the improvement of Lodges at present difficult of access, and to the promotion
of their proficiency in the work of the ritual.
My visits have been as numerous as possible, and principally to Lodges
and districts in outlying portions of the -State, their condition requiring more
attention than those in the immediate vicinity of San Francisco. As far as
possible, I have encouraged the plan of holding Lodges of Instruction rather
than having a degree conferred, feeling that the limited time would be thus
spent more profitably to the Lodge officers. The fact that the brethren h~ve
in all cases shown a willing disposition to study and adopt, as far as they were
able, the authorized work of the ritual, their eagerness to obtain the correct
work; and their loyalty to the Grand Lodge, are features worthy of the highest
commendation.
The company of the M. '. W. •. Grand Master on most of my visits has
served to create a lively interest among the brethren, and his words of encouragement and advice have borne an abundance of fruit.
VISITATIONS.
In addition to the following record of visits I have devoted much time to
the Inspectors of several districts who have visited the city, as well as to
individual officers of various Lodges.
I have been ably supported by Inspectors W.R. EVANS and B. F. JELLISON,
of the Twenty-fifth and Twenty-sixth Districts, respectively; also by Bro.
JOHN A. BECKWITH, Worshipful Master of Live Oak Lodge, No. 61, and
others. From our combined efforts I feel that some progress has resulted.

The foregoing will show that while time would not admit of my visiting all
the Lodges, or even all the Masonic Districts of the State, yet all sections of
the State have been reached, to the extent of visits to one or more Lodges in
twenty-three of the thirty-eight districts of the State. The disadvantages of

54

Procee<lings of the

[Oct. 8,

the district.ti remotely situated a.re many. I am sorry to say that a very few
of the District Inspectors are not as proficient in the work as they should he,
nor as they would be if they were given an opportunity to acquire it from a
competent source. It is, therefore, not surprising if the Lodges a.re not able
to render the work as it ought to be rendered. I have visited few Lodges
where some feature did not present itself that I had never heard of before, and
I must attribute that fact to the necessity of utilizing brethren who have taken
the degrees in various sections of the East, and who have perhaps occupied
chairs in the Eastern Lodges, and these brethren have unconsciously introduced phraseology and floor movements entirely foreign to what the Grand
Lodge prescribes. Now, assuming that it is the object of this Grand Lodge to
have our beautiful ritual worked with uniformity and not allow the work of
the various other Grand Jurisdictions to stamp out its individuality, and,
further, that ultimate economy is a desirable feature, I submit the following
plan of action : Pay a sala.ry amounting to enough to justify a Grand Lecturer devoting his
entire time to the work, which would give him ou an average, say ten days to
each district (some districts will require more, some leBB), but make it his duty
to visit every district and stay until the Inspector is perfect and give the
officers of the Lodges, who are accessible, as much general instruction as
poesible. I would furthermore recommend that each Inspector select the
Master or some Past Master of each Lodge, who will perfect himself in the
entire work and appoint him an autli.ority on the work in that particular
Lodge, for the convenient reference of its officers, subject, of course, to the
correction of said Inspector. These Past Masters could sit with the Grand
Lecturer and Inspector during the former's visit to the district.
I believe that with this system in effect for a period of two years, more will
be accomplished than the present plan will yield in ten. I might, with
profit to the Craft, have spent weeks where I was only able to spend days. If
the work is once firmly planted in each district it is likely the present system
can a.gain be resumed. It is apparent that this Grand Jurisdiction has been
growing more rapidly than some of us realize, and while the present plan may
have been ample for the needs of several years ago, it certainly is ina.4eqnate
.
now, particularly considering the tremendous area of the State.
The proposed plan wonld place the work of the office on a more busmeSBlike basis and make the teaching of the work more a matter of duty than of
the Grand Lecturer's individual convenience. The matter of limiting the
Grand Lecturer's expenses, it seems to me, is a mistake. If he has been diligent and has expended his limit, he is then constrained to cease work rather
than pay his own expenses ; hence some work might be left undone which
otherwise wonld have been performed. If, on the other hand, the work is not
pushed with energy and little traveling is done, then the limiting of expenses
is a nseleSB precaution. In other words, the limit of work should not be
circumscribed by a limited amount for actual and reasonable t ra.veling expenses.
This suggestion is not the result of the authorized amount for the pa.st year
being too small, because the limit was not nearly consumed ; but my expenses
were less than the Grand Lodge can reasonably expect those of my successor
to be.

_\"bile on the subject of expenses, a number of instances ·have come to my
notice where Inspectors have failed to visit certain Lodges because they have
not been asked to, and the invitation is apparently withheld on account of the
t.odge's inability to pay the Inspector's expenses, even for one visit a year,
In two instances I found Inspectors who would not accept expense money
proffered by some Lodges, because other Lodges in the district had not offered
to pay, or had not paid. If an Inspector's purse is long enough to stand it
without curtailing his usefnlneSB, presumably no one can object; but, the
Inspector being willing to contribute his time and talent, it would seem that
an occasional week's boa.rd and actual necessary outlay of cash is not an
unreasonable return for his services, and surely most of the Lodges can stand
a solid week of instruction at lea.st once a year. General Regulation No. 15
covers the case and permit! the Inspector to visi£ a Lodge at the Lodge's ·
expense whenever he deems it neceSBa.ry in the faithful discharge of his duties
but the Inspector hesitates, from a sense of delicacy, to force an expense upo~
the Lodge, and he cannot always afford to make a trip at his own expense,
A Lodge should not be allowed to offer economy as an excuse for permitting
the .work to become warped into distortion, and I recommend that each Lodge,
durmg the coming year, extend an invitation to its Inspector to pay it a visit
at a time mutually convenient, for the purpose of instruction; that the visit
be as protracted as the circumstances require, and that he also be asked to
present his bill to the Lodge for actu~ expense incurred, and that it be acted
upon just as the Lodge would dispose of a bill for rent or fuel.
In conclusion, let me express my warm appreciation of the uniform courtesy
and expreBBion of confidence vouchsafed by all the brethren whom I have met
and their ready disposition to render assistance in my efforts to carry out th~
work imposed upon the office of Grand Lecturer. The year has been one of
infinite plea.sure and great profit to me as a. result of personal contact with so
many genial and enthusiastic Masons.
Respectfully submitted.

'

HARRY CHARLES BUSH,
Grand Lt.aurer,

To the M. •• W'. •• JAMES BAUNTY STEVl!.NS, ·
Grand Master of MasonR of CaJ,ifernia:-

The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home herewith
submits its fourth annual report, embracing its transactions during the past Masonic year.
We highly appreciate the fraternal courtesy shown to us by yourself and the
members of this Grand Lodge, bv your patient forbearance with the delays that
have been caused by the unforeseen difficulties and perplexities which have heretofore beset us in our efforts to carry to a successful completion the great trust
which you committed to our charge. Permit us to assure you that there are no
other members of this Grand Lodge who are more anxious or willing to expedite
this work than the members of the .Board of Tl'Ulltees.
We are happy to announce that the obstacles which have heretofore impeded
the progress of our work have been overcome, and that we are now prepared to
carry forward the work of improving the grounds and of constructing buildings as
rapidly as the necessary funds are provided to pay for the expenditures, as the
expense bills fall due.
The question of an available water supply, which had not been decided at the
time of our last annual report, has now been successfully solved. We have
secured, from the owner of lands adjacent to our premis~s at Decoto, the perpetual
right to the waters of certain springs which are situated at a sutlicient altitude to
carry the water, by gravity, to the highest portions of the buildini:is which are to
be constructed. The supply, as determined by W. R. ECKART, C. E ., whoije
observations and conclusions are embodied•. in bis written report, now on file
in the office of the Grand Secretary, will be amply sufficient for all the domestic
requirementR of the Home, and also to supply a ~torage reservoir, to be reserved
for emergencies and to protect the buildings from destruction by fire. When this
water system is completed and paid for, the institution will be relieved of any
further expense for the purchase of daily water 11upply or for artificial power for
pumpin11.
After having completed the negotiations for an adequate supply of water, the
Board of Truste•s reconsidered their action relative to the sale of the Decoto
propertv, as reported by us to the Grand Lodge at its last session, and, without a
dissenting Yoice, voted to establish and maintain the Home on the lands and
premises which we now own at Decato. At the same meetinir the Board, by vote,
decided to proceed at once with.such prelimmary improvements on the property
aB are necessary to construct the wa;ter system and to prepare the grounds for
laying the foundation of the building_
We also contemplate the immediate construction of a driveway from the county
road to the proposed site, and the planting of fruit and ornamental trees. In this
· connection we are pleased to announce that the brethren of .Alameda Lodge, No.
167, located at Centreville, within whose jurisdiction the Home is located, have
generously agreed to plant ten acres of our land to fruit trees, and to cultivate the
same and care for the trees for an entire year, and then to tum the orchard over to
the Board of Trustees free from all expense to the Board.
Being thus equipped and ready for the actual work of constructing the Home,
we again appeal to the charitable impulses of all Masons and all Lodges throughout
the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California, for additional contributions of
funds in such generous amounts as shall insure the speedy completion of the Home,
and exemplify the open handed hospital'ty and broad charity which have always
been characteristic of the people of Cali ornia.

Grand L0<J,ge of California.

Relative to the $845, which was referred to in our last annual report as due
from W. F . .PllRRY, we beg to state that we have been unable to oollect the
amount in money, but, throU,lth the efforts of our attorney, Bro. C. L. PATTON,
who served without compensation, the Board of Trustees effected a settlement of
the claim by securing the assignment of a trust deed to certain lands in Lassen
county, which lands are to be sold under the conditions of the trust, and the proceec!s, which are estimated to be ample for the purpose, to ~ applied to the payment of the claim.
It is with sadness that we refer to another visitation to the membership of this
Eoard by the reaper Death: Bro. .A.r.BllRT HANSl!.N departec\ this life on the
twenty-ninth day of April, 1895. The vacancy thus caused in the Hoard was filled
by the appointment of FRANK MARION ANGllLLOTTI, Past Master of Marin
Lodge, No. 19L
We also regret that another vacancy was caused by the resignation of Bro.
GUSTAVUS LANGFORD SPEAR, who was unable longer to dischaTge his duty as a
member of the Board on account of ill health." This 'vacancy was filled by the
appointment of Bro. CHARLllS LEWIS PATrON, Past Master of CaJ,ifornia Lodge,
No. I.
In addition to the foregoing statements, we herewith submit the reports of
our Treasurer and Secretary, showing receipts and disbursements during the
current year, also the amount of available cash which we have on band for immediate use. In addition to the cash on hand we have unpaid subscriptions amounting to $20,406.64, which amounts should be paid as rapidly as practicable, for all
of these sums, and much more, will be needed before the work of construction and
equipment can be completed.
The business depression and financial stringency which have prevailed for the
last two years, to the detriment of our subscription list, are now happily passing
away, and with returning prosperity we look confidently forward, believill,lt that
the brethren and Lodges throughout this Grand Jurisdiction will see to it that the
necessary work of this noble charity is not delayed for lack of adequate funds for
its completion and equipment.
Fraternally submitted.

In writing the report your committee have endeavored to carry out their idea

ALABAMA.

The Grand Lodge of Alabama held its seventy.fourth Annual Communication
in the city of Montgomery, December 4, 1894,-the M . '. W. ·.FRANCIS L. PE'l'I'US,
Grand Master; R. ·. W. ·. H. CL.&Y ARMSTRONG, Grand Secretary. Two hundred
an:I ninety Lodges were represented. There were present four Past Grand Masters, two Past Grand Wardens, and the Representatives of fourteen sister Grand
Jurisdictions.
•
The Grand J.odge was opened in Ample Form, with pr&ytJ by the reverend
Grand Chaplain.
In hie Address, the Grand Master gave thanks to the Great Ruler for abundant
harvests and a decided improvement in ihe general condition and prospects of the

1895.]

Grand Lodge of California. ·

75

people of Alabama. Renewed interest, he said, was manifest in Masonic affairs,
and the year had been one of prosperity. He pByB the following compliment to
the MBBone of Alabama :-

amendment of the Constitution, to say that the fact that a person follows a certain
oocupation is of itself conclusive evidence tha.t he lacks the aualificatione of a
good reputation.
·

One thing which may not properly have a place in this Ad?ress, BI!d which yet
ie so striking that I cannot forbear making "?ention of _it as illu~tre;tml!'. the firm
foundation of our Order, and the Jove which its members bear to it, is this : . Du~­
ing the past two years, poReibly the tierceet political struggle ever known m this
State has been carried on amongst our people. So heated has this struggle been,
and so high have men's passions run, that friendships of a lifetime· have been
broken up. The relations between churches and pastors have been ~e.stroyed,_and .
· even family circles have been broken up by the fierce heat of political pase10~ ;
ret through it all no note of discord bas entered any Masonic Lodge. No Masonic
Lodge in Alabama bas been affected by this fierce struggle, and this should be a
monument to the Masonic Lodges of Alabama.
They have met in the times of the greatest trial within their Lodges BB friends
and as brethren, and nothing outside the doors of the Lodge room has affected
this beautiful Masonic feeling. It hBB created within my breBBt a sentiment of
added reverence and love for the Craft, and I feel sure that a house builded on ~o
firm a foundation, and able to withstand the shocks of the past two years, will
never be shaken. In the past year,-too, we have been greatly blessed in the.~ t~e
officers and members of this Grand Lodge have been all spared to meet aga1.n m
this assembly. The destroying an~el has pBBeed us by and allowed ua agam to
meet together to consult and advise with each other ae to the beet interests of
Masonry in Alabama.

The Report on Correspondence is presented by Bro. PALMER J. PILLANS (veteran). He gives a review of the doings of fifty-six Grand Masonic Bodies-full of
practical information and wise comment. In noticing Arkansas, be quotes Bro.
SAM H. DAVIDSON, and endorses his opinions in opposition to a Cipher Ritual in
its many forms, and thinks the Mason or Lodge using the pesky thing should be
"stood up;" but Bro. PILLANS says we are constantly informed "that we are old
fogy, behind the age, and that Masonry is a progressive science," etc. Under the
awful threat of "you're another," we side with the protestants DAVIDSON and
l'ILLANS. The loose methods adopted in the dissemination of the cipher is the
:first objection ; the second and greatest is the much more careless methods of the
individual recipient. We have heard of their being worn out from carrying in the
side pocket, and then the copies that are made for convenience-oh, Lord I
Under California, Bro. PJLLANB notices the illnee~ of Grand Master GRITMAN.
He quotes, in full, Bro. BELOHER'B report on the communication·of Grand Master
ARNOLD, of Pennsylvania, announcing hie withdrawal of the Representative of the
Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania near the Grand Lodge of California; comment•
favorably upon the acts of our Boards of Relief. He notes the pro1?r~ee in the
matter of the Home, and says " this looks well, and with our brethren of California, in matters of charity, there is no Ruch word known to.them as fail."
In his notice of Connecticut, he closes with these words, writing of Bro. J OBEPH
R. WHEELER: ' 1 We regretfully leave him (most probably we will meet no more
here). Alas I how true your words, Bro. PlLLANS, 'we shall meet Bro. WHEELER
no more here.' "
Under Illinois, Bro. l'JLLANS indulges in a few words which strike the average
mind as peculiarly truthful and pertinent, and the application may be made to the
doings of most any of o'ur Grand Bodies. We quote:-

Could the Masone of Alabama have received a greater compliment! The
Grand Master "set his face firmly ." against the ltl'Bnting of dispensations to confer
degrees out of time. A number of interesting decisions were rendered, but being
controlled by the local law are not important in other jurisdictions. We quote the
following, however, BB an exception, as founded on good law under any code claiming to be Masonic:I received a letter in which it was stated that an applicant for affiliati!'n had
been blackballed, and BB the letter stated, for no good cause, and it was stated
that the members of the Lodge were of opinion that they knew who bad <:BBt the
black ball, and desired to know whether or not tht>y could not proceed agamst the
member:
I replied : The ballot in a -Masonic Lodge ie strictly a secret ballot. No member has a right to inCJ.uire or to be informed how any other member h!!-8 voted on
any application for mitiation or affiliation ; in fact it is not proper for a memb~r
himself casting a blackball to state in open Lodge that he has done so, or his
reasons for so doing. No man, however pure, or good, or desirable as a member,
bas a right to become a member of a Masonic Lodge without the unanimous consent of every member present when his application comes up, freely expressed. by
the secret result of the ballot. It is needless to say that your Lodge has no nght
to inquire who cast a black ball and why it was cast.
And here is another good common sense decision by the Committee on Jurispmdence, to whom the subject had been referred:We are a11ked if the fact that a man is engaged in the business of selling
spirituous, vinous or malt liquors is of itself a ~ound for rejecting the applicant.
There was a ruling of this Grand Body in 1855 to that effect, but in 1866 it was de.cirled that as the business of retailing ardent spirits was licensed by the State,
that it wBB not in itself inconsistent with Masonry to follow such a business. We
do not think that it is within the power of this Grand Lodge to impose any other
qualifications upon the candidate for degrees than those imposed by Section 7,
Article VI, of the Constitution. By that section a man is required to be a man,
free-born, of the age of twenty-one years or upwards, of good reputation !'-nd of
suffioient natural intellectual endowment, and with means of honest subsistence
and free from certain corporeal deformity. It is for each member of a Lodge to
satisfy his conscience as to whether a candidate possesses these qualifications, and
we do not think that it is within the power of this Grand Lodge, without an

. The Jurisprudence Committee _commend him, the Grand Master, for hie position; but why commendation should have been awarded him for doi.ng ezactly a.a he
ia required tt• do is not <J,Uite clear to us, for fools are not wanted in the Fraternity,
but are expressly prohibited.

from our Dean in Masonry, Bro. DRUMMOND. The subject of the remarks was
the late anti-saloon Masonic legislation in several jurisdictions. Bro. DRUMMOND
writes:That depends. When the use of anything becomes a public'curse/the general
weal demands that its Ul.'e be prohibited, although there may be many who do not
abuse it; human laws must have reference to the mas•, even if they limit the
rights of the few. So, if evil practices exist among Masone to such tan extent as
to di~race Masonry, it is no innovation to enact laws to prohibit those practices.
It is mherent in Freemasonry to preserve itself, and the exercise of this power,
when necessary, is no innovation, but rather the performance of a duty enjoined
by its fundamental principles.
To which Bro. PILLANS responds :To which we agree, but are not ready to concede that such conditions ~xist.

Address. After an expression of gratitude to the Heavenly Father for preservation, he uported the death of Past Grand Lecturer Bro. D. B. WARREN, and paid
a warm and earnest tribute to his memory.
The Grand Master reported his official acts, among which many decisions of
local importance only were rendered, and some peculiar methods developed.
Some quaint questions and answers were reported, from which we quote:Queation. A member of our Lodge skipped a bail bond, ran ofi and went to
Texas, and while there attempted to draw money from 11 bank on a forged check,
under an assumed name. Can we prefer charges against him here in our Lodge
where he is a member, or will we have to prefer charges in.some Lodge in Texas?
Answer. You should prefer charges in the Lodge where be is a member, and
expel him before the matkr .gets cold. Then you can advertise him in T exas if
you choose to do so.

I have been cordially invited to visit several Lodges and assist in laying corner

Grand Lecturer, visited a itood many Lodges. Bro OATHOUT is a good worker
and makes a lasting impression wherever he goes-a itenial companion to travel
with. Lodges treated us kindly and gave us plenty to eat, which is ..1ways acce_11table to me. I have assisted in conferring many degrees during the ]ear. The
brethren of all the Lodges I have visited have treated me with fove an re9pect.,

cipher out any plan except to adopt the amendment to the Constitution that is
now before the Grand Lodge or vote down the mileage and per diem, and I do
h.ope and pray that the amendment will be adopted by this Grand L od_ge. While
some of our hrethren may think that there has been money wasted m building

The Lodge of Instruction exemplified the third degree before the Grand Lodge,
omittin1t the lecture on account of press of business.
The Report on Correspcndence is presented by Bro. LEWIS R. J AOKSON, Grand
Chaplain and Chairman of committee. The report is a well written, "crispy"
review of tbe doings of American and Foreign Grand Lodges the style is terse
and vigorous, without surplusage or filling.
Our proceedings are favorably commented on; the Rep0rt of Bro. JAMES W.
.ANDERSON on Correspondence, and the Oration of Bro. EUGENE DEUPREY receiving special praise. He considers the Grand Lodge just in refusing the use of
Lodge funds for social purposes. He endorses the Georgia decision that only a
Master of a chartered Lodges become a Past Master upon his retiring from office.
He is enthr..siastic in his admiration of the brethren of Kentucky for their successful establishment and support of their Home for the widows and cbildren of
their deceased brethren.
Under Montana he bolds that when a Mason in good standing, clear of dues
and charges, asks to become a member, and the Lodge by ballot elects him, and
thus grants his request, the transaction is complete. His obligation binds him to
support the by-laws.
Like many other questions which will arise, Bro. JAOKSON, the necessity for
signing the by-laws depends upon the law of the Grand Lodge under which you
acquired or hold membership. For instance, the law of California, uniform code
of by-laws, Sec. 3 of Art. 4, declares that "every person raised to the degree of
'Master Mason in, or elected a member of this Lodge, shall sign the by-laws
thereof."
Under New Jersey be makes affectionate reference to the death of Bro.
VEHSLAGE, the beloved Chairman of Correspondence for that jurisdiction.

Grand J,odge. Bro. SINGLE:TON adds :.
A farmer, who had hired a new boy to wait on his reapers in the field, gave
him a bucket of cider and told him to put it in the spring to keep cool. When the
cider wae wanted he told th~ boy to bring it. The hoy said "I have put it in the
spring." "Yes, I told you to do so, but bring it along." "But1" said the boy," I
but don't you
. have poured it in the spring." "You did ! Well, that's all rignt,
do it again."
Now, the Grand Master obeyed his prerogative. The c,ommittee said it was
not right and so future Grand Masters of South Dakota. will govern themselves
accordingly.

Deputy Grand Master, presiding, the R. ·. W.·. ANDREW M. WoLIBIN, Grand Secretary. Three hundred and ninety-eight Lodges were represented, out of three

16,235 Master Masons.

The Grand Lodge was opened with prayer by the Grand Chaplain. The Grand
Master opened his Annual Addre88 with the following tribute to the dead Grand
Master, JOHN s. DAVIDSON:
My Brethren: On Sunday afternoon, March 11, 1894, the ·wires brought tbe
sad news of the death of our beloved Grand Master. Thou11:h not wholly unexpected, for I knew of the fatal malady that cut short his brilliant career and deprived M&l!Onry of its brightest light, yet I could not realize that he who had

roared around it, was no longer at the helm. F or more than ten yea.I'!!, in common

There was a natural shrinking from so 1Ireat a burden and so 1"f9po11sible a position,
for to hold the reins of command over four hundred Lod~es and seventeen thousand Masons requires the best energies and the best brain of the best man in all
the State; while to assume charge of the Craft, just following such a Mason and

.ASBurances from all over the State that I would have the support of my brethren
were soon received, and, with the determination to do all that man could to sustain the honor and dignity of the high office so sadly and suddenly cast upon me,
and remembering that my lahors would be lightened by the charity of my brethren, and, more than all, recalling that the designs upon the trestle-board had

During the past year dispensations were issued for the formation of eleven new
Lodges.
From the following decision of Grand Master DAVIDSON it will be seen that
Cerneauism is without honor or profit in Georgia :A man who had heretofore received any of the degrees of Cerneau Masonry cannot be made a member of any subordinate Lodge of this State, unless he is healed
of this infirmity by proper petition to the Grand Lodge. (This decision being
based on the report of the Com mittee on Cerneauism, made to the Grand Lodge,
and found in Proceedings of 1889, p. 53.)
Seventy-two decisions are reported by the Acting Grand Master, t wenty-seven
having been rendered by Grand Master DAVIDSON pr10r to his death. The following, by the Acting Grand Master, is in the line of sound doctrine, and cannot too
often be "emphasized : "Ne~ther. the W orshipful Master nor any member has the right to q uestion the
ballot 1ll any way or comment on the result of the ballot. The Worshipful Master
must declare the result, and there the matter ends. He is not permitted to say
any more about it, or to in any way inquire by whom any ballot was cast, by hint,
comment or innuendo. It is the privilege of every Mason to cast his ballot in
secrecy. It is forever secret. It may perhaps seem unnecessary to have announced
this decision, but the matter of inquiry into the nature of a ballot has come before
me in so many different shapes that I have deemed it best to emphasize this
decision.

We have been painfully impressed with the cloud of gloom that has hung
during the year over all of the Grand Jurisdictions of .America, owing to the
general stagnation in business by reason of the financial depression, affecting business of every .character, but we have been more gloomiz. overshanowed with the
solemn reflection that we are soon to convene the Grand odge of Georgia without
JOHN S. D AVIDSON, Most Worshipful Grand Master. Darkness must for a time
ensue when the brightest luminary is withdrawn, the chill of a dark winter night
broods over m, and our proceedings of necessity pt1rtake of the natnre of our
surroundings. If we had only known that the last communication was his last
with us, bow different the greeting-how different th~arting. May his noble
spirit linger with us to encourage and to stimulate us. We would hear hi• cheerful
voice again from the Grand East reminding us that "sorrow endureth for a night;
joy coineth in the morning." No pen can describe our sorrow, no voice express our
loss, no mind conceive the shock to Masonry in this jurisdiction by the removal so
suddenly of our great chieftain and leader; but our faith assures us that Israel's
God will provide for and comfort us, in this our time of need.

The Grand Lodge of Idaho held its twenty-seventh .Annual Communication at
Boise City, September 11, 1894,-the M. ·• W. ·.JAMES A. PINNEY, Grand Master;
the R. '. W. ·. W. C. WroKERSHA.11, Grand Secretary. Twenty-one Lodges were
represented. Four Past Grand Masters were present with the Representatives of
twelve sister Grand Jurisdictions.
.An Emergent Communication of this Grand Lodge was held May 23, at Boise
City, for the purpose of laying the corner stone of a building to be known as the
"Idaho Soldier'• Home." Idaho Commandery, No.1, acted as escort to the Grand
Lodge. The ceremonies were imposing, and passed off with satisfaction to the
participants and the public.
In Annual Communication, September 12, the Grand Lodge was OPened in
Ample Form.
The Grand Master delivered his Annual Address. After ~n impressive
opening, in which he reminded the assembled brethren of their obligation to the
.Almighty Father for preservation and proteJtion during the past, he asked for
their co-operation in striving to maintain the exalted position enjoyed by their
Grand Lodge among the jurisdictions of the nation.
In sorrow the Grand Master reporte!l the death of Past Deputy Grand Master
CHARLES W. CABE and ten other brethren of this jurisdiction. He read from the
death roll the names of the departed brethren, and paid earnest and eloquent
tribute to their memories. He also reported the unusual number of eminent
brethren of sister jurisdictions who had passed away during the year, and extended, on behalf of the Grand Lodge, the sympathy of the brethren of Idaho to
the bereaved Masonic househlllds.

~HKREAB, In ~883 the M. ·. W. '. .Grand Lodge A. F. and A. M. of Idaho adopted
a series of resolutions on Mormomsm, based on the statement or assumption at
that time, "that the teachings of Mormonism were opposed to the law of the
land," and providing "that no person acknowledging allegiance to the so-called
Mormon Church, or Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, shall be admitted to any of the privileges of Masonry within the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of I<iaho ; " and
WHERll'-AS, Said Church has satisfactorily demonstrated to the civil authorities
of the government, both National and State, that the teachings of the so-called
Mormon Church, or Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, are not opposed
to the law of the land, but, on the contrary, that the members of such Church are
a law-abiding, loyal and moral class of people, attached to the principles of the
Constitution of the United States, and well disposed to the good order and happi·
ness of the same ; therefore be it
Reaolved, That said resolution of the Grand Lodge be and the same is hereby
~pe8:led .and set _aside; and members of said Church possessing the requisite qualifications otherwise be and they are hereby declared eligible for admission as members of the Masonic Order within this jurisdiction, and to all the privileges of
Masonry.

The Report on Correspondence is by Past Grand Master JOSEPH RoBBINS-a
most inte~esting paper, thoroughly treating the questions arising in our several
families of Free and Accepted Masons, from the standpnint of the ancient charges
and regulations, as set forth in harmony with the original plan of Masonry. Bro.
ROBBINS reviews forty-nine American Grand Lodges, with those of England and
South Austr,.lia. As to matters for discussion-food for thought-Bro. RoBBINB
seems to have HD abundant supply on hand. He writes:Besides the perennial questions which crop out over the field in every year, and
which claim attention because every year there is in part a new generation of masters coming on to be perplexed by them, several matters have claimed unusual
attention.
In commenting on the Masonic Congress and its msulta, he says :It is t~e of any body of men that what it does not do is quite as imfortant and
often quite as significant as what it does. This is peculiarly true o a Masonic
body; and when, in a body of Masons as large and as representative as the
Masonic Congress of 1893, doctrines are advanced or propositions submittted, possibly reflectin~ the action of Grand Lodges who affect to recognize no \imitat1ons
upon their sovereign will and no higher law than the law of pre"9Dt expediency, it
is reassuring to find the constraint of the ancient law so profoundly and generally
felt the.t it needs no other expression than non-action. This must be taken into
account before we admit the justice of the most frequent criticism of the Congress
-that it accomplished so little. It is yet too early to estimate ita results. It
would be strange, indeed, if it should contributa nothing towards a more inclusive
consensus of expression, when, after supplementing long years of discussion by
correspondence committees and others, in print. by a comparison of views at the
short range of oral debate, it is found that ita formulated conclusions are in harlDOllY with the original plan of Masonry.
The records of the year show the most prolific cause of serious friction between
Grand Lodges to be the want of uniformity in their regulations respecting rejectetl
candidates. The majority of Grand LodgAs forbid the making of a rejected candidate save in the Lodge which rejected him, without a waiver of the jurisdiction
to which he subjected himself when he put his petition in their hands. Other
Grand Lodges provide that after a stated period such jurisdiction shall cease, leaving any other Lodge within whose territory he has resided for the prescribed
length of time free to entertain his petition. This period is generally fixed at one
year from the time of rejection, and usually, perhaps in all instances, so far corresponds to the time during which the rejecting Lodge is itself forbidden to again
receive hi~ petition. A person rejected in a State where jurisdiction over rejected
candidates 1s perpetual, removing into another State where the regulations make
such jurisdiction only temporary, and being made a Mason there, complaint naturally follows from the Grand Lodge of his former home that the rights of its constituent Lodge have been disregarded. The reply naturally comes back that he
has fully complied with the requirements of the law in his new home, and that
therefore the Lodge there was the solll judge in the matter, and, having made him,
he is a lawful Mason, standing upon an equal footing with all other Masons.
Both Grand Lodges are right according to their own laws, and each claims to be
right according to the law of MW!onry. Both are equ•lly sovereign bodies, and
each with a show of truth accuses the other of attempting to give its own regulations extra-territorial force- the one by making a Mason of a man who has 00en

pronounced unfit by authority whose competency to decide the other does not and
cannot gainsay, the other by denying-if, as is probable, it does deny it-the
validity of bis making when it knows him to have been made by a Lodge whose
·Masomc acts must be given full faith end credit so long as the Masonic compe·
tency of the Grand Lodge of which it is a constituent part is recognized.
When relations between Grand Lodges become thus strained, each must sullenly bear what it feels to have been an outrage on the part of tbe other, which is
intolerable; or open rupture of fraternal relations and estrangement muet follow,
which is too intvlerable to be contemJ>lated as a permanent possibility; or comity
must suggest some modm vivendi by which peace and good will may be preserved.
To this object Mississippi, under the lead of Past Grand Master SPEED, has
addressed herself by the adoption of uniform rules, so called because designed to
bring about a uniform practice, if not among all Grand Lodges, at least among
such as may give their adhesion to them. The subject is one of such importance
that it should have the most careful and deliberate consideration before it is determined that je•lousy of their own sovereignty absolutely forbids concession on
either band.

Bro. MILi.ER indulges freely in criticism of the legislation of the several Grand
:Bodies, wherever he believes it necessary in vindication of the original groundwork
and plan of Masonry; and, although he pleads guilty to youth and inexperienoe,
he certainly wields his pencil with the skill and force of a veteran.
Under Arizona, Bro. MILLER demurs to the aSBertion of Grand Master ORHSBY
that ·"If the world had never had any religion other than the teachings of
Masonry it would be as well off as it is to-day if every one lived up to its prect'pts.
He says:Masonry, as now exemplified in the Lodges of the American Rite, notwithstanding the barely concealed slurs of loose speaking and inconsiderate votaries

Most of the ruling by the Grand Master is determined by the local law of

not be resorted to in subordinate Lodges.
And we think the same a safe rule to follow.
The Grand Master says, in reference to physical qualifications:I liave received several letters requesting dispensations to confer the degrees on
maimed candidates. I have simply cited the applicants to the provisions of the
Constitution as defined in Article VIII, Section 4, and said tp them that the Lodge
must be the judge of the qualifications of candidates, having that provision of the
Constitution before them. I am not an advocate of tbe " perfect youth " doctrine.
. I believe io the internal and not the external qualifications of a man to fit him for
Masonry, but at the same time I am not an advocate for committing our mysteries
to those who cannot teach, or be taught our means of recognition.
All right, Bro. STATON, we think the only safe rule is that the petitioner shall
be able to comply "lireraUy" with the requirements of the several degrees.

The Committee on J:urisprudence, W. LARUE THOMAS, Chairman, referring to
the Mississippi pro.p osition for a uniform regulation in certain matters, report as
follows:-

In regard to the circular received by this Grand Lodge (which is filed herewith,
and which we desire made a part of this report) we say : Kentucky has always,
in its Masonry, maintained the doctrine of territorial jurisdiction, and accorded to
other Grand Lodges, what it has reserved to itself, the right to pass upon the fitness of all candidates for initiation or membership. The child of Virginia, and
the mother Lodge of the west and south, this Grand Lodge has never claimed a
power to act outside its own jurisdiction. It will not aBBume to control the action
of Mississippi, nor will it allow its own action to be controlled by any other body
of Masons. Recognizing the fraternal feeling which prompted the Grand Lod~e
of MiBSissippi to issue the circular referred to, the Grand Lodge of Kentucky
respectfully declines to take any action thereon.

Our Grand Lodge Constitution does not allow the suspension or expulsion,
from th.£ righta of Masonry, of a member for non-pa:yment of dues. We assume
that a brother is expelled in Georgia only upon due trial, upon cha~es, the gist of
which is that he willfully fails to perform a Mruionic duty which he 1s fully able to
perform; if so, it is not so bad · as in some jurisdictions (like California), where
they suspend a brother without trial or even the filing of charges. If one brother
· kills another he cannot be suspended without due trial; it is only Masons who
are unable or unwilling to belong to a Lodge that are suspended from all Masonic
rights without trial.
·
It may be that we are too strongly imbued with the idea, "Once a Mason
always a Mason ; " but it does seem to us that, under any circumstances, eT;pulaWn.
for non-payment of dues belittles Masonry. We bold that the privilege of being a
Mason is a very high one, of which one should be deprived only for a very serious
offense; by deprivation of membership one loses Lodge rights and privilegee, as he
should if he declines to pay for them; but when we expel ont' for non-payment it
seems to us that the value we place upon being a Mason is measured by the few
dollars of his arrears. Or else the punishment is grossly disproportionate to the
offense."
.

The following action was had in regard to dual membership: R. ·. W. ••
CHARLES HARRIS presented the following report, which wa.e accepted, and the
amendment, as recommended, was unanimously adopted:The committee to whom was referred the proposed amendment to Part 5, Sec.
13, respectfully submit the following report and recommendation :Section 13, of Pa.r~ V~ as it now stands, restricts a brother from being a member of more than one LOOge.
The proposed amendment removes this restriction to the extent of giving him
the privilege of holding at the ea.me time membership in a foreign Lodge.
This amendment is intended particularly for the benefit of brethren, members
of Lodges in this State, whose business may take them to foreign countries to reside for a considerable length of time, and who, for their own advantage, and for·
the service they may render Freema•onry in those countries, may desire to become
members of Lodges in those countries, without being compelled by the law of this
Grand Lodge to first sever their membership from the home Lodge.
Your committee are in full accord with the spirit of the proposed amendment,
but would recommend its adoption in a form somewhat less ambiguous tb1Ln that
in which it was first offered--a form in which, while it will continue, as here·
tofore, to restrict a. brother from being a mem her of more than one Lodge in this
State, will oppose no barrier to bis holding membership at the same time in a
Lodge, if he may so desire, in a foreign couutry where he may reside.
We therefore recommend that Section 13 of Part V be amended by inserting
after the word "Lodge," in the second line, the words, "in tbie Commonwealth," so
that when amended the Section shall read as follows, viz :-

unanimous vote :WHEREAS, Certain unauthorized practices tend to corrupt the work and lectures
of this Grand Lod~, and deceive the Craft; and, WHEREAS, Certain printed books,

from the rights and privileges of ·Freemasonry, or to be otherwise punished, by

BROTHER OUOKSON'S RESPONSE.
MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER AND BRETHREN :-I thank you for the
honor you have again conferred upon me by again selecting me as one of the Grand
Chaplains of this Grand Lodge. I regret that my co-Chaplain, Brother HORTON,
is not permitted to be here this evening. He is a man of many engagements and
of much wor)i:, and found it inconvenient to be here to-night, and so desired me to

l

Grand Lodge of OalifornW..

131

apologize for his absence. For myself, there are few privileges which I enjoy more
deeply or more sincerely than my affiliation with Masonry. Our brotherhood is
too large for any sect or for any creed ; and, at the risk of differing somewhat from
so eminent an authority on theological and Masonic symbolism as the newly.
appointed Deputy Grand Master, I venture to say that the triangle was a triangle
long before the Trinity was thought of ; and, if I had the faintest notion that the
triangle I wore this afternoon was the symbol of the Trinity, with all due respect,
I should have handed it back a~ain to the· Deputy Grand Master.
We are here as a united brotherhood. We stand upon our merits as men, and
not upon any connection, or supposed connection, with this church, that, or the
other. I trust that our sympathies are broad enough to include all the churches,
and to maintain loyal and brotherly fellowship with the ministers of all denominations.
For my own part, I enjoy the fellowship, I think, more deeply and more widely
as I grow older, of the men who differ from me. It is the easiest thing in the
world to be on the best of terms with men who agree with you in every particular.
There is very little merit in that. But to be able to listen patiently and respectfully to men who think differently from you, to pay respect to their differences,
and to hold their right of private judgment in due and becoming reverence, is a
virtue which is none too co1Umon. I wish it were commoner than it is at the present
day.
A feeling of brotherhood is the one sole bond offellowship'which binds together
Masons in all parts of the civilized world; and, for my own part, I never could
quite understand the attitude of any Christian church in its opposition to Masonry ;
for it seems to me that Masonry, .rightly understood, comprehends and embraces
that which is common to all the churches, and that which is best in Christianity;
and I think that the feeling which prompts the Catholic Church to be hostile to
our brotherhood must rather be a feeling of envy, a feeling that we are perhaps a
little too strong and a little too close in our fellowship, that we are a formidable
body as compared with the Roman Catholic Church, and that our brotherhood is
as large and as powerful, when it cares to exert itself, as any existi1,1g affiliation in the
world ; and it is not of much use for the church to try to deal with us in any spirit
of hostility. It may put us under its ban; it may curse us, if it chooses; but that
kind of business is innocent enough in these days, fortunately. It may do what it
chooses ; but we have bef!n here a little too long, we are too ancient, too deeply
rooted, too firmly fixed in human life, to be i'reatly disturbed by the anathemas of
any,priest or of any church. And so the bitterness, the ill-feeling, which sometimes
comes to the surface in the church, reminds me very much of the anger-the
fruitless anger-displayed once by a Somersetshire far111er. He tried desperately
hard, but to no purpose, to tear up an oak sapling by the roots. He pulled at it,
and puffed and blowed for a long time, but could not move it. At last in futile
petty anger, he said, "Domn the pigs that didn't yut thee when thou wert an
aeorn I"
Now, it seems to me that the hostility towards Masonry, in its 'futility, partakes very much of the anger of the Somersetshire farmer. We are not moved by
hard words ; we are not to be disturbed by misunderstandings and misrepreSAntations. Our work is clear and definite, and distinct enough, anJ. we shall
probably go on without consulting the churches, and without consulting anybody
outside of our own Order. It is our work, individually and collectively, to maintain in our several capacities the great practical virtues of Freemasonry ; and as I
read my morning papers it seems to me that there never was atime when Masonry
should stand more firmly for conduct and character than at the present day. If
we do no not stand for that, if our essential principles of Truth and Justice and
Mercy and Brotherly Kindness be not the essential features of our federation,
then I know not for what we can stand before the world; and in all our great
cities of America there is abundant need for the patriotic citizen, trained in the
school of Freemasonry.
·
There is abundant mason for men who are both able and willing to serve the
State, and to serve the State willingly, to ve of their strength and their time,
and of their means, to the maintenance o pure government, with a view to securing in all our cities, and in our States, a government that governs, for that, it
seems to me, is what we most of all need in these times. When I think of the
various institutions which are broullht into existence to enforce the laws of this
country, those institutions seem to me to be a permanent reflection either upon the
incapacity or the lack of character of the government itself. When we have our
watch a111d ward societies, our municipal leagues, and what not, these societies are •
