Then I confess I heard, with a good deal of satisfaction, the statement of the
Grand Master that some effort was to be made to associate practical charity with
Freemasonry. Our .goo~ fello~shiJ? is, of course, very satisfactory and very

there should he eomethmg more permanent, eomethmg more dumble something
more lasting than thai : and I trust that the large fund which has akeady been
~u~cri~ed ~or ch~ritable P?rpoeee will eventual~y lead to the establishment of some
1Dstitution ID which the children, the orphan children of Masone, or aged or infirm
Masons, may receive some lasting and permanent benefit at our bands.
It always seemed to me that one of the chief attractions of Freemasonry in
England was the. magnificent way in which Masonic charities were supported there.
I have s11t at a dmner on St. John's Day in Bradford, and have seen $5 ()()()taken
from t~e qinner table for the maintenance of ~asonic charities, in the way of
Masomc gifts. No one !'BB pledged to any specific sum, but we all gave, according
to our means, to the ma1Dtenance of the Orphan School for Boys, and for the

Then there was one other feature in connection with Masonry which touched
me more tenderly and deeply than almost anything else. I well remember the
toast at all our dinners in England, "To aged and sick and infirm Ma11ons all over

That w~ o!1e of the s~ndard sentiments i!1 all our meet!ngs, al!d. that is one thing

are absolutely dropped when we enter the Masonic Temple, and our hearts ~

me, may be materially develope<l without interfering with our l!OOd-fellowsbip or
'
with the pleasure of these gatherings.
However, I must not drop into preaching. I came here to-night in defiance oJ
authorities which I am bound to respect, and came from a sickness from which I
am just recovering. When I came from home I snid that I did not feel well

MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER :-This is a fraud. I have been waiting
to hear brother WELCH and Brother WELLS, and pick up ideas from them, and,
having the last word, to scratch their backs with my toe nail as bard as I could.
Instead of that, you have called me up_at this inopportune time, so that now I
have got to catch it instead of them. Under the circumstances, I feel very much
as a little girl in Boston did some years ago, when Boston was "gooder" than it is
now. She said her prayers in the evening, as usual, and, at the conclusion, said,
"Good-by, God. I am going to New York to-morrow." But you have caught
me, sir, when I am exposed to my enemies, with nobody to shield me or protect
me.
I have listened wilh feelings of pleasure to the remarks of your excellent and
worthy Grand Chaplain, and I think that he has given you some very good advice,
anrl has encouraged you in the way you should fr<>· I think that Masons ought
always to remember that the grPat fact which gives life, not existence, but gives
life and vitality to Masonry, and causes it to spread all over the world, is involved
in two propositions :-one, that Masons are to be true to the country in which
they live; the other, that they are to establish institutions where brethren of all
sects and creeds, not atheists, m•y meet tog.ther upon a common footing, and
become acquainted and esteem each other's virtues more and more; and there is
no kicking at any creed ; there is no kicking at any body of men ; there is no intolerance or bigotry to stir the Masonic Body in the least particle from the great
fundamental principle of its organization, or cause it to withhold the right hand of
fellowship from those who are willing to come together and meet upon the level
and part upon the square. In all these troubles, and in all these trials that we
have to go through, Masone should always remember that, because that is their
bond of strength, that is their power, which will exist ae long a~ humanity shall

exist.

Now, to go back, and start anew: when that great principle was announcedand I need not go historically back of that-Masonry spread at once in Germany,
in France, in Holland, in Great Britain, in Ireland, in Scotland, and in the
United States, and then in the colonies, and all the world took it up. You can
find Masons in India, you can find them in China, vou can find them in Japan,
you can find them in Persia, you can find them in Arabia, you can find them
among the Indians out on the plain•, .you can find them among the Indians in
,South America; all recognizing the Masonic sign, and all ready to extend the
right hand of fellowship and brotherhood to those whom they meet as their
fellows.
\Vith that bond of Masonry our merchants and our ehipmasters and our sailors
have in times past traversed the whole world and brought back the rich treasures of
every country, and found themselves in every city, wherever they might be, in the
presence of friends who would take care that they were not cheated, but who would
see that they got fair play. It is a great thing to belong to an Institution that is
so widespread and so uni versa!, and yet does not derogate one iota or hair's
breadth from the fidelity which you owe to your country and to the institutions
·
of your country. Your loyalty is unimraired by it.
Wby, in the days of the Revolution, you talk of those great men, Washington,
and Lafayette, and General Knox, and Stark, and Putnam, and Hancock, and all
the great names that filled this country with their energy and their force ill Revolutionary times; tbP. boncis of Masonry tied them together, and they trusted ePch
other, and, became they trusted ea.ch other, they dared to go forward, and, because
of them, .America became free.
No, it was not we, it was uot our grandfathers and our great-grandfathers in
themselves, but, above all, there was the Unseen Hand, the Divine Force, the
Great Will, before which all the earth trembles, and all the earth moves, and all
the earth has its bein(I', that carried those men forward in tbe path which led to
the freedom of this country ; and it is with you a guiding star, a pillar of cloud by
day and a pillar of fire by night, guiding the whole people of the world up to a better
future, to a higher civilization, to a more perfect equality, to a greater prosperity,
to a more thorough happiness-to everything which can make earth the nearest
approximation which can be made to a Garden of Paradise or of Eden.
Now, I am pas•ing away. Men who are gray amongst you are also passing
away. On you this mantle of Elijah is to fall, and you are to go on and do the
work. Do not forget it I It is a moral precept on your minds ; it is a moral duty
on your consciences ; it is a great thing that you are still, as you have been for

The Oommittee on Jurisprudence present this very interesting case lo their
report:Morning Star Lodge, No. 65, of Canisteo, Steuben Coouty, lo the Tweuty-third
Masouic District, applies to the Grand Lodge for relief from its present embarrassmeut, arising from the fact that since the last election and installation or its officers,
the Master and Beuior and Jouior Wardens have removed from the county and district
in which the Lodge is located, and are consequently unable to attend the Oommuoj,
cations of the Lodge. The question presented is, how can the Lodge, in the absence
of these three warranted officers, continue ite meeting and work 7 These officers are
represented as being ready and willing to do aoythioir within their power to assist
the Lodge in its dilemma, bot they are confronted with Section 12 of the Statutes,
which forbids a Master or Warden to resign; and Section 13, whiclt enumerates the
only cases in which a vacancy in office in a Lodge can occur, does not mention
removal from the district or State as one of such cases. Hence we are compelled to
hold that the removal of their places of residence by the Master and Wardens of this
Lodge does not create a vacancy in any ofthelr respective offices.

It seems strange to as that in revising their organic law our brethren of New York
did not provide for cases like the one above quoted, by striking out Sec. 82 of Art.
xn, relatfog to .. tennre of office."
Jo California we provide that vacancies may occnr by death, resignation, soepen·
sion or expulsion, or removal from the jurisdiction. We have never heard any good
reason urged in support of the prohibition to Master or Wardens of the right to
resign in case of incapacity from any cause.
Oar brethren of New York say he may die but must l!Ot resign. We consider the
restriction a violation of the fourteenth amendment to the Constitntion, and insist
that a Mason in good standing, be he a Master or Warden, has as clear a right to
resign as he has to die or go away. However, its none of our bnsinees and we pass.

The new Grand Master, R.·. W.·. Bro. MATTHIAS H. HBNDBBSON, then addressed
the Grand Lodge. Io the coarse of his address he said :Onr system of work differs from that practiced by the other jurisdictions of this
country. So marked is this difference that Pennsylvania stands alone among the
American Grand Lodge• as having a ritual entirely her own. It ls simple and impressive, without sopertluous verbiage, yet explaining folly and intelligently every
sign, symbol an<l attribnte the candidate receives. We make no attempt at dramatic
display, but endeavor by sound practical teaching to impress the troths of Free·
masonry upon our members. Oar work needs oo defense and we make none for it.
It was practiced when Hasonry was young, and has come down to us from the mists
or antiquity. We are proud to transmit it as we have received it without innovation,
spot or blemish. The efforts of the Grand Lodge in recent years have been to first
ascertain the true work and afterwards promulgate it. Io this it has been remark·
ably successful,. and a high degree of proficiency has been attained. The Temple
School of Instrnctioo and the schools located in other parts of the jorisdiotloo have
done admirable work in this respect, and the practice adopted In 1890 of requiring
proof of proficiency before advancement has been most beneficial, p.nd it can no
longer be said that Pennsylvania does not instruct her candidates. The advantages
of the practice accrue alike to the Lodge and the indivldoal, To the former by
insuring it an intelligent class of members, whereby It gains m reputation, and to
the latter by giving him all that he hlls paid for and enabling hiQl to make himself
known among strangers and enjoy social and fraternal beoefi~.

While this decision was warranted, in view of the fact that the Grand Lodge
ha8 never taken any action upon the subject, we believe it in the interest of
M..sonry that the Secretary of a Lodge in which a member is suspended or
expelloo should at once communicate the fact to the Secretaries of all known Masonio bodies with which the party is affiliated, and to secure this we recommend
the adoption nf the following standard resolution:Ruol·ved That in case of the suspension or expulsion of a member of a Lodge
the Secreta~v thereof shall forth with give notice under the seal of the Lodge to
the Secretary nr Recorder of all other Ma.sonic bodies with which said suspended
or expelled members are known to be affiliated.
The organizations of Chapters and Commanderies are directly interested in the
Lodge stflnding of their membership, and any rule having for its object the
furnishing of tha required information is important to each organization, and will
itid harmonious relations between the bodies. The rule is a good one.

Do yon see any parallel between the lesson of this cask thus situated, thos pro·

pause and consider. What is Freemasonrv? Simply an inetrnmeot for the good of
others. How is it. held to the human race? Only by the atroog chaiod of brotherly

We know of the merit of the representative system, proven in many instances, and
while we would not force it upon anothtir jurisdiction, would regret to see it discontinued, while many wish to retain it as a reminder of the olcl days when, a Grand
Representative, as special messenger, was the means of communicating important
business interests between sovereign Bodies. In the language of Bro. BELCHER, "the
system of appointing representatives has been adopted by the Grand Lodges of the
world, and has been recognized by all for more than a half a century; hence when it is
proposed to abolish this established system, we do not so much consider what it has
accomplished as what it might do under different conditions. Referring our M.·. W.· •
brother to the parable of the fig-tree, we would •ay to him, "give these representatives
a chance to do the work appropriate to their oftice before. abolishing the office."

CONCLUSION.
"And I sit and think when the sunset's gold
Is fl.usbing river and hill and shore,
I shall one day stand by the water cold,
And list for the sound of the boatman's oar;
I shall watch for a gleam of the fl.apping sail,
I shall hear the boat as it gains the strand,
I shall pass from sight with the boatman pale,
To the better shore of the spirit land.
I shall know the loved who have gone before,
And joyfully sweet will the meeting be,
When over the river, the peaceful river,
The Angel of Death shall carry me."
Once more, brethren of the Grand Lodge of California, we have received the
solemn admonition.." Be ye .also ready I" and we are again called to "drop the sprig
of acacia" and mourn the loss of two Past Grand Masters, Brothers JOHN MILLS
BROW.NII: and WILLUM CALDWELL BELCHER.
Bro. JOHN MILLS BROWNE was our Grand Master during the years 1875to1879.
He was a magnetic, scholarly Mason, a fine presiding officer, and his administration
of Grand Lodge affairs was eminently successful. He retired from office amid the
unanimous acclaim by his brethren of faithful service rendered. Bro. BROWNE being
in Government service, was called to Washington to complete bis uninterrupted
term of forty-one years in the U. S. Navy, and, as a crowning.,honor for his faithful service, he was !j.ppointed by President CLEVELAND and re-appointed by President
HABBIBON to the head of the Medical Department, with the title of Burgeon Gen·
era!. An ab~ence of fifteen years bas made him a comparative stranger to the
younger members of the Grand Lodge, bot to the members of twenty years, and
upwards, service, there is no one held in memory's grasp whose record brings to
mind pleasanter remembrances of Masonic association.
Of Hro. WILLLU[ C. BELCHER, we can hardly realize that he has left us forever.
We find ourselves looking for him in his accustomed place, and wondering that the
veteran cl,ui.irman has no reports to deliver.
Bro. BELCHER'B service commenced in the year 1860, when he was elected Senior
Grand Warden. In the following year he. was chosen ])epnty Grand Master, but
owing to the absence of Grand Master ENGLISH in the Frazer river country, the
discharge of the Grand Master's duties devolved upon Bro. BELOHER. He was
re-elected Grand Master for the years 1862, 1868 and 1864, and since the close of his
term has been continuously in service as Chairman of the Committee on Jurispru·

denoo. The Grand Lodge of C&lifornia can truly say that in the death of Bro.
BBLOHEB it loses one' who has been through all the past years its guide, counselor
and friend; his reports have attracted the attention of the Masonic world, and are
classed with. the best in our literature. WILLIAM C. BELCHER was a great lawyer,
and his love and veneration for the system of Freemasonry, with his special attachment for this Grand Lodge, made him a great Masonic jurist. There are but few in
the world who, having the ability, would give the time from their business demands
to the study, the analysis and application of the principles and groundwork of
Masonry as did our late brother.
The writer was associated for many years with Bro. BELCHER in his · committee
work, is witness of hia unselfish devotion, his firm, unyielding advocacy of the
right, and his unswerving attachment t.o the Grand Lodge at all times. May his
memory remain with us always, as the sweetness of the summer's last rose.
• Another year has passed, with its joys and sorrows, its pleasures and disappointments; the Great Reaper has been busy in striking from the rolls of the living those
for whom we had formed the most sincere attachment, and whom we shall greatly
miss as we tramp through the short time allotted to us here, but in the words of our
last service, "We can trustingly leave them in the hands of a Beneficent Being who
has done all things well." Peace to their memories.
In closing this report, we submit t.o our co-correspondents our best wishes for
their temporal and spiritual welfare with the salutation of the Monks of old, who, in
the discharge of their daily duties, met and exchanged their accustomed greeting of
memento mori.

Bro. CHARLES LEWIS PATTON, Trustee of the Masonic Widows' and
Orphans' Home, presented the following :The B9ard of Trustees of the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Homr, in response
to the request of the Grand Lodge, submit the following supplemental report:The ~nic Widows' and Orphans' Home Tract is locatt'd in Alameda County,
on the mam county road from Oakland to San Jose, about eighteen miles south of
• Oakland and one and a half miles north of Niles, and within half a mile of Decoto
.S 'tation on the main line of the 8. P. Co. It has n frontage on this road of about
one mile. There are five trains each way between San Francisco and Decoto on
the S. P. R. R. The Haywarde Electric Road also rune from Oakland to Haywarde
(five miles from our property), and we have every reason to believe that within a
year or so this road will be extended so that it will pass our tract, which will give
us half hourly transportatioh to and from Oakland.
The property was purchased in the spring of 1893, and contains 267.46 acres of
land. It cost $33,093.00, or approximately $124 per acre, and is free from incumbrance. Of these 267 acres there are about 80 acres of line level bottom land
which is, very productive, and will bear comparison with an.y land in the neighbor'.
hood. The California Nursery Co. conducta what is said to be the largest nursery
in the world within half a mile of this property, and their soil is of the same character. The only criterion as to the value of this level land is the sale recently
made of some land of a similar character near it at $350 per acre in ten acre tracts.
The Trustees feel safe, therefore, in valuinj!' this 80 acres at $200 per acre.
There are about 117 acres of rolling hillside land which is arable and suitable
for raising vegetables, grain, or deciduou~ fruit of any description. From the beet
information the Trustees can gather this 117 11cres· Is worth about $100 per acr1:.
The remaining 70 acres are suitable for pasture, and there is considerable wood on
it suitable for firewood, and it is worth say $30 per acre.
If these figures are nearly accurate the value of the land would appPoximately
be as follows :80 acres of 9ottom land at $250 per acre ............. . ... $20,000 00
117 acres of rolling land at $100 per acre ............ .· . .. . . 11, 700 00
70 acres of pasture land at say $30 per acre .. . . . . . . . . . . . . 2,100 00
Or a total valuation of. .......... . ... .. . ..... ... $33,800 00
The latest transfer in this vicinity of any land of a similar character tp ours was
the sale of about 57 acres within half a mile of our ~ite for $8,500. Thie property
conta.ine about the same proportion of level and rollinll land as ours, and was
bought by Mr. MAY, who now owns 1,300 acres adjoining our tract.
We would also add as a. fact having some weight in the matter of value, that at
the time this property was purchased, it was mortgaged to the San Francisco
Savings Union for $17,000 or thereabouts. It is well known that this company
never loans more than h~lf of the estimated value of country land. Calculated on
this basis the value of the land wnR at that time about $34,000. The Trustees,
therefore, feel that the price paid was not exorbitant.
At the last meeting of the Grand Lodge the Trustees reported that there was
some doubt as to the availability of this site on account of a question existing as to
the adequacy of the water supply. There is not nor h~ the~e e,·er been any quee·

1895.J

Grand Lodge of CaJ,ifOTnia.

213

tion that by sinking wells about fifty feet deep on the level j!'l"Ound and pumping, a
supply of water adequate for any purpose could be obtained ; but it bas been the
desire to procure a water supply without .the necessity of pumping, and to that
end we employed Bro. W.R. ECKAR1', who, after a thorough examination of the
l{roun:I, reports that by purchasing two springs from Mr. JOHN QUIGLEY, who
owns the adjoining property, a supply of water amounting to at least 9,000 gallons
per day can be piped to any point of our land which we may choose for a reservoir
site.
Prof. RISING, of the State University, after analyzing the water from these
springs, reports that the water from either of them, properly protected, is undoubtedly of good quality for domestic purposes. Mr. QUIGLEY made a written offer to
us of these two springs, with sufficient land around them for every purpose, and a
perpetual right to erect, lay and maintain the necessary improvements, pipes, etc.,'
across his land, for $2,000, and the citizens of Decoto have offered to subscribe the
~.000 to purchase these rights from Mr. QUIGLEY, provided this site is adopted for
the Home.
The supply of water will be amply sufficient for from 125 to 150 persons, and·
can probably be increased by proper development of the sprinirs. Of course there
is not sufficient water for irrigation; but after a thoroul!'h investigati~n of the
au bjflct, the Tn1etees are satisfied that it is absolutely unnecessary to irrigate an
acre of this land for any ordinary purpose, and that cereals, fruit or Vllj\'etablee of
all kinds, can successfully be raised without irrigation.
There 'are now three tenants on the place, each one of whom gets sufficient
water from a spring near bis place on our property for all Jomestic purposes, and
these springs would furnish a water supply, but pumping would be necessary,
which the Trustees desire to avoid.
Respectfully submitted.

Your committee, to whom w~s referred the transcript of the record of trial of
EDOUARD LARTHX, expelled by La PMfaite Union Lodge, No. 17, on April 5th,
1895, have had the same under consideration, and report as follows : This case was before the Grand Lodge at its last .Annual Communication, when,
for errors in the proceedings, the judgment was reversed and the cause remanded
for retrial. [Grand Lodge Proceedings, 1894, p. 728.]
The transcript now before the Grand Lodge shows a. new trial, resulting in a
judgment of expulsion. It further shows the most pa.insta.killlf effort on the part
of the subordinate Lodge to comply fully with the law governing tria.ls, and, but
for one omission, would not be open to the slightest criticism. The record fails to
show that any vote was taken by the Commissioners on the question· as to whether
or not the accused was guilty a.s charged ia the specifications, the only vote as to
guilt being on the question of unm&l!Onic conduct. It is needless to sa.y that a
verdict of guilty on the specification is absolutely essential to the validity of a.
judgment of expulsion. The transcript shows very clearly that the accused was
proven guilty, as charged in the specification, of having embezzled funds of the
benevolent society of which he was Secretary, and that he should be expelled, and
following precedents established by this Grand Lodge, your committee offer the
following tesolution and recommend it.. JMloption :Ruolved, That the judgment of La Parfam Union Lodge, No. 17, given on
April 5th, 1895, whereby EDOUARD LARTHE was expelled from all the rights and,
privileglll! of Masonry, be and the same is hereby reversed, and that tbe said
EDOUARD LARTHE be and he hereby·is, by this Grand Lodge, expelled from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry.
In the ca.l[le of Bro. DAVID ALBERT SHAW, acquitted by AzWJa Lodge, No. 305,
a. document entitled "Transcript on Appeal " has been placed in the hand• of
your Committee. There is no showing that any notice of appeal to the Grand
Lodge was ever given. Sec. 10, Art. IV, Part VI, ·constitution, provides
how and within what time an appeal may be ta.ken, and unless an appeal be ta.ken
in the manner there provided, the Grand Lodge will.not review the proceedings,
except in cases where a. judgment of expulsion or suspension has been pronounced.
Where an appeal is necessary to bring the matter before the Grand Lodge, it is
obvious that there should be a s.howing that the appeal has heen properly ta.ken.
It is possible that in this case an appeal was properly ta.ken, and that the proof
can be supplied. Your committee feel that the case shonld be continued to the
next Annual Communication, to allow the accuser to supply this proof, if it exists,
and therefore offer the following resolution, and recommend its adoption:Ruolved, That consideration of the case of Bro. DAVID ALBERT SHAW, acquitted
by AzWJa Lodge, No. 305, be deforred until the next Annual Communication of this
Grand Lodge.
Your committee, to whom' was referred the transcript of the record of the trial
of J08EPH DANIEL JOURDAN, of Misaion Lodge, No.169, suspended by Abell Lodge,
No. 146, within whose juriadiction he was th1m residing, on January 5th, 1895, have
had the ea.me under consideration, and report as follows:The accused has appealed from the judgment. The transcript shows no error
in the proceedings. The main charge 11oga.inst the accused was that during the year
1894, he, on divers occasions, the particular dates being unknown to the accuser,

consorted with women of disreputable character. The accused presented " written
answer in which he states "that during the year 1894 he was engaged in the saloon
business at Ukiah, and that certain women of the town, of bad reputation, purchased liquors from him habitually, and in the course of his regular business he was
frequently called upon to visit the house where said women resided, and frequently
met and recognized said women in other places, but he emphatica.lly denies that he
ever resorttd to said house or consorted with any woman for the purpose of prosti·
tution." The allegations of the charge are amply sustained by the testimony and
admltted by the a.newer. So far as the testimony goes, it appears, as alleged in
the answer, that the conduct of the accused, a. married man, was, to some extent,
inspired by a. desire to promote his business interests. In order to sell them liquor
and collect his money therefor, it was necessary for him to visit their hoW!08, spend
money thereat, recognize and converse with them wherever he met them, and to
generally treat them a.a friends. But it must be remembered that a Mason has no
right to subordinate Masonry to his own busineBB interests, ha.a no right to do any
act that will reflect discredit on the Order, even th,mgh it may benefit him a. little
fina.ncially. If a. Mason has not a. sufficient regarci for the Fraternity to restrain
him from the commission of act.a that must bring a. blush of shame to the faces of
his brothers, and strike a blow at the reputation of the Order, the sooner it is
known that his acts are discountenanced the better it will be for the fair name of
Masonry. That the acts of the accused were of such a character cannot admit of
question. It may seem a waste of time to state these simple truths, but some ha.ve
evidently been admitted as members who have not begun to appreciate the nature
of the obligations they have as•umed. The conduct of the accused was unmasonic,
and the fa.ct that it was, in some d~ee, prompted by busineBB reasons, makes it no
less unmasonic. .Your committee feel that the judgment of suspension should
be . affirmed, and, therefore, offer the following resolution, and recommend · its
adoption:.
Resol'Ved, That the judgment of AbeU Lodge, No. 146, given on .January 5th,
1895. whereby JOSEPH DANIEL JouBDAN, of Misaion Lodge, No. 169, was suspe~ded
from a.11 the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby affirmed.

In the matter of the petition of JAll&B VELSIR, expelled by Pentalpha Lodge,
No. 202, on May 19th. 1890, to be restored to all the rights and privileges of
Masonry, your Committee report as follows :-

Due notice of the application was ltiven to PentaJ,pha Lodge, No. 202, and that
Lodge had, by more than a two-thirds vote, &eked for the granting of the petition.
The petitioner was expelled for having willfully disobeyed a summons to appear at
a meeting of the Lodge for reprimand, which punishment he bad previously been
adjudged to suffer for unmasonic condnct. The original charge against him was
that he had made an unprovoked assault upon hie wife, striking her several times,
and the circumstances surrouoding·the act were such that a public prosecution had
been instituted against him, resulting in a plea of guiltv of assault in the Superior
Court and judgment thereon. The commission having found him guilty, adjudged
· the very li~ht penalty of reprimand as the punishment. He was duly summoned
to appear for reprimand, but refused to obey the summons; declared that he would
not go into the Lodge-room again, and that they could do what they pleased in the
matter. He was vecy properly expelled for this, and his only excuse now for this
most serious offense is that he did not realize the seriousness of the matter, for
various re&eons, including family troubles.
Willful disobedience of a M&eonic summons i11 an offens~ that cannot be lightly
condoned, and it seems to your committee that something more than the excuse
above referred to, and the recommendation of the expelling Lodge, is necessary to
justify the restoration of the offender to all the rights and privileges of M&eonry.
There is nothing here to indicate that if restored, the petitioner would come any
nearer to living up to the obligations of M&eonry than he did before his expulsion,
and if there has been no change, he certainly should not be allowed to be a member
of the Order. It should devolve opon one who seeks restoration to show that he
realizes and repents his offense, and is honestly endeavoring to lead such a life &a
will in itself be a recommendation for his readmission to the rights and privilegf'.s
of which he w&e properly deprived.
Your committee offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption :Resolved, That the petition of .TA.MKS V ELBm, expelled by Pentalph,a Lodge,
No. 202, on May 19th, 1890, to be restored to all the rights and privileges of
Masonry, be and the same is hereby denied.

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 9,

The accused wae fonod guilty opon four epeciflcatlooe. It is doubtful wlietber the
evidence is sufficient to sustain the verdict of guilty on either the fourth or firtb
specifications, but It is oooeceesary to devote any attention to either of these,
inasmuch as the verdict of gnllty oo the first and second Is amply sustained by the
testimony. The substance of these two specifications is that the accused, in the town
of Sanger, where he lived, associated in pnblic'with a woman well 1<nown as a pro1ti·
tote, received bAr into hie own household, where she lived for some weeks in com·
pany with hie wife and family, accompanied 'her and hie wife together to San
Francisco, where they all stopped at the same hotel, and in general associated with
her as an acquaintance.
Such conduct does not become a Mason, who bas in hie care not only hie own
honor, bot the honor of the Order to which he belongs. He h&s no right to do any·
thing which will reflect discredit upon Masonry, and when be is guilty of any ench
aot, the interests of Masonry demand that be should no longer be known as a member
of the Order.
Although the errors found in the record of the proceedings of the first trial have
been rectified, your committee cann.o t recommend the transcript in this case as a
model for future proceedings. The errors now fonnd are, however, all immaterial,
and cannot have operated to the prejudice of the accused.
Your committee offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Re80?tled, ihat the judgment of Sanger Lodge, No. 316, rendered on December
6th, 1894, whereby ROBERT J. PADBN was expelled from all the righte\nd privileges
of Masonry, be 1t.nd the same is hereby affirmed.
All "!hlch is reapectfnlly submitted.

Flin MABION ANGELLOTTI,

Your committee, from information furnished by the Grand Secretary and from
the foregoing tabulated statement, find a decidedly marked improvement in the
number of degrees conferred by the subordinate Lodges, and the consequent
increase in membership theuin during the. past year, as compared with the year
immediately preceding, and, from the showing made, the Grand Lodge has every
reason ·to congratulate itself upon the flourishing condition of the Craft in Cali·
fomia.
Your committee would again urge upon the Masters and Secretaries of subordinate Lodges the great importance of forwarding their returns within the time
prescribed and required by the Constitution, and also at the same time their dues
to the Grand Lodge. Each year, for several years past, your committee has
endeavored to impress upon the MASTERS of Lodges that, in a me.asure, responsibility for the strict observanoe of this rule rests upon them, and that it is their
duty as much, if not more, than that of their Secretaries, to see that the returns to
which they certify are not only correct as to the matters therein contained, but
that they are properly attested with the Lodge seal, and, further, to see that the
dues accompany the returns forwarded to the Grand Secretary. We are pleased
to report that a great improvement in this respect is shown during the year just
past, there being fifty.four delinquent Lodge.a as compared with seventy-two of the
preceding year ; but still the number of errors occurring in returns, inetancee of
the omission of signatures thereto, in some cases a failure to affix the seal of the
.Lodge to the returns, and neglect in forwarding the Grand Lodge dues until
reminders by the Grand Secretary were necessary, is so unreasonably large, that
in justice to the Grand Secretary, by reason of the unnecessary increaae in the
business of hie office occasioned thereby, your committee feel justified in again
oalling attention to these delinquencies, in the hope that great improvement in the
future will he made with referenoe to the errors to which attention is here called,
and we would again recommend the adoption of the same resolution presented last
year, as follows :Re10Zved, That the Grand Secretary he instructed, as soon as he shall forward
the blanks for the returns to the subordinate Lodges, to notify the Inei>ectors of
the several districts that he has so done, and that it shall then become the duty of
the said Inspectors to see to~it, as far aslliee in their power, that the l..odges comply
with the requirements of the'Oonstitution in this regard.

We are glad to be able to inform our brethren of Kentucky and Wyoming that
we have experienced no "trouble" or "vexation " by adopting the Grand Repreeentativeeystem; but, upon the contrary, our intercourse with the Representatives
of other Grand Bodies has been of the most cordial and· fraternal character. Yet
we do not believe that the system is nece88ary to maintain the comity existing
between the Grand Lodges. Still we like the system and would regret to see it
abolished.
We respectfully recommend that the co01mie•ione accrediting Representatives
from this Grand I.JOd11e to the Grand Lodges of Kentucky and Wyoming, by their
request, be withdrawn.

Relative to the United Grand Lodge of Victoria.
Tbe Grand Secretary has placed before us a communication from the Grand
Secretary of that Grand Lodge, in which he save : "I am directed again to write
and renew the application for recognition and exch..nge of Representatives from
the United Grand Lodge of Victoria, and the hope that the same cordial recognition and mutual exchange of Representatives may be accorded to the United
Grand Lodge of Victoria as have been by our sister Grand Lodges in Australia."
It has been the settled policy of this Grand Lodga in reference to new Grand
I.JOdgee to ascertain what wae the condition of Masomy in the territory over which
the new Grand Lodge claim~ jurisdiction; how many I.JOdges there were there and
under what obedience they held ; how many of them joined in the establishment
of thii new Grand Lodge, and, if less than all joined, under what obedience those not
joining hold ; whether the new Grand Lodge has been recognized by the Grand
I.JOdges by which its constituents were originally chii.rtered ; what proceedings were
had and taken at the Convention looking to ite organization, and what claim of
jurisdiction it makes, and also a copy of ite Constitution. In regard to these
matters we have no information.
We therefore recommend that the Grand Secretary be requested to ask that
Grand ·L odge to furnish ue with the nece88ary information ae above eet forth.
With the hope that that information will be furnished, we recommend that no
further action be taken at this time.
A proposition hae been made by ihttnmlle.I.JOdge, No. 249, to consolidate with
Sincerity Lodge, No. 132.
The provision of the Constitution which relates to the consolidation of Lodges,
(see Section 11, Article II, Part III), provides that "two or more Lodiree located
near each other may consolidate into one upon such terms as way be agreed upon
by themselves; but of such proposed consolidation the members of each Lodge
shall have at least three months notice before the stated meeting at which such
proposition is to be acted upon, and shall require the assent in writmg of at least
three-fourths of all the members of •uch Lod1te to adopt such proposal for consolidation."
So far. as the proceedings in Greenville Lodge are shown there is no record that
the requisite three months' notice was given to the members of that I.JOdge, although
there ie an instrument attached which shows that eleven members out of the fourteen consent to the consolidation.
Upon the part of Sincerity I.JOdge, No. 132, the record shows that the Worship·
ful Master notified the members that at the stated meeting in September, 1894, the
proposed consolidation would come up for final action; that tha proposal for conaolidation was signed by twelve out of the fourteen members who were within
reach; that upon a vote being taken there were six ayes and one no; while the roll
ahowe there are twenty members of such Lodge.
.
Thus it will be seen that in the attempted consolidation there is a total absence
of about all of the constitutional requirements to effect the object intended.
The consolidation must be effected by three-fourths of all the members of each
Lodge, given in writing, and three months' notice previous to the dtated meeting at
which the proposition is to be acted upon.
·
The action of the Lodge is not sufficient compliance with the Constitution governing this proceedinj!'.

In that very apt illustration, in those words of application be1mtifully spokan,
more is presented and said than volumes of discursiveness could really ac~omplish
in impressing the deep and telling truths of that Order founded upon the principle
so forcibly written in the Scripture : "These three, but the greatest of these is
charity." What are fhe chains which hold the cask which has placed within man's
reach messages of cheer, messages of hopes, messeges of consolation and messages
of happineos, when he has fully performed, or has in a great measure performed,
hia dutie1< as a Freemason. They are the knowledge we have, the knowledge we
must acquire, the knowledge we must possrss in order to hold this depository of
sweet words written by the members of our Craft in the past, recognized by the
members of our Craft in the present. If we will not h~ed the warninj!'S, not only of
the present, I.Jut the warnings of the measureless past that, in a few words, have
expre~ed "knowledge is power," and see to it that we follow this motto as the
guiding star for our actions in adding to, protecting and building up the Order, the
chains will soon be parted, the cask of messages float away soon to he battered by
the waves of opposition into pieces which will soon float here and there of no use
to man, of no use of any kind, lost-utterly lost. It seems to me that these are
lessons of the hour, and we must not fail to grasp the opportunities which are given
us to know more, and, by knowing more, be armed against opposition, no matter
from what source it may come. .
It id not for OD!l who is appointed to the position of Grand Orator that he should

study, to learn what bas thus been accomplished. It appears to me that the duty,
as I understand it, of the one who fills the position of Grand Orator of any jurisdiction, is to call the attention of the members of the Masonic Order to any evils
which to him may seem to exist, and thus cause such evils to be destroved if possible, and if the evils are not ao immense as to him they may appear, still seri<ius
~arm is not accomplished, but good may come. If "e are to protect, if we are to
entrench ourselves bt>hind battlements that cannot he assailed when the foe
appro11-ches, we must be well armed, well clothed, well fed in knowledge, nnd why
should we not lie so armed, fed and clothed, for we only have to seek knowledge of
that splendid Institution created for charily which, by another, has been beautifully and truthfully said to be "Masonry-its laws are reason and equity ; its
principles benevolence and love; its religion purity and trnth ; its intention peace .
on earth ; and its dispositien, good will toward men.''

The M... w.·. NATHANIEL GREENE CUBTIS then ad.dressed the Grand
Lodge, as follows : MosT WORSHIPF UL GRAND MASTER
AND BRETHREN OF 'l'HE GRAND LODGE:~

It hath pleased the Supreme Ruler of the Universe in His infinite wisdom to
call our beloved Past Grand Master, WILL:LAM l.JALDWBLL BELCHER, from hiR lai;Jors
here on earth to that Celestial Grand Lodge where the weary, toil-worn craftsman,
will find eternal rest. On the morning of the first of September, in this city, the
Angel of Death cast the dark shadow of its wings over his earthly tenement and
laid its icy hand upon his great warm heart, and his immortal spirit winged its
flight to that God who gave, it, 1here to dwell forever in eternal rest.
When the sad tidings of hie death was flashed along the wires, on hill-top and
mountain, in valley and callon1 in city and hamlet, it cast a deep gloom and profound sorrow all over the land. He was widely known and everywhere universally
beloved and respected. I am glad that I am here to-day to offer my humble lrihute
of love and esteem to the memory of our deceased brother. His pathway all aloIJg
the journey of life was a track of Light, where we may walk with safety, emulate

When Grand Secretary ABELL died, our late distinguished brother, Past
Grand Master BELCHER, said to me that it would be worse than folly for any

Mason living in this jurisdiction to pronounce a eulogy at hiR funeral ; that no one
could do justice to the great life work which had distinguished Bro. ABELL; the
splendor of his Masonic achievements, the work he had done for the Order, the
purity of his purposes, reached beyond the limits of the voice of any living Mason~
And to-day, Most Worshipful Grand Master, as we gather for the last time a.round
the bier of our departed brother, it seems to me that there are few, if any of us,
who can fully or fitly speak at Bro. BELCHER's funeral. It i~ most true he is dead
in the flesh, but the genial warmth and the beautiful character of his spiritual life
cannot and will not die. He went down in a ripe old age. ·He ha.G lived more
than the three score years and t en allotted to man, but the whole of his life was
devoted to his fellow beings. Qld as he was, he yet seemed to us to live in the
spring-time of youth. Many of us had known him for over a third of a century,
and to us he always seemed young. The same benignant countenance, the same
lofty, erect carriage, the same geniality of feature and wonderful intellectuality of
character, remained with him through every period of his life.
I can see him now as he used to pass up the main hall to his seat in the East,
where, as Chairman. of the Committee on Juri•prudeoce, he did M asonic duty.
His deci•ioos while on thnt committee form distinguished landmarks in the Masonic
law of California, and they will be referred to by our Masonic brethren for all time
to come.
Bear in mind, my brothers, that he was a distinguished and illustrious Mason
in this jurisdiction when at least one-half of the members now present were not
born. Bear in miod, also, the long period of his Masonic labors, his devotion to
our Order, his dignity of manner, and you cannot and would not, if you could,
forget the man. It should be our hope, our ambition, that our lives will be as full
of fn1itioo as was his ; t hat they shall be as ample in goodne~s, as wise in action as
was his. If so, the story.of our existence will be a benediction to the Order and we
shall not have lived in vain. He fought the good tight. With us he bas finished
hiR course, but he has left behind him something we should all emulate as an
example and follow as a guide. We will remember him for what he bas done and
we will carry through life the recollection of his goodneM
s and greatness. I once
heard a very distinguished and lovable woman say of him, "I am proud of Judge
BELCHER." I ventured to ask her the reason, and she answered, "He was brave
enough never to marry." "Why, madam," I said to her, "you are a wife and a
mother; why do you say that? " And she answered, "He is one of the few men
whose hearts are too great for any one woman to monopolize; he is intended for
all mankind." And so he was.
I once heard him say to a friend who wished to join a particular churob, that
he waR pleB!!ed to have him do so, but as for him he said he felt that creed or sect
might narrow his field for good. That he felt as though the battle of life was not
fully fought unless he fought for all. He believed in humanity. He believed in
the brotnerhood of man, the fatherhood of God. He believed that the best way to
serve his fellow man was to dry the tears of the widow, to bury the dead and to
care for the orphan. Doiug tbeRe things, he thought he was accomplishing the
great purpose of life, and he was practicing that true religion which was taught by
Christ while on earth.
The story of his life can never be fully t old, for he was one of those few characters who did good in secret. Twice, when I was Grand Master, he volunteered
to go to some brother whom we both feared was going wrong, and each time his
persuasion tended to redeem that brother. He was not one of those who told the
•tory of his good deeds. He let not his right hand know what his left hand doeth.

Past Grand Master MoBBis MA.ROH ESTEE, from the Special Committee on the deaths of Past Grand Masters BBLOHER and BnoWNx, presented the following reports :To the M. ". W. ". <hand Lodge of Oaliforni,a, :Pa~t Grand Master WILLIAM CALDWELL BELOHER died in this city September
1st, 189/i, at the ad vanceJ age of seventy.four years. He was born at Stockbridge,
State of Vermont, December 12, 1820, graduated from the University of Vermont
in 1843, taught school in the Academy at Bridgeford, in the State of Vermont,
and at the ·Academy at Plattsburg, in the State of New York, for a number of
Years. He then studied law; and was admitted to the bar in Vermont in the year
1852.
He came to California in the spring of 1856, settled in Marysville, and commenced the practice of the law with his brother, Judge I. S. BBLOB:&R, under the

260

. Proceedings of the

[Oct. 11,

firm name of BELCHER & BELCHER. Subsequently he· removed to San Francisco,
and beca.me the lea.ding member of the law firm of MASTICK, BELCHER & MASTICK.
In Masonry, he has always been a conspicuous figure. He was Grand Master
of this Grand Lodge for the years 1862-3--4, and was Chairman of the Committee
on Masonic .Jurisprudence for more than twenty-eight years.
As a lawyer, he stood at the head of the profession. He was honest and capable. No one who knew him ever questioned his integrity; and no one who ever
practiced la.w with him doubted his eminent ability. He possessed to a high
degree the courage of his con victiona. In debate he was strong and convincing.
If in the wrong, he sought to be right. If right, he wa• fearless, and asserted
himself with all the vigor of his forceful manhood.
The gentleness of his disposition, the simplicity of his manners, added to his
tall, commanding person, made him at once a most conspicuous and most lovable
man. He combined in a high degree the opposite_qualities of goodness and greatness. His learning was as varied as it was profound. He seemed to grasp the
whole field of literature-not superficially, but thoroughly and exhaustively. He
was a linguist of more than common attainments, for he was both a Latin and
a French scholar, and was deeply versed in the literature of both tongues. He had
accumulated a large library of mi•cellaneous works, and they were selected with
rare judgment and perfect taste.
His mind was eminently judicial. He believed the law was intended only to
secure justi~e, and he thus became an eminent eqnity lawyer. He despised pretense, trickery and deception; beCl\UBe he was himself the soul of frankness and
honor. He was well versed in affairs, and had studied the political history of bis
country, and knew by heart the careers of our most distinguished pub~ic men,
although he avoided politics and refused public station. He was conspicuously
loyal to his co11Dtry, obedient to his God, and just to all men He possessed,
in a large d~, a sincere and hopeful religious sentiment, which with him
amounted to conviction. His was that religion which recognized broadly the
fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. No sect could narrow bis conception of religious duty, or limit his love for his fellow-men.
He was the noblest of our Craft-the first Mason in our jurisdiction. For
more than thirty-five years he helped to build our Masonic structu,·e. Nor did he
toil in vain~ Behold the work of his wining hand, bis generous heart, his wise
head. But that band has now paused ; that heart is stilled; that bead is no longer
the storehouee of thought. And yet, in a loftier sense, he is not dead. The spirit
cannot die. His good deeds survive him, and they will be remembered while
truth and virtue and honor hold dominion among men. They will be remembered
by Masons so long as Masonry remains faithful to the great trust confided to its
keeping, and so long as justice and equality, liberty and law, control the conduct
and mark out the social and political action of American freemen.
Past Grand Master JOHN MILLS BROWNE died in Washington during the
last Masonic year. He was born in Hinsdale, New Hampshire, May 10, 1831,
was graduated from Harvard University in March, 1852, entered the service of
the United States as an Assistant Surgeon March 23, 1853, and continued in that
service until May 10, 1893, when he was retired.
He occupied many conspicuous positions in the branch of the service to which
he belonged, and for many years before his retirement was Surgeon-General of the
United States Navy. He was Surgeon of the "Kearsarge" in the memorable battle with the "Alabama."

1895.]

(}rand Lodge of Galif<Ymia.

261

In the Masonic Order he had filled every position of honor and trust. He was
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Masonry of this jti.riediction for the years
1875--0-7 and 8. He was a man of varied att..inments, and of a warm, ((enerous
and impulsive nature. In private life, h~ was kindly and affable; as a speaker,
.
he was eloquent and penmasive.
He was appointed Surgeon-General of the Navy by both Presidents CLEVELAND
and HARRISON, and conducted himself in that high office with rare wisdom. For
many years he was a conspicuous character in Washington, and to his last hours
poesessed, in an eminent degree, the confidence of the heads of the department to
which he was attached.
As a man, he was upright and honorable; as a Mason he stood at the bead of
our Order-one of its most distinguished characters, beloved by all who came in
contact with him.

Bro. NATHANIEL GREENE CURTIS, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports :To the M.·. W.'. Grand Lodge of Califqrnia :-

Relative to decisions upon questions of Masonic law, reported by the Most
'Vorsbipful Grand Master, which have been referred to your committee, we are
constrained to disagree with him in granting permission to Lodges to appear in the
regalia of the Order for the purpose of attending divine service. Brethren should
not appear in public clothed in regalia, except upon occasions which are Maaomc
and in attending funerals. We are of the opinion thatthe discretion uf the Grand
Master in grantinglsuch permission should not have been exercised.

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 11

The Grand Master received a number of communicntions from Masters of
Lodges, relating to the rights, etc., of dimitted Masons who apply for affiliation and
are rejected. In each case the Grand Master referrer! these anxious inquirers to
the constitutional provisions regulating the proposition · In most of the cases preaented to him the applicants had carried their dimits for from five to fifteen years
before presenting the same to any Lodge and applying for affiliation. To reach
the exigency of such cases, the Grand Master recommends that this Grand Lodge
amends the Constitution so as t o make it conform to the provision of the Constitution of New York, which provides that no dimit shall be granted to a brother until
he shall have first affiliated with another Lodge.
Yonr committee can see no reason for disturbing the terms of our Constitution
relating to this subject. It is sufficient to meet all qaestions which may arise.
We are of the opinion tliat the recommendation of the Grand Master should not
be concurred in.
Information was rAquested by Paaadena Lodge as to the obligation resting
upon the Lodge to contribute to the relief of the widow of a Mason who had resided
in Iowa, an,l who had been dead for forty vears, and who had been a non -affiliated
Mason for se\'en years prior to his death. This aged lady had removed from Iowa
to PasadP.na for the purpose of benefiting a son who was afBicted with consumption.
Had the former brother been alive and in the circumstances his widow is found, he
would not be entitled to aid, and certainly no greater rights can be poBBeBBed by
her. The Grand Master replied that the Lodge was under no obligation ·to make
the contribution. In this we think he was correct.

At the annual election for officers in Athens Lodge, No. 228, votes were cast by
members who were in arrears for dues, the votes were canvaSBed and the Master
declared the officers elected. Prior to the next stated meeting a brother insisted
that the Master should declare the election illegal.
The Grand Master decided the election must stand. In rendering his decision
the Grand Master makes use of the following language : "While it is true under
the provisions of Section 2, Article IX of the Uniform Code of By-laws of Lodges,
delinquents should not be permitted to vote, in this case delinquents having been
permitted to do 80 would not justify the Master in declaring the election illego.l."
In this connection, at least referring to the same subject, Woodland Lodge, No.
156, states that, "previous to voting the Master announced that brethren in arrears
for dues were not entitled to vote." There were twenty-six votes cast and only
twenty-two brethren present who had paid their dues. In view of these facts the
questions are asked: Was the election legal? Has the Lodge a right to install the
officers 80 elected!
In both cases the Grand Master decided that the elections must stand. Which
determination we think was correct.
It is true that no brother, who is in arrears for dues, is entitled to vote, yet, we
are of the opinion that, in permitting those who are in arrears to vote, the responsibility rests upon the Master solely, and his irregularity should not vitiate the
election. We, however, look upon it as a duty, for the benefit of Lodges, to say to
all Masters that th~y should not permit a brother to participate in an annual election unless he is clear of the books.

The son of the Secretary of a Lodge died and the father was without means to
bury his dead. The Master of the Lodge advanced the money to defray the
expenses of the funeral. The Lodge objected to reimbursing the Master for the
money thus advanced, for the reason that the Secretary had no claim against the
Lodge, and that the amount should be considered a loan upon the part of the
.
Master.
The Grand Master thought that this was a matter altogether proper for the
consideration of the Lodge; if its Secretary, or any other member, under the circumstancP.s stated, was unable to meet the necessary expenses of burying the child,
it was the duty of the Lodge. ,to help him, and it was the duty .of every member of
the Lodge to see that be received the neOOBBary aSBisbnr,e, That the action of the
MRSter was propPr, as the representative of the Lodge, in making the advance
when it was impracticable or inconvenient to call the Lodge together to act upon
the case, and that the Lodge should repay to the Master the money thus a~vanced.
If, however, the money was advanced as a loan, then the Lodge was under no
obligation to repay the amount.
Tbe position of the Grand Master is well faken upon both propositions. From
the statement of the matter we think the Master acted for the Lodge. Probably
the charitable instinct of the Master which prompted him to render the aid as he
did, was not strictiy in accordance with the practice of the Order, yet we should
remember that charity is one of the cardjnal principles of our Order, and that which
is done in the name of charity is blessed. The Master having rendered the relief
we think the Lodge should reimburse him.
The Trustees of Athens Lodge, No. 228, made a loan of the funds of the Lodge
to irresponsible persons, and which have resulted in its lose. The question is asked :
.
Are the Trustees responsible for the amount?
The Grand Master thought that if the Trustees exercised their best judgment
in making the loan, and acted in good faith, they incurred no liability. In other
words if the Trustees exercised that judgment which an ordinary, prudent business
man ,;.ould with ref'erence to his own affairs, that no liability would a_ttacb. We
think this is the law of the case briefly stated.
Question. Can the Tyler of a Lodge, he being a member in good standing,
debate and vote on questions before the Lodge!
The Grand Master said yes, and that it was the duty of the Master to relieve
him sufficiently to exercise the right.
We cannot see that the Tyler, becnuse he has taken upon himself the responsiNe
duties of that place, should have favors extended to him whereby he would be
released from his obligations as a member of the Lodge. It is not only the right
of the Tyler to exercise all the privileges of a member of the Lodge, but it is his
duty, as well as all mem hers of the Lodge, to participate in the transaction of the
Lodge'• business.

name. The Grand Ma~ter was g,sked if a Lodl!'e could receive a petition signed by

Charges were preferred against the Secretary of a Lodge, and the question Wf!oB
asked who should notify the members of the special meeting called to elect Commissioners?
•
The Grand Master replied that the Secretary should issue the notices, and act
in his official capacity until the Commissioners were elected; then he should be
temporarily suspended from office, and a Secretary pro tem. appointed to discharge
the duties of the office to the conclusion of the trial. The Secretary is not supposed
to know against whom the chargea are preferred.
Your committee layd this down al! the proper practice.

Question. Is it required that the Master-elect shall be qualified to give the
work and lecture of the Senior Deacon, to be entitled to be installed as Master?
The Grand Master thought not; so we think. Though we would suggest that
the Master should be sufficiently proficient in the work as an entirety to enable
him to instruct his officers, as well as to correct them as to any mistakes which they
might make.
A brother had for a numb<ir of years remained suspendtod for non-payment of
dues. He beciLme sick, and, thinking his life fast drawing to a close, expressed a
desire to be restored by his Lodge, that be might die a Mason in good standing.
The request was made known to his Lodge at the next stated meeting thereof,
when a brother moved that the delinquent's dues be remitted, and the motion was
carried without opposition. Prior to the next stated meeting, the Grand Master
was asked if, at that meeting, the vote by which the dues were remitted could be
reconsidered? He answered, No.
In another case, the question as to a reconsideration of the action of the Lodge
was referred to the Grand Master, as follows :"A brother was suspended for non-payment of dues at the stated meeting in
December, 1894, the Lodge rafusing to grant him further time. At the stated
meeting in January, 1895, a brother, who felt aggrieved at the action of the Lodge,
made the statement in open Lodge, ' That he had seen the Grand· Master, and had
talked the . matter over with him, and that the Grand Master would very likely
order us to rescind our action, or he would take our charter.' Upon this statement
being made, a member made a motion to rescind the action of the Lodge. and to
remit the dues of the brother to January let, 1895, Rtating 'that if we had to reinstate the brother, we had better do it voluntarily than to be ordered to do so by
the Grand Master, or !Ose our charter.' The motion was carried, and the brother
was reinstated. Soon after this action was had, the Master of the Lodge called
on the Grand Master and stated that by reason of such action the harmony of the
Lodge had been disturbed," and asked his advice as to the best way to proceed,
with a view of restoring harmony. The Grand Master assured the Master that
the statement made as above quoted as coming from him was incorrect. The
Grand Master stated to the Master that tbe·suspension of the brother was a mat-

ter with which the Lodge had a perfect right to deal, and that he did not thin~ be
bad any right to interfere. The Master then asked, 'Can our Lodge reconsider
the vote by which the brother'~ dues were remitted?' .The Grand ~aster .answ~red
that the Lodge, having acted unier a misrepresentation of facts, its action 1111ght
be reconsidered."
The action of the Grand Master in both propositions was correct.
In the first proposition, under all rules, the motion to reconsider would rome ~oo
late ; and again, the action of the Lodge was in the dispensation. of a char1ty
which was commendable. Further, the action of the Lodge created, ~r r~tber
restored the brother to a new status in the Lodge, and conferred upon h1~ rights
of which he could not be deprived onlv by his own act in causing a forfeiture, or
by due process of law.
In the second proposition, it is very evidant that the action of the Lodge was
reached through a misunderstanding of the facts, and the members werfl influenced
by misrepresentations.
Question. Can a Lodge set ap,.rt, for social purposes, money received for rent
of their halls?
The Grand Master says No. Such funns are part of the revenue of the Lodge,
and a sum, not exceeding five per cent. of the total revenue for the preceding Masonic year can be used for such purpose.
We thi~k that no greater latitude should be allowed in the use of the funds of
a Lodge for the purpose referred to than is noticed in the Grand Master's reply.
The money referred to becomes a part of the funds of the Lodge as much a• though
they had been received from the payment of dues. We approve of the position
·t aken by the Grand Master.
Question. Can a Mason, holding a dimit, place himself in standing by paying
dues to a Lodge?
The Grand Master answered, No.
Under our Constitution, something more than mere paying of dues is required.
An unaffiliate should present to a Lodge bis petition for affiliation, pay six months'
dues-if he has resided in the State six months or more-and the affiliation fee,
if any. If rejected, be may renew it under the provisions of the Constitution
anrl the decisions of tnis Grand Lodge, and thus keep himself in standing.
The Master of Santa Ba1·bara Lodge, No. 172, desires that all persons who
may be made Master Masons hereafter, shall be required to pass an examinati~n
as to his proficiency in the degree, in open Lodge, within six months after receiving the degree.
We are of the opini~n that this proposition is impracticable. Should this become a regulation we see no means to compel its observance. The ~flicacy of the
law is in the means of enforcing obedience. This could not be reached. Self.
pride should prompt a brother to perfect himself in the work of the Master's degree,
but, if he neglect so tu do, we are utterly powerless to compel him.
We recommend that the resolution be not adopted.

of gross inaccuracies, and were the meetings of the Lodge conducted as the minutes

hea~d the Master of the Lodge and one of its members, the Masters of two neighbormg Lodges and the Inspector, we are convinced that all the proceediDgs of the
Lo?ge were regular, and that the minutes are very inaccurate, and we do not
beheve the Lodge should Le made to suffer through the fault of this one brother
If a charter is granted, the Lodge will be able to hold an election of officers and
the mistake in the selection of a Secretary will be corrected ; if they have to continue under dispensation, they cannot change their officers, and it will be a death
blow to the ~odge. Be!ievinl? it to be for the · best interests of Masonry we
offer the followmg resolution and recommend its l\doption : -

Resolved. That a charter be granted to Whittier Lodge, with such number as the

usage of the Grand Lodge directs.

The Grand Master then delivered his Annual AddreBB to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :BRETHREN OJI' THE GR.AND LoDGE : -

I extend to you a fraternal greeting and congratnlat.e you on the auspicious
opening of this, our forty-seventh Annual Communication.
Our relatiollS with neighboring and foreign jurisdictiollB are of the most
cordial and friendly nature. Our returns show, for the present year, a net
increll.lle of over seven hundred in,the membership of the subordinate Lodges.
Our financial condition, notwithstanding our large expenditures, is better
than it was at the time of our last Annual Communication. Three new
Lodges have received charters, two others have been orge.nired and have
received diapensatiollB, and no Lodge hll.8 been called upon to surrender its
charter. The financial condition of the subordinate Lodges is, as a general
rule, favorable, although some are suffering from causes incident to the commercial and industrial depression which is now so generally prevalent. It is
gratifying to see, among those who are ll.llsembled here to-day, so many whose
faces have become familiar because of their frequent attendance upon our
Annual Communications; many of whom have grown gray in the service of
our Order - some -0f whom have pa.seed their vigor and are now venerable in
years. We offer up thanks to the Source of all our blessings that so many of
our vet.eran workers have been spa.red to honor us with their presence and to
a.id us with their wise and conservative counsel. So far 11.8 we are informed,
during the past year the grim reaper, Death, hll.8 not invaded the ranks of the
present or the past elective officers of this Grand Lodge. While we have thus
been spa.red u.ny such a:ffiicting dispensation, it is meet and proper that we
should bow in reverence wiPt our s~ter jurisdictions who have been called
upon during the pa.st year to mourn over the bier of those who have been
translated from the Grand Lodge on earth to the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge on High. ·
.
e therefore pause in our deliberations to offer a. fraternal tribute to the

In the enactment of new laws there is often a tendency to adopt; new

this Addreu. · The result of such legialation is to confuse the Craft and add

And, my brethren, in the final business of this Commtr.nicatioo-the eleo·

brethren anwng whom no contention should exist, except that noble oonten·

In reviewing the anneal addreasee of my illustrious pred--:M, I find,

My experience in this pattianlat line has not been unlike that of those who

Second-That a large majority of the questions submitted for official rulings
related to matters that are clearly defined and regulated by direct provielons

Third-That there is too great a tendency among some of our brethren to
strive to evade the mandates of the Constitution, when such manda.tee con·
flict with the special purposes which they wish to accomplish. Frequent instances have occurred during the year in which I have been requested to issue
a speci.I dispensation to permit a Lodge to ignore some s~ction of .the ?onstitution-particula.rly such sections as relate to the physical qualifications of

D.BCISIONB.

The following is a brief summary of such rulings as I have to submit for
your con•ideration :
Any person, eligible to receive the degrees of Maaonry, may present hi1
petition for the degrees to a Lodge other than that Lodge in whose jnriadictioo he resides, by complying with the provisions of Sec. 2, Art. III, Part III
of the Constitution, and upon receiving the consent of a majority oi the
members present at the time that hie request is voted upon.
My purpose in reaffinning this decision is to correct a mieappreheoaion
whi~h seems to be very general among our brethren. They have manifeatly
overlooked the fact tha.t the amendment to Sec. 2, Art. ill, Part III of the
Constitution, which was adopted in 1892, nullifies the decision referred to in
Section 605 of Anderson's Manual relative to waiver of jurisdiction over ap·
plicant~ for the degrees.
An applicant for the degrees in Masonry, who is otherwise wort.by and well
qualified, is not ineligible because of a suspicion of African taint in his blood.
There is no requirement in, Masonic law nor in Ma.sonic tradition for refusing
to receive the petition of a worthy applicant, or for refusing admiuion to a
Masonic Lodge of a Mason of recognized good standing, merely because oi any
particular color of his skin.
Lodge funds cannot be used either to purchase jewels for retiring officers or
to purchase portraits of such officers to ornament the walls of a Lodge-room.
A retiring Master has no right to demand or receive from the funds of hie
Lodge any sum whatever in return for hie services a11 installing officer of hie
eucceBBor in office.

AMENDMENTS TO BY-LAWS.
A large number of amendments to By-Laws have been submitted for my
approval, as will appear in a classified form in the report of the Grand Beere·
tary. These amendments were mainly for the reduction of the fees for the
degrees, and a reduction of the amount of annual dues of the members of the
Lodges. In all cases in which Lodges have proposed to rednce the amount
of the dues, I have required of the Secretary a full statement of the financial
condition of his Lodge. Where the resources of the Lodge justified such a
reduction, I have approved of the same ; but I have refused approval in a
number of instances, for the reason that the reduction proposed would leave
little or nothing for charity after the current expenses of the Lodge were
paid.
AMENDMENTS TO Co1iSTITUTION.
I recommend that the Constitution be amended as follows:
First-The striking out from Subdivision 10 of Section 1, Article IV, Part
II, the·words, " once in every two months ;" and
Second-The repeal of all of Subdivision 4 of Section 2, Article V, Part
IV, relating to the bi-monthly circular from the office of the Grand Secretary,
for the reasons :
.First-That in 1891 the Grand Lodge ordered a discontinuance of the pub·
lication of suspensions for non-payment of dues. Under that ruling, the
Grand Secretary seldom has anything to publish.
Second-It is impossible for the Secretaries of the subordinate Lodl(es to keep
a complete black-book, for the manifest reason that, as the law now stands,
they can know nothing of the suspensions for non-payment of dues, except of
their own Lodges.

THE RITuAL.
Having received notice from the Grand Secretary that the supply of copies
of the printed monitorial work was nearly exhausted, I directed him, when
he ordered a new edition printed, to insert, in the proper place, a full explana·
tion of the hieroglyphical emblems which are referred to in the unwritten
work of the Third Degree.
To those who are familiar· with the unwritten monitorial work as adopted
and promulgated by the Grand Lodge, it is evident that the work, as exem~lified b~ many of the Lodges at the present day, contains numerous expressions which are at variance with the original authorized text. Some of these
variations have been adopted inadvertently, others intentionally.
Zeal on the part of teachers of our ritual is commendable, but a misdirected zeal which. leads an official to assume that, upon his own dictum, he
has a right to amend or modify the phraseology which has been adopted and
promulgated by the Grand Lodge, cannot be condemned in too strong Ian·
guage.
•
If we are to maintain a uniform work in the degrees it seems appropriate
and essential that a permanent committee, or tribunal, should be created
whose members shall be the custodians and censors of the text of the un·
written work.
I therefore recommend that, at as early a date as may be practicable during
the present Communication, a committee be appointed from among those breth·
ren who are familiar with the authorized work and with the rulings of the Grand
Lodge relative thereto, whose duty it shall be to ascertain if the work as now
tau~ht is strictly the work as adopted by this Body. Also to make a careful
compilation or digest of the rulings and decisions of the Grand Lodge relative
to the adoption and promulgation of the unwritten work of our ri.tual, and
that the result of these investigations, together with recommendations as to
the best method of preserving and of teaching this portion of th~ ritual in its

579

economical ma.inte~ce, we will thereby remove from the several Boards of
Relief one of their most perplexing and expensive responsibilities, leaving
only cases of temporary emergency for their charitable considerati on.
Efforts to perfect such a plan on lines of economy, which indicate a reasonable probability of its early realization, must certainly commend themselves to
the favorable considerati on of all who are familiar with the necessary bur·
dens which are now imposed on the members of the several Boards of Relief,
a.s well as of a.ll others who a.re seeking for the most beneficial and economical methods of dispensing charity.
Such a. plan will find its. realization in the completion and endowmen t of
the Widows' a.nd Orphans' Home. The sum of $110,000, which has lieretOfore
been paid from the funds of this (irand Lodge for charity, would have endowed
such a. home with a. munificent hand. I do not question the wisdom nor the
beneficence of these donations in the past, but rather would urge upon you
to wisely consider and carefully determine as to how we shall provide for the
needy in the future.
·
This Grand Lodge is now possessed of a location for such a home. It is
free from debt. It ha.s a broad acreage, with enough tillable land for the
requiremen ts of the home. The climate is equable and healthful. The location of the administra tion building is sightly and commanding. It is of easy
access by rail. During the present year the Trustees have acquired a.n ample
water supply for domestic purposes. Pipes have been laid which conduct the
water to the premises. Roads have been built, the grounds ha.ve been graded,
a.nd the foundation s of the administra tion building are now in process of con·
struction. To-morrow the comer-ston e will be la.id by the Grand Lodge with
the usual formalities of the Craft. Tbs uncomplet ed structure will thenceforward stand as a. mute yet eloquent appeal to the charitable impulses of
every true Mason throughou t the jurisdictio n of California., until the last nail
is drfren in the structure, and until the hospitable doors of the home are
thrown open to offer a. gratefUl welcome to those who !I.re otherwise homeless
and a.re bereft of the comforts and necessities of life.
I present the foregoing propositions for your considerati on, with the confi.
dent hope a.nd expectation tha.t there may be no longer anv question as to the
wisdom and importance of urging this beneficent charity-th e Masonic
Widows' and Orphans' Home-to a speedy a.nd snccessfUl completion.
CONCLUSION.

In the foregoing statements and recommendations, I submit the official

acts of my administra tion to your impartial consideration. In the discharge
of my official duties it has been my purpose to be charitir.ble, imparti&l. a.nd
just ; to render such decisions and rulings as a.re consistent with the intent as
well as with the text of the law ; to advocate an adherence to the text of the
unwritten monitorial work a.s originally adopted and promUlgated by the
Grand Lodge, and to sanction only a consistent obedience to the requiremen ts
of the Constitutio n and Regulation s.
In retiring from office, at the close, of the proceedings of the present Communication , I shall do so with the consciousness of having exerted my best

The undersigned respectfully submits his sixth Annual Report, giving in
detail the transactions of his office since the la.st Annual Communication, and
presenting all such matters appertaining to that office as may reqnire action
by this Grand Body, or may, in any way, be of interest to its officers and
members.
As soon a.a possible after the close of the la.st Annual Communication, two
thousand two hundred and fifty copies of the proceedings thereof-being the
increased number ordered last year-were printed and distributed, or reserved
for future binding, in the customary manner, viz.: one copy to ea.ch of the
present Grand Officers ; one copy to each of the elective Pa.st Grand Officers ;
four copies to each of the Grand Bodies, American and Foreign, with which we
are in correspondence ; four copies to each of the Lodges of our juriBdiction ;
and six hundred copies reserved for future binding, to form Vol. XXII of our
proceedings.
The proceedings of all the Grand Lodges of the United States and British
America for the year since la.st report, have been received and placed in the
hands of the Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence, as have also
those of New South Wales, England, South Australia, Scotland and Victoria.
