At the last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, the charter of
Fall River Lodge, No. 270, at Glenburn, Shasta. County, was revoked, and
Bro. WILLIAM C. SELVESTF.R, late Secretary thereof, was authorized to settle
up its a.lfa.irs. Bro. SELVESTER has managed to pay the debts of the Lodge
with the amount realized from its aesets, presenting a clean balance sheet, but
nothing more. So the affairs of that extinct Lodge may be considered as
finally settled.
At date of last report there were two hundred a.nd sixty-one Lodges borne
upon the roll of the Grand Lodge, with a. membership of seventeen thousand
four hundred a.nd thirty-one. Since that time two dispensations to form new
Lodges have been granted. One Lodge (Fall River, No. 270,) has had itll
charter revoked, which leaves a net gain of one Lodge, and added to above

Of the proposed amendments to the By-Laws of Lodges which have been
received during the year, the approval of the Grand Master in forty cases
have been filed in this office. Of these, two, being from Lodges Nos. 57 and
124, proposed changes in the time for stated meeting. Two, being from Lodges
Nos. 143 and 158, proposed to increase the monthly dues. Six, being from
Lodges Nos. 57, 161, 206, 229, 308 a.nd 324, proposed to reduce those dues.
One, being from Lodge No. 216, proposed to increase the affiliation fee. Two
being from Lodges Nos. 127 and 284, proposed an affiliation fee where hereto'.
fore none had existed. One, being from Lodge No. 9, proposed changing powers of Charity Committee. One, being from Lodge No. 30, proposed to rescind the assessment of one dollar upon the death of a member; and twenty.
five, being from Lodges Noe. 38, 50, 91, 93, 95, 114, 132, 141, 146, 166, 175,
179, 193, 205, 206, 235, 240, 245, 249, 258, 284, 285, 288, 291, 297 and 321,
proposed to reduce the fee for the deirees.
Proposed amendments to the By-Laws, relative to the reduction of dues of
members, from Lodges Nos. 12, 134, 249 and 292, were disapproved by the
Grand Master, for the reason that the rate of dues proposed was thought to
be too low for the Lodges to maintain a healthy and useful existence.
The approval of the Grand Master being but a temporary authorization
the foregoing amendments, as required by our laws, have been placed in th;
hands of the Chairman of the Committee on By-Laws of Lodges, and will be
submitted to the Grand Lodge for final action, as have the books of By-Laws
of the two Lodges now working under dispensation.

1896.J

Grand· Lodge of (Jalifornia.

590

presented. from the R. '. W. '. Bro. WILLIAM RoNALDBON, Grand Secretary of
the Grand Lodge of New Zealand, dated at Christchurch on the twenty-fifth
day of March, 1891, praying for recognition from our Grand Lodge and an
exchange of Representative s. At that time the request was denied, it not
appearing that recognition had been granted by either of the Grand Lodges
under whom the constituent Lodges of New Zealand had heretofore held
obedience. From documents received at this office it appears that the Grand
Lodge of England grantci recognition to the Grand Lodge of New Zealand,
by an almost unanimous vote, at a Special Communication called for that
purpose on the twenty-ninth day of July last, and the matter of our recognition of that Grand Body has again been submitjed to the Committee.
At the last Annual Communication a like request was presented from the
United Grand Lodge of Victoria, The Committee on Juriapmdence, to whom
the matter was referred, reported, in part, as follows :It has been the settled policy of this Grand Lodge in reference to new
Grand Lodges to ascertain what was the condition of Masonry in the .territory
over which the new Grand Lodg~ claims jurisdiction ; how many Lodges there
were ther~ and under what obedience they held; how many of them joined in
the establishment of the new Grand Lodge, and, if less than all joined, under
what obedie;11ce those not joining hold ; whether the new Grand Lodge has
been recogmzed by the Grand Lodges by which its constituents were originally chartered; what proceedings were had and taken at the Convention
looking to its organization, and what claim of jurisdiction it makes, and also
a copy of its Constitution. In regard to these matters we have no information.
We therefore recommend that the Grand Secretary be requested to ask
that Grand Lodge to furnish us with the necessary information as above set
forth. With the hope that that information will be furnished, we recommend
that no further action be taken at this time.
A copy of th.e above report and recommendation was mailed to V. •• W. '.
Bro. JOHN BRAIM, Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Victoria, on the
twenty-fourth day of December last, and, although all the information desired
by the committee has not come to hand, from a programme of the proceedings
at the installation of the Grand Officers ol that Grand Body held at Melbourne on the fonrth day of May last, it appears that Represe~tatives have
been exchanged with England, Scotland and Ireland, all of the Grand Lodges
of the Coloriies and British America, and also by thirty.six of the Grand
Lodges of the United :States of America. The request for recognition and an
exchange of Representative s has again been referred to the Committee.
The matter of the "Washington Memorial Observances," proposed to be
held at Mount Vernon on the fourtl)enth day of December, 1899, is still in
the hands of the committee as unfinished business.

ProceedingB of the

[Oct. 13,

Bro. OHABLBS PARSHALL OVERTON, Ohairman of the Masonic Board
of Relief of the Oity of San Francisco, presented the following :To the M.'. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia:In view of the fact that the matter of the finances of this Board was
brought to the attention of the Lodges of this Sta.te during the past year, it
would seem proper at this time that some report be made in addition to the
'
·
customary account of receipt& and expenditures.
Moreover, our experiences have suggested the advisability of certain changes,
and have raised certain questions which it would seem in order to submit to
this Grand Lodge for ita determination.
From the circular letter sent to a.ll the Lodges throughou~ the State, under
date of June 12th last, asking aid from the Grand Lodge's funds, the financial
straits in which thi9 Board has found itself are well known. The responses to
our letter were prompt and courteous, and, in nearly every single instance,
favorable; but a technical objection to the legality of advancing to us any part
of the funds of the Grand Lodge during the receBB of the same, prevented the
plan from being carried out, and it was not deemed expedient to call a special
session of the Grand Lodge solely for this purpose.
However, the investigations made. at that time by the Grand Master and
the Finance Committee, satisfied them a.a to the justice as well a.a to the necessities of our case, and they suggested our borrowing the fundll needed for the
continua.nee of our work, they promising to recommend the repayment by this
Grand Lodge of such loans as we might be able to secure.
At a time when we were practically without funds for the continuance of
our work, the firm of Halsted & Co., to whom this Board is already indebted
for many substantial favor11, tendered to us, without solicitation, the sum of
five hundred doliare as a loan, without interest, to be repaid out of our first
available appropriation. It is need.Iese to e&f this offer was promptly accepted
and an appeal was then made to the city Lodges for such further amount& as
were necessary. The prompt and generous responses of these Lodges has
furnished us with eight hundred dollars additional, enabling us to continue
without interruption the dispensing of necessary charities and the burial of
the dead, and we would Tespectfully ask that the appropriation to be given us
at this time be ma.de sufficient to cover the a.mount of our indebtedness.
As one of the reeulta of our experiences during the past year, it appears to
ue that a change in the manner of apportioning the appropriation from the
Grand Lodge should be ma.de, in view of the fact that the personnel of this
Board changes on the first of January of each year, while the appropriation ie
ma.de available in October, a.nd it would seem more desirable and more just
that e&eh Boa.rd of Relief receive int&et from the Grand Lodge the appropriation for the year in which it conducts its affairs.
·To inaugurate this system, which I am confident will be highly ad van·
tageous, it will be necessary at this time to arrange for appropriations to cover
a period of fifteen months, i. e., from October first of this year until the end of
1897, by giving this Board sufficient to last it until the close of its term, and
making a separate appropriation which shall be available for the Boa.rd of

1896.]

Grand Lodge of OaUfrwnia.

603

1897, and thereafter ma.king the appropriation available for each calendar or
·
Board year.
I would, therefore, respectfully recommend that at this time an appropria
tion be made sufficient to cover the indebtedneBB of the present Board and ~
.carry it until the first of January, and that a separate appropriation be ma.de
for the Board of 1897, the same to become available when the Board of 1897
assumes office, and that the appropriations hereafter be made available at the
beginning of e&eh Board year, to wit, in the first part of January.
After ma.king careful calculations, we now ask for thirteen hundred dollars
for the repayment of amounts borrowed, and one thousand dollars for use
during the remainder of our term; and that the Grand Lodge make such an
approp~iation for. t~e use of the Board of 1897 as it may deem right and proper.
While recogmzmg fully the thrift and enterprising nature of the Scotch
~e~pl~, ~et ~or experience with applicants claiming membership under Scottish
Jnr1sd1ct1on is such as to convince us, as well as other Boards of Relief, that a
grea~ laxity exists, a~ least in some of the seaports of Scotland, regarding the
quality of the material from which Masons are made. It appears to be the
custom to take in sailors, cooks and stewards of vessels lying in the port for
no reason that we can imagine except to get the small initiation fee; and we
are repeatedly beset by applications from negro stewards and cooks who are
without eufllcie.nt in~elligence to comprehend any of the principles of 'Masonry,
except that wh'.ch giv011 them pecuniary aid; and we respectfully recommend
th~t the Co~m1ttee on Correspondence of this Grand Lodge get such facts in
this connect10n as. can be obtai.ued from our Boards of Relief, and enter into
correspondence with the Grand Lodge of Scotland respecting the quality of
Masons which a few of thf'ir Lodges launch upon the Fraternity at large.
The quest.ion of ~ranting relief to Masons out of standing is one th 11t has
been exhaustively discuBBed by this Board without reaching a conclusion, and
we would respectfully ask a ruling by this Grand Lodge. Of course we understand that where the applicant has wi!Uully or carelessly allowed himself to
lapse from standing and makes application only when hie necessities impel him
to do so, that such a case should meet with no consideration · but the latest
instance coming under our notice is one that has caused a diviei~n of sentiment
among the members of this Board. It is that of a man who came to California
from an Eastern city, bringing with him considerable monev which he invested
and lost in business here. He was unable to keep up hi~· dues in hie home
Lo~e and. too proud to acknowledge his condition, hoping some time later to
r~tneve _hi~ fortun~s and again place himself in standing. Long-continued
s10kness ID the family exhausted his remaining means. Knowing himself to
be out of standing he would not apply to those who had been hie brethren
pr~fe.rring, as he himself eaid, to star\·e. But his wife, threatened with
eV1ct1on from their home and driven to desperation by the straits in which
they found themselves, and by the hnnger of five little children, and believing
her hu~band to be a Mason, without his knowledge has applied to this Board
for a.ss1sta.uce. By a telegram we learn that the husband has not been in
standing in his Lodge for two years. For the g11idance of this nnd succeeding
Boards, we respectfully a.sk a ruling by the Grand Lodge on this case.

Which was ordersd to be referred to the Oommittee on Finance.

ProceedingB of the

At the meeting of the Board held August 2d, 1896, the financial condition
of the Board being under oonsideration, Bro. J. c. CUNNINGHAM, of Southern
California Lodge, volunteered the Board a loan of $200, which enabled us to
continue our relief work, although we have been forced to refuse in many
cases where we think that relief should have been extended.
We would also present the following table, compiled from our reports to
the Grand Lodge during the past four years, as showing the increased de·
mands upon the Board, due, largely, to the increase in population : -

In the year 1894 we made a loan of $400. In 1895 we were permitted to
overdraw to the amount of $125.65, as reported to the Grand Lodge that year.
This year, with a loan of $200, our b·a lance stands at $110.28, making our total
indebtedness at this date $310.28, a.a above reported.
We would also note that in the years above referred to the assessments
upon the Lodge members had been as high as twelve cents per mouth per
member. This year we have rigidly adhered to the amount recommended by
the Grand Lodge.
We are pleased to report that the claim of this Board against Atlanta
Lodge, No. 59, State of Georgia, has been paid in full, to the satisfaction of
all parties interested.

worthy case ha.a failed to receive at lea.et some aid from us, we a.re yet
conscious of having been compelled in many instances to bestow charity with
too scanty a hand, owing to lack of funds. It was the judgment of our
Board at its last meeting that at the coming session of the Grand Lodge at
least $60() should be appropriated for our use during the corning year.
All which is respectfully submitted.
EDWARD H. HART, Chairman.

The Board has under its care the widow of M. Phelps, formerly of Hiram
Lodge, No. 43, and have ·paid for the relief of herself and family $99.15, included in above account, the which, the Board is informed, Hiram Lodge is
not in condition to repay, and the family will continue a charge, to some extent at least, upon this Board.
The item of $120 in last above table was for the care of a brother of the
jurisdiction of Nebraska, whose Lodge refuses to pay the bills which were
necessarily incurred by this Board, and must be paid by it.
Demands have been increased during the past year over the years preceding,
owing to an influx of strangers seeking employme nt on pv.blic enterprises .
We have been as careful as possible to avoid unworthy claims upon our funds,
and by a small expi;nse incurred in telegraphin g have saved some money and
avoided imposition. We do not think that any application of a worthy
brother has been neglected.
Respectful ly submitted.
A. N. DAVIDSON, Chairman.
JAMES H. LINDSLY, Secretary.

MORNING SESSION,

l

Wednesday, October 14th, A. L. 5896. )

The Grand Lodge was called on at nine o'clock, the Grand Master
presiding.
The Grand Master briefly announced that the business of the day
would be the laying of the corner-stone of the Masonic Widows' and
Orphans' Home at Decoto.
The Grand Lodge was then formed in the customary manner, and
proceeded to the street to follow the other Masonic Bodies in the
march to the Oakland ferry.

At the site a platform had been erected on a lev.il with and sur·
rounding the corner-stone to be laid, sufficiently large to accom·
modate the Grand Officers of the Grand Lodge, the various officebearers of that Body whose duties were connected therewith, the
Masonic choir, and the musicians necessary for the occasion.
The Grand Master was seated in front of the centre of the platform,
immediately accompanied by the Grand Officers and office-bearers of
the Grand Lodge.
Upon a table before him, properly draped, were placed by their
several bearers the Holy Writings, the Book of Constitutions, the
Golden Vessel containing Corn, the two Silver Vessels oontaining
Wine and Oil, the Three Large Lights, the five Orders of Architecture,
the working tools of the Principal Architect, and the Casket containing the deposits to be placed beneath the corner-stone.

lasting monument of the practical charity of the Craft. It will convince the

The Junior Grand Warden then p,oured the Oil upon the stone,

Thrice happy· is he whose footsteps led him this day to this favored
spot in the sunny Alameda hills. Thrice happy he who, with us, may witness
this sacred consumm11otion of hopes long deferred, of prayers long nnanswere<if
of wishes long unrealized. We stand on the hilltops o'erlooking our domain,
every foot of which speaks of Faith, Hope and Charity. We stand at the
closed groove, in which is sunk the keystone, noble symbol of patient faith
kept alive by the love of our brethren. We stand aloft, gazing on the rich
valleys of this dear, dear land; we watch the silver lines of the waters beyond;
we watch these kindly faces, beaming wit h pleasure at the fulfillment of this
holy task, and, surely, our fi rst thought is- God is good ; the Master who
steels the a.rm for the sowing time permits us to stand on the threshing floor
and sing our song of praise !
Brethren, this is a. sacred hour. W ell may we tarry to learn its lessons.
T£ere are few such periods in our busy lives. Usually we grapple with
problems that often remain unanswered until we have gone our last journey.
We hanker after power, riches, glory ; we illustrate, in the mighty weakness
of onr reputed strength, the unhallowed selfishneBB of our ambitions and desires. Life is a battlefield strewn with the corpses of unsatisfied ambition,
of wrecked hopes, of defeated schemes ; and in our journey to the beyond we
oft meet the cripples, whose maimed bodies tell the woeful tales of disaster to
the one, conquest to the other. We live to conquer; to reach the goal in the .
mighty race for power and fame; to set our foot on the neck of the vanquished,
This we call success, forgetting that there is a measure with which all are
measured-a. scythe that mows the ranks of men and knows not the difference
between the conqueror and the vanquished. Death is the victor. SucceBB is
but the glimmer of a. moment, a bright presence lighting up our little world
but for a. brief day. We pass on, to make room for others. We descend
into the ocean of oblivion; its waters engulf us, a.nd on the shore stand new
generations, awaiting, wonderingly, th'e time whon they, too, shall follow.
What remains? Faith remains, hope a.bides, a.nd charity, also-and the greatest of these is charity?
Do not think, brethren, that it is my intention to convert this moment of
success into one of extreme melancholy. We a.re indeed happy that our enterprise hath prospered. We are moved to give thanks and praise to all who
have contributed to this lasting monument of Masonry, and thereby havo

eayingMay the blessing of heaven descend upon this a.nd a.11. good works ; ~d
ma.y our loved Fraternity long exist to pour ~orth the Oil of Joy upon t e
hearts of the widowed, the fatherless a.nd the distressed.

1896.]

Grand Lodge of California.

631

of the democracy of spirits levels, within Masonry, all classes and conditions.
All are alike before the Supreme-the Master and the Apprentice, he who sits
in the flood of Oriental light and he who gropes in darkness, he who wields
the scepter and he who obeys orders, he who commands and he who toils.
Banded and linked together by the power of that leveling principle, duty receives a different interpretation, There may be a palace for the one and a
hovel for the other; but the denizen of the palace mUJ1t know the fate of him
who dwells in the poor ma.n's hut ; they are responsible to one another, for
Ood has made them alike; they share a common destiny; both live, and both
suffer, and both shall die, and both shall live again. Brethren, we are respon
sible to one another, and unless that link of responsibility holds us together,
Masonry is not worth a thought. Rich and poor, learned and unlearned,
strong and weak, high and low, these are the nomenclatures of life's battles,
representing the victor aud the conquered, the sound in body and the maimed;
we know them not in Masonry; we are a democracy, standing before the
Supreme Grand Master, girt with but one armament, uniform to all, the armament of virtue, of character and of good deeds ! That is our creed. He who
hath a better to offer let him step forward and improve the ideal, which is the
design of God himself. And now, since we a.re thus constituted, with a ,firm
belief in the justice of equality, we render no humiliating service to the
families of our brethren who have departed on their la.st journey-we do but
honor ourselves, we do but justice to ourselves, when we provide this shelter
for them. Charity is kind, but the word charity is not so Ma.sonic as the
word justice l We do justice to our orphans, to our widows, when we remove
them into surrouadings where they may witness the. strength of our teachings ;
it is jUJ1tice to give them shelter, justice to clothe them, justice to educate,
justice to love them ! If I could, I would remove the word charity from our
vocabulary. Faith, Hope and Justice would suit me better . .Justice interprets
the rela.tion.s of man to man according to the design of law ; it imposes
righteous duty, whereas in these modern times the word charity is misconstrued as intending to place the poor and forlorn in the capacity of recipients.who with shamed face give thanks for the munificence that enables them to
live. That is not charity-it is rank injustice. Our charity, our justice, is
not only kind, but it offers to the poor our gratitude for that we are enabled
to demonstrate the strength of our teachings. Our charity, our jUJ1tice, is of
that character that illustrates that all we have is not ours, that all we know
is not for ourselves, that all we a.re able to accomplish is not for our own glory.
In our Masonic democracy, at least a part of our possessions actually belongs
to our brethren, and that is, or should be, the charity without which there is.
neither faith nor hope ! For such charity we need no thanks, for it is the
tithe of the Mason to a God whom he thanks for all his goodness and mercy !
In this spirit, brethren, let us labor on, illustrating to the world the
glorious fact that Masonry weakens and finally eradicates the selfishness of
human nature. We stand on the threshing floor; but the harvest is not yet
complete. .Much remains to be done; much faithful toil is yet to be expended. But the goal is in sight - the beginning of the end has approached.
In our imagination the walls of this glorious monument are raised; in our

I

632

Proceedings of the

'(Oct. 14,

hearts are already resounding the benedictions that here shall fall from praying lips. From whose lips ? From those homeless ones who here shall
find a home ; from those bereaved ones who here shall find their friends ;
-from those fatherless children who here shall recover their parents and
protectors. Ah, brethren, may God be thanked for the impulse that brings
such labor to fruition; may the Master of us all be praised for the seed
planted in these sunny hills ! For the work is unselfish, it is God's work.
Nothing can be compared to such evidence of loving kindness. Men erect
monuments to commemorate or perpetuate various phases of nsefnlness.
Here stands a university, there a chapel, over yonder the arts claim their
asylum and science has her temple. But everywhere man, more or less,
strives for himself and to some degree perpetuates the warfare of mankind
against itself. Here a.lone,-here alone none but the Creator can profit ! Here
alone-here a.lone, brethren, the suspicion of selfishness fades before the
bright star of hope and faith that rises upon these hills. Here the tenderest
sentiments of humanity shall find rich illustration, and the atmosphere shall
not be tainted with the impure motive of every one for himself. Here shall
rise a temple of humanity, and every Mason a priest therein; here shall rise
an altar of love, and its censers swung by grateful women and happy children,
from whose lives we shall have removed the bitterness that prevented them
from seeing the good in man which comes from God. Think yon the labor
is worthy of the illustrious order which claims our allegiance? If so, continue to strengthen our hands. Yon must find the means to prosecute this
great work to its consummation. Your intelligent legislation must devise
permanent provision for the Home to be erected here. Your personal contribution, in money, is needed and desired. For love is a great, good thing;
but starving love, helpless love, motiveless love is little more than a name,
little more than a fancy, which hath a trick of self-deception and in the end
means nothing whatever. Our charity and lov_e are, must be, evidenced in
the material support we shall give this institution. Now that we have begun
in earnest, the consummation rests with you ; on yon the obligation to permit
the workmen no rest until, like the glorious temple of old, it shall rise in
majesty, a lasting monument to the Masonry of California. Brethren, heed
this ad vice. The Ma.son's love is substantial; not theoretical ; his charity is
continuous·, not sporadic ; his affections are tireless, for beneath them all rests,
as a strong and safe basis, his sense of duty that tells him that this work is
right-and that right must live and prosper and succeed.
The consecration of this comer-stone, brethren, emphasizes once more
the Mason's duty to the State and to the Fraternity which honors him
by elevating him to its service. To the State first, not last, for the
Mason's loyalty to the dictates of honor and manhood is but an illustration of that allegiance he owes to his country. Our beloved whQ
here shall find their abiding place will be taught that the Mason's greatest honor consists in serving God and. his country. To make men good
Masons, they must be taught to become good citizens. That humanity that
knows no class nor condition, that sense of equality that looks beneath the artificial divisions of mankind, that cosmopolitanism that is identical with

1896.J

..

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

633

Masonry, these also will be taught to the flock, who from this hallowed spot
may graduate themselves to become leaders of men. Therefore, brethren, our
duty first to California, mother of us all ! Our duty to the noble State, redeemed from Craft ignoble, whose fostering hand raises the manhood of our
children ! Our love to the glorioli.s, sun-kissed land, the cradle of honorable
enterprises and of the Fraternity that makes all men kindred indeed ! Long
may she prevail, the noble mother, proudest and fairest among her sisters,
who compose the holy band of priestesse8 in the temple of liberty, equality
and Fraternity! Beneath the hallowed pennant of the bear, and the greater
flag of America's united sovereignties, may this Ma.sonic enterprise come to
glorious fruition, aud this comer-stone prove as firm as the eternal rocks
'gainst which the storm-laden waves of adversity dash in vain! And now,
all hail to the Grand Lodge of California, mother of noble institutions, protectress of honorable enterprises, sacred teacher of our Masonic manhood!
All hail to the venerable exponent of Masonry in California, beneath whose
protecting hand we are penmtted to consecrate this pile to humanity! In it
the traditions of Masonry live again. Called into life in the days of gold, its
wisdom sought permanence 'midst the coming and going of gold-loving wayfarers, and secured a home for Masonic teachings on the Western shore; its
strength supported its young apprentices until they become Masters, whom
California did and does delight to honor ; and its beauty attracted the noble
youth, whom it taught the grand lessons of ·speculative Masonry. And these
lessons, are they really the esoteric knowledge the world may not know? Two
words constitute both its ritual and its philosophy. To the Mason the Delphic
oracle contained no mystery. Know thyself; That is the sum of our teach-·
ings. Knowing is acting, doing. Therefore we give honor to our Fraternity,
our Grand Lodge, the venerable and worshipful brethren who constitute its
leaders and teachers, for that we are permitted, under Heaven's blessing, to
illustrate our self-knowledge by an act of unselfishness that shall redound not
to our glory, but to the glor.y of Him whom Masons worship-the Supreme
Architect, to whose divine care we commit the designs of our architects, the
labor of our crafts, and the success of this noble enterprise.
Most Worshipful Grand Master, I thank you.

The Report on Correspondence is again by the veteran correspondent and Paet
Grand Master, PALMER J. PILLANB, who reviews fifty-six Grand Bodies or Masonic
Legislatures ; gives us an abstract of their doings with his opinions upon the quality
of their work. Bro. PILLANB makes favorable report of the general condition of
the Fraternity throughout the world; he reports a healthy increase of membership
in the records of nearly .all of the juriedictiollll, with a tendency to an improved
condition in the matter of non-affiliation. He sees, however, in the distance, a
cloud of threatening import that may lead to a moat serious disturbance in this
great Fraternity. We quote bis words and commend them as worthy the serious
consideration of those brethren who would "propagate the knowledge of the
Art," by other than the authorized and warranted method, i. e.-"from mouth to
ear:"There has, however, oome to the front a question which we, with some others,
deem of vital importance to the welfare of the Order. The Grand _L odge of
MaBBachueetts, venerable though she be, after great labor in perfecting her rituals,
for the preservation of "m1iformity of work" within her jurisdiction, bas re<luced
the same to paper in cipher. The result was to have been anticipated. There are
now very many copies of this authorized work. in and around Bo:iton, the original
having been unwarrantably ueed for 11;ain. After in •estigation the two brethren implicated w11re ~xpelled. and thii use of any cipher made a Masonic offense. \Vould
1t not, however, have been infinitely better to have locked the stable before the
horse was stolen? These copies of the ritual are still in existence, and thPy contain what had been deolared by Grand Lodge to be the true and proper work. But
whence does this or any other Grand Lodge derive its power to reduce the ritual
to cipher? is a question which should recur to every Mason, even the youngest E.
A., though still in the N. E. corner.
We indeed have always thought that we were bound under nocircumstance.s to
write out the work, lest by any accident in so doing we discover it to others. At
least we were surely so taught at the very threshold of Masonry. This injunction
was oftentimes reiterated io the several degrees we took, lest we should be guilty,
even inadvertently, of this heinous offence. But now we see GrR.nd Lodges authorizi••g this thing. Whence is this power of a Grand Lodge derived? Is it claimed
for these bodies that they have the consciences of the brethren within their keeving?
Can they absolve the brethren? If so, whence their power? We are, unfortunately
perhaps, of those who deny such powel'!I to Grand Lodges.. We thinkthe•e bodies
should themselves do nothing euhversive of the ancient requirements of Masonry,
while they at the same time demand this of their subordinates.
Secrecy and circumspection was our first and fundamental instruction, and
frequ•ntly were we reminded of them, so that we became to esteem them, more·
particularly secrecy, as fundamental landmarks of the Order. b secrecy not?
'£hen who baa the power to do anything that might by any poBBibility, and under
any circumstances, enable others to know any portion of the esoteric work? "It
is not in the power of any man or body of men to make innovations in Masonry."
But is not this putting this arcana of Masonry within the reach of the profane an
innovation in the bo11y of Masonry!
We specially direct the attention of bretbreu who read this introduction to the
review of Maosachusett.a, We~t Virginia, Oregon anti Mississippi, that they may
see for themselves the enormity of the act. We see it stated that the Grand
Mester of Kentucky recogni:iles the right of a Grand Lodge to enact any laws
which it may deem proper, on the score of its supreme sovereiJ1,'Dty. But if this is
so, then France had the right to strike out the pr11n>quieite of a belief in Deity,
nor had she committed a very much -graver Masonic offence than this. Indeed, no
Grand Lodge is of such absolute independence as to alter or change the ancient

stituent Lodges were represented, six Past Grand Masters were present to impress
upon the brethren "the dignity and high importance of MBBonry," and fifteen

The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with prayer bv the Grand
Chaplain and music by the choir.
After appointing the standing committees the Grand Master delivered his Annual Address. He returned thanks to the Supreme Being for Hie care and protection, and invoked His continued blessings upon their labors. He voiced for all
their gratitude that their official circle had been spared, although ten good and true
brethren had been taken to join the great majority. After a tribute to their memories he advised the setting apart of mourning pages devoted to the record of their'
lives as men and as Masons.
The Grand Master was enabled to report the visitation by him of every one of
the eleven Lodges on his Grand Lodge roll. Thie might not seem a task of unusual merit in many jurisdictions, but in Arizona it means very many hundreds of
miles of weary travel through a country liberally sprinkled with cowaus and ruffians. He says the prosperity of the Lodges keep pace with that of the Territory;
no complaints of financial distress are heard, although a small loss in membership
is reported.
The official transactions of hie office were very light. No decisions of importance were rendered, although the Grand Master seems to have observed a close
supervision over the Masonic doings of hie eleven Lodges, numbering a total of
503 Master Masone.
The Grand Secretary reports the receipt of the following circular, which we
quote here, as the subject is one of deserving interest to Masons individually and
collectively :-·
To all Grand Lodges of Free and Accepted Masons, Grand Chapters of Royal
Arch Masons, Grand Councils of Royal and Select MasterR, and Grand Commanderies of Knights Templar in the United States and Provinces of British
North America:
The undersigned, in behalf of their confreres of the Guild and the Grand
Bodies that, in this behalf, they serve and represent, ask not merely your approval,
but your material aid to secure a complete Masonic library for each juri!ld.iction,
which shall include full sets of printed annual proceedings of all corresponding
jurisdicti .. ns.
The Grand Secretaries and Grand Recorders, with some assistance-most of
which can be secured by volunteers-will undertake the work of supplying a list
of their wants and a catalogue of duplicates on hand available for exchanges. If
the work is systematically and thoroughly done by some central committee, it is believed that the first aim-the compilation of full sets for our Grand Bodies-can
aoon be accomplished, and much done toward building up Masonic libraries in all
jurisdictions.
Where reprints are needed, we believe in most jurisdictions the work will be
undertaken at home, especially when assurance is given that copies will be subscribed for to cover the cost. While in some cases a number of years must be
covered by a reprint, yet the jl'l'eatest part of the work will be accomplished by
the exchange of existing material-transferri ng it from places where it is going to
waste to others where it will be of applicable value.
.
With the central clearing house in charge of an efficient officer, with li•ts of
wants and duplica.tes before him, the work of transfer <Jan he euily and speedily
accomplished. It would be right that each jurisdiction undertake to bear the expense of sending by mail or express, which e•·er would be cheapP.r, that which it
receives. For a short time, while the heaviest of the work is being done, a moderate compensation should be paid to one devoting bis entire time to the work, and
money would he needed for postage, printing, etc. We propose that each Grand
Body be asked to contribute five dul/a?'B towards the general expense of such organization, and that other permanent Masonic Library Associations be admitted to

In his Address, the Grand Master reminded the brethren of the rapid flight
of time; of those with them one year ago who had since obeyed the summons
and closed their labors on earth. His view of the condition of the Fraternity
was not encouraging. He said a state of apathy existed, and a lack of interest
was apparent throughout the jurisdiction; the ballot box was not guarded as in the
olden time; too many of their members were Masons in name only, and he appeal.
ingly says : " My brethren, these things ought not to be. We must arouse from
our apathy ; guard well our outer door, and return to the Ancient Landmarks
with full purpose of heart, or, failing in this, the disastrous consequences are not
only apparent, but are appallingly imminent. •Ichabod' will be inscribed on our
altars and Freemasonry will become but as a sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal."
·

He had granted three dispensations for the formation of new Lodges, and arrested the charters of three Lodges for cause.
Of decisions, the Grand Master reported several which are not of Masonic in·
terest, unless maybe to set forth the minimum of Masonic intelligence needed to
sustain a Lodge of Masons in Arkansa!MQuestion. A party residing within the jurisdiction of Lodge A ~titioned
Lodge B for initiation aad was duly elected, but failed to appear for mitiation.
Be afterwards petitioned Lodge C, and, on application to Longe A, that Lodge
waived its jurisdiction in favor of Lodge C, which latter Lodge also elected the
canrlidate, but, failing to hold a meeting at the time designated for that purpose,
the candidate was not initiated, and afterwards petitioned Lodge A for initiation
and was elected. Of which of these three Lodges is the candidate the material?
Question. A brother charged with drunkenness appeared for trial, and by his
counsel demurred to the charges, because no committee bad been appointed to wait
upon and admonish him. 'l'he Worshipful Master &ustained the demurrer and disniissed the charges. Did the Worshipful Master do right?
Quat·ion. Does the fact that a Master Mason who is not in goorl. standing in
his Lodge exclude his daughter's chastity from Masonic protection, the father be·
ing an expelled Mason?
Anawer. It does not. While expulsion deprives a brother of all his rights and
privileges as a Master Mason, it does not, therefore, absolve the brethren from
their obligation, and the brother who violates the chastity of an expelled brother's
daughter, knowing her to be such, is guilty of a violation of his obligation, and
upon proper proof of such offense, should be expelled from his Lodge.
The last decision was not concurred in by the Grand Lodge, During the opening ceremonies the Grand Master was informed of the death of R. '. W. ·• Bro.
JASPER M. PlNNEI.L, Senior Grand Warden, which sad. event occurred at his home
in De Witt the preceding night.
R. ·• W. ·. FAY HDlPBT.BAD, Grand Secretary, reported the names of the emi·
nent dead of sister jurisdictions. Among others, the most eminent brethren
HICKMAN of Montana, GoDFBEY of Ohio, CHADWICK of Oregon, FRIZZELL of Ten·
neesee, and ISAACS of Virginia.
"Death, so called, is a thin1t which make men weep,
And yet a third of life is p11Rsed in aleep.''
The receipts of Grand Lodge for the year were $8,801.20; Grand Lodge ex•
pensea (including salary of Grand Secretary, $1000) 82,651.85.
The chief object of interest with the brethren of Arkansaa is the Masonic
Temple, and they are struggling bravely to place it upon a self-supporting plane.
'rhe amount of $3,!iOO paid for interest was a heavy weight upon the resources of
the past year, but with the steady strong pull they will accomplish it.

'fhere is one subject further to which your attention is called in considering
the development of Freamasonry-a subject which has been most deeply impress~d
upon my mind in the discharge of my official duties as President of the Masomc
Charity foundation. I refer to the relations of the. mothers, . wives, widows,
sisters and daughters of Free Masons to the Craft. It is popular ID some quarters
to decry the formation of societies by them having any reference to the Craft. No
Mason will deny that by his most solemn obligations they stand in special relation
to him and are entitled to his assistance and protection.
It follows that it would be wise that sure proof should be proyided by which
they may with certainty be able to claim and prove themselves entitled to such assistance and protection. The Craft has made no such provision. . The e'.'igencies
of the early days did not require it. Masone were few and their relations well
known. Now all this is changed.

"It is a good rule in rell'ard to everything to inquire, ascertain and possess
some degree of knowledge before we adjudge a case. Our institution originally
was probably founded by males who were operative mechanics, in whose rnAChanical pu~uite females were physically and naturally unfitted to take part. Hence,
and not on account of mental endowment, physical prerequisites, free birth,
mental or moral qualifications, females were excluded. But shall we say that the
Free Masone Lodge is an unfit place on any other account than that for female
morale, female purity or female piety? ·Never. The ancients _Provided for .t~eir
parti~ipation in all the benefits of the institution but those particularly pertammg
to membership.
"And they bound every member of it to award on proper demand to all worthy
Masonic mothers, sisters, daughters, wives and widows peculiar immunities and
benefits, but they fail to provide them with the means of m•king tbemeel vee
known as such. These degree! supply the omiseions; and do that only. except
giving moral instruction and conveying religious ideas, such as Masonry everywhere gives and conveys. and also such knowledge of real Masonry as the Monitors
universally afford to the uninitiated in the really ancient systems. That is all

The Semi-Annual Communication was held at MaaonicTemple, May8, 1895,M. ". W. ". DAVID G. DIXON, Grand Master; R. ". W. ". WM.. R. SINGLETON, Grand

Grand, Lodge of California.

There were present twelve Paet Grand Masters and the representatives of twentyfour sister Grand Jurisdictions.
Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with prayer by the Grand Chaplain.
A petition was granted for the formation of a new Lodge to be ca.lled Takoma
Lodge, located in the town of Takoma Park.
The action of the Grand Lodge of Kentucky in repealing the representative
system, having been referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, that committee
reported as follows :The Grand Master of Kentucky bas used pretty strong language in expressing
bis opinion of the_Grand Representative system, but your committee eee no just
grounds for any expression of "contempt" for a system which has received the
sanction of nearly all the Grand Lodges of tbe world for the past thirty or forty
years, whilst under it very many of the most distinguished Masons of our time
now hold or have held commissions as Grand Repr6sentatives of other Grand
Lodges than their own.
If it be determined by the Grand Lodges generally, or by a majority of them,
that the Grand Representative system baa not proved usP.ful in any way, but on
the contrary, has tended to interfere with rather than promote harmony and
fraternal feeling among the Grand Bodies .; if it has failed to do away, in some
measure, with that isolation from each other which their individual eoverei1<I1ty
tends to foster, then it baa not realized the hopes and intentions of those who
were instrumental in instituting it, nor of the many eminent brethren who have
given it their sanction.
If such should be the verdict, this Grand Lodge, with the others, can quietly
resolve to take no further part in it. But there seems to be no good reason to revile the system or exprelis "contAmpt" for it.
As there is no question of Masonic law to be considered in this case, but a mere
matter of expediency, and aa each member of your Jurisprudence Committee has
the honor of holding a commission or commissions as Grand Representative of
other Grand Lodges, and feels honored in having been selected as such, and in having been received by this Grand Lodge in that capacity, it follows that they are
to be looked upon as mterested parties in this matter. They therefore prefer to
offer no recommendation, either in favor of or against the longer continuance of the
Representative system by this Grand Lodge, but would recommend that the matter
be referred to a committee of three members of the Grand Lodge, who are not the
Representatives of any other Grand Lodge, to consider this matter and report at
our next annual meeting.
Referring to the communication from the Grand Lodge of Mississippi, in reference to the adoption of uniform rules aa to jurisdiction over candidates, the com·
mittee say :your committee believe that the adoption by all the Grand Lodges in our
country of some uniform rules governing their respective jurisdiction over candidates (if such a thing could be brought about) would result in great good, and that
the action of the Grand Lodge of Missiasippi, looking to that end is to be com·
mended. Yet it is by no means apparent that any rules could possibly be framed
which would meet with approval by all or even a majority of the Grand Lodges.
. Custom, constitutional provisions, and the jealous regard which each cherishes
for its own sovereignty would, we fear, militate against any general agreement.
Yet, notwithstanding the difficulties in the way, we may hope that a consummation so much to be desired mav eventually be brought about.
The "uniform rules " submitted by the Grand Lodge of Missieaippi are not, in
all res1>_ects, such as your committee could approve.
In Rule I it will be noticed that when a rejected applicant for the degrees subsequently remo''es to another jurisdiction and applies there for the degrees, the
Lodg-e to which be applies requires the one which rejected him to furnish "the
grounds upon which such rejection was made;" and if the grounds of the objection should be furnished the Lodge to which he makes his new pAtition, "it shall
juJge the sufficiency thereof and proceed in its discretion ! " If the grounds for
the rejection are not furnished within six months, it proceeds with the petition
"as in other cases."

The Grand Lodge was opened In Ample Form, with prayer by the Grand Chap·

Grand Master SHANNON delivered a very able and lengthy address. Of the condition of Masonry in Georgia, he says :Numerically we may not have increased, but the personnel of the membership
was never better. The dead branches have been lopped ofl, and the body of the
llMonio tree is living, growing and bearing only healthy, mor.l fruit. Good men
and troe have been added to our ranks, and to-day the 18,000 .Masons of Georgia
stand a band of law observing, God fearing meu, honored even by those who are
ignorant of the mysteries of our Order, bot who approve the practical working of
onr ancient Craft. Thus we should ever be a happy, loving society of friends and
brothers.
Happy Grand Master: Long may be enjoy the loyal support of brethren so devoted to the original plan and designs of Masonry.
The Grand Master's report of bis omcial acts if the journal of an active and vigorous administration. He appears to have held himself subject to call for the discharge of any Masonic dnty; his visitations were many, for the laying or corner-stones,
purposes of dedication , or the performance of other Masonic ceremonies. He granted
some seventy dispensations for various pnrposes. Of the District Deputies he says
he has found them faithful and efficient, always ready to dispense information among
the less informed brethren, and he commends them to Grand Lodge as a hard work·
ing and able set. or officers, who richly deserve the thanks or the Fraternity. He
bad granted dispensations for the formation of three new Lodges.
He bad rendered some two bnndred decisions dnrinll' the year, thirty of which he
reports for the pnrpose or emphasizing well known principles of Masonic low, and
says it Is doe to &he Craft to state that the rendermg of so many decisions by him
ls due not so much to Ignorance on the pa.rt or Mastera with reference to the laws of
the Fraterni1y es to the desire for information aa tq the i;>roper construction thereof.

knowledge of the Esoteric work." All honor, the greatest honor, to Grand Master
GODDARD.

Of perpetual jurisdiction the Grand Master said, with undeniable truth:. -

Grand Lodl}e of Calif<Yrnia.

1896.]

673

"The question of perpetual control over rejected material is now engaging the
attention of nearly every Grand Jorisdiction. It has been fruitful of many disputes,
and no doobt will continue to be for vears to come. In Illinois we recognize personal
jurisdiction over rejected materiel, wherever disposed, and the same is not affected
by the lapse of time. In other words, when a candidate is once rejected by a Lodge
in our jurisdiction, we hold that he always remaius the Masonic (rejected) 1>roperty
of the rejecting Lodge notil released by a clear ballot. He may have been only
twenty-one years of age, and thoogh he may locate in another part of the world, and
Jive a life of purity and full of good deeds, the relation is unchanged. A brother who
was so fortnnate as to be made a Mason first, and thereby given the opportunity to
cast an nnfavorable ballot, may hold the brand against the applicant so long as they
both live, regardless of merit or a change of location or circumstances. Thus to
reject is to acqoire perpetual ownership-certainly a strange law, and one not sup·
ported by the Ancient Regulations.
The question has been thoroughly considered and discnssed. There is no new
argument to present. My desire is only to record a suggestion that while it is rea·
sonable and proper to retain control so long as the rejected remains in oor jorisdlcdiction, there should be a limit to the length of time of such control when he leaves
our State and locates in another territory.
By my request our Grand Secretary has corresponded with the other Grand
Jurisdictions of the United States, asking their position, and of the forty-five reports
received, " .sixteen" recognize the law of perpetual jurisdiction, and "twenty-nine"
do not.
And yet the Committee on Jnrisprodence, after consideration, make this extra·
ordinary report : "Your committee is of the opinion that the observance of this
system of •inter-jurisdictional oumity' (that's a new name for it) tends to protect
the rights of Individual brethren, promote harmony, and conserve the principles of
11 common brotherhood. Yoor committee is also of the opinion that a change in so
Important and long established featore of the general Masonic law woold be in the
nature of an innovation, and not warranted by the best interests of the <Jraftatlarge.
Therefore unwise, and not desirable."
And that's the plea of perpetual jurisdiction-an innovation sanctioned by twenty.
nine Grand Lodge ayes to sixteen noes.

Among his decisions, we note thl' following, which we consider a very dangerous one:Oan we Initiate en Indian who cannot speak or nnderstand the Engllsh langnage?
Yes; provided yon have a good interpreter.
A case of jurisdictional claim and denial has been exercising the brethren of
Missouri and Indian Territory since Angust, 189(, and all on account of one BEN F.
L.l.FAYBTTB, claiming to be a citizen of Missouri and within the jorlsdictlon of
I>ecatur Lodge, No. 400, Pierce Oity, Mo., which Lodge he petitioned for the degrees
of Masonry. This coming to the knowledge of the Grand Master of Indian Territory
he at once informed the Grand Master of Missouri that Mr, BEN F. LAF.1.Y.KTTR was
a resident of Indian Territory, and had been residing in the jurisdiction of <Jhecotah
Lodge for six or s9ven years. He requested the Grand Master of Missonri to cause
all proceedings to be at once stopped.
It would seem to be a case of Mr. LAFAYBTTJC 1B maintaining his residence at his
former home in Missouri while permanently engaged in bnsiuess in the Territory,
The laws of both Missouri and the Territory require twelve months' residence in the
State. Under this law Indian Territory claims tllat Mr. LAFAYBTTB, or any other man,
who bas lived In the Territory for twelve months, and is now living there, if he wishes
to become a Mason, mnst petition a Lodge In that jurisdiction.
Grand Master CoTLB says, in closing his last Jetter:There are abont 40,000 white men in this jurisdiction who have lived and done
bnslness io other conntries besides this, and hnndrede of them now do their banking
in Kansas, Missouri and Texas, and have otller business interests in those States and
many ot.ber places, but still we claim, and the Masonic world says we have the right
to this claim, that if aur of those men wish to become Masons they must petition a
Lodge in this jurisdiction. This position we are bound to maintain ; otherwise we
would have no jurisdiction over any white man living in this Territory.
The claim of Indian Territory appears to be well founded, and we anticipate no
arrest of amicable relations between the parties to this fraternal contest.

In reporting bis exercise of the powers and duties of Grand Master during the
recess of Grand Lodge, he indulges in the following comments upon the liberal nse
of that wonderful lever for the removal of obstacles and the exaltation of the Supreme Head known as "The Grand Prerogative":In years irooe by, when I was young in Masonrv,I looked upon the Grand Master
of the Grand Lodge In Iowa as 11 being endowed with superhuman power over the
Craft. When clothed In the jewels and regalia of bis office be arose in the Grand
East, be appeared to me as the embodiment of all Masonic power and authority,
as one who could suspend or enforce the Jaw at will, and wbo•e every order most be
implicitly obeyed by the Orart. Many years of service in the ranks of the Order
had izreatly modified my early Impressions as to the powers of the Gr~nd Master,
bot it was left for one year's service in the office to impress upon me with fall force
his true condition, and the very limited powers with which he is clothed. While
the Grand Master is the executive officer of the Oraft for his term of office,. yet his
duties and his powers are carefully prescribed by Jaw, and he is bound to r11spect
and obey its pro'Oisiom to the same ex.tent as the youngest Entered ,ipprentice.
Italics ours.
He reports many applications for the use of his "prerog," and closes lhe subject
with these fitting words:1 have been asked to grant dispensations in many other cases where I had no
authority under tbe law to do so. I have in all such cases refused the d1speusatlon,
believing that the interests of the Order at large would be better promoted by a
compliance with the law than by attempting to suspend it, or to so construe it as to
1,11eet special circumstances.

The Grand Master is opposed to the Wiaconsiu rules for the dissemination of
charity. He closes his dissenting argument with the words: "I am In favor of the
broadest Masonic charity when voluntarily exercised, but am opj>Osed to any law or
role that provides for charity under compulsion."
The Grand Master says :Many years ago the Grand Lodge recognized the Grand Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons and the Grand Commandery of Knights Templar of Iowa, a.nd now by
expresa provisions of law holds fraternal relations with each of said bodies. Which
condition seems to be threatened by the approval of the Grand Commaodery of an
obsolete ruling of the Grand Encampment of the United States concerning the
status of oon-alJiliates, by which members of the Lodge who are also members of
the Commandery are placed in an unpleasant position by lieiog compelled to hold
fraternal intercourse with Masons who cannot visit the Lodge, walk in Masonic proce88ioos, receive Masonic aid or burial. This Is the result of a report by Grand
Commandery approving the Grand Encampment ruling, making it the law of Grand
Commaodery that 11 non-affiliate Mason may not only hold membership in the Com·
mandery but he may petition for and receive the Orders of Knighthood while he Is
11 non-affiliate.
As Brother SPEED, of .Mississippi, very pertinently asks: Now what is to be
done? We answer: The ooo-cootribntiog non-affiliate cannot sit in a Commaodery
in California because the highest power in Masonry, the Grand Lodge, forbids its
members to hold Masonic intercourse with suspended Masons-Grand Encampment
to the contrary notwithstanding.

The Report on Correspondence is again presented by Worshipful Brother CoxB,
who submits a thorough review of the Masonic world, with a valuable and interest.
Ing paper on Mexican Masonry by Grand Secretary PARV!lf. Bro. Con finds the
subjects dividing tbe attention of correspondents to be the method of dispensing
charity, fraternal relief, perpetnal jurisdiction, and Mexican Masonry. The last
seems to be attracting the most attention, although the majority seem disposed to
"make haste slowly," and thereby avoid possible mistakes. The qaeetion of reoognition is one of vital Importance, not only to the Masone of Mexico but also to
American Freemasonry, whose influence would tend to elevate and secure that sta·
bility so desirable in our neighboring Republic in its political as well as Masonic Interests. We trust Bro. Con will enter into the discassion and give the Fraternity
the benefit or hie judgment npon this important proposition.

Master's tribute to the memories of the illustrious Paet Grand Masters BROWNB and
BELCHER, has good words for Grand Secretary Jolll!fso11 and hie methods, and
compliments the Board of Relief.
Bro. Coxz notes the defeat of the resolution requiring all Master Masons, hereafter raised, to pass an examination in open Lodge within six months, and says : In Iowa we make the examination a condition of voting, holding office, or dimitting-and we think wisely. The law works well.

Bro. MATTHEW M. MILLBB, Chairman of Correspondence, made an exhau"tive
and interesting report upon the subject of the recognition of the Gran Dieta Sim·
bolica of the United States of Mexico, which was adopted by the Grand Lodge,
The committee, after a recital of the facts and mach information obtained from
Grand Secretary PABvlN, of Iowa, and others having personal knowle.d ge of exist-

686

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 15,

ing conditions relating to Masonry In Mexico, close their r• •i¥ltb the following
summary, which, as we have said, was concurred in by the { ' AW'Lodge of Kansas:
From the foregoing your committee would summarize 8.s' follows :1. The Symbolic Lodges of Mexico entered into the organization and formation
of the Gran Dieta, and tile latter was duly and regularly organized as a sovereign
Grand Body over the bymbolic Degrees of Kasonry within tile Grand Jnrlsdictlon
of Mexico, in February, 1890.
2. The charges made against the Gran Dieta se a sovereign Grand Lodge are
shown never to have been true as to its Constitution and By-Lawe, and It bas by
solemn enactment decreed that the Holy Bible, square and compass eboold be used
on all Masonic altars in the Symbolic Lodges of the Repoblic of Mexico, and that
all cbartere held by so-called women Lodges be at once withdrawn, and no recogni·
tion of women as Masons ever be made.
3. We also find that practical recognition bas been given to the Gran Dieti1 by
American Masons residing or sojooroiog in Mexico, and that American visitors to
Mexican Lodges find the work to be practically the same as that of the Lodges o!
the United States; that the recognition of the Gran Dieta by the Grand Lodge of
Texas bas been productive of a better feeling of amity between the two jurisdictions; that recognition has also been formally made of the Gran Dieta by the Grand
Lodge• or New York and N ortb Dakota, ancl that the Grand Lodge of Missouri, by
advising its subordinate ToUec Lodge, No. 520 to accept a charter from the Gran
Dieta, bas in the most impressive manner certiHed to ltd legitimacy and regularity,
and borne testimony to the fact that it regarded and considered the Gran Dieta a
body of character and stability, and entitled to the allegiance of all the Symbolic
Lodges within its jurisdiction. We also find from the testimony of Masons known
to ns that the "good of Masonry" demands that we extend a helping hand to our
brethren of Mexico,
We therefore recommend that the Grand Symbolic Diet of the United States of
Mexico be duly recognized by this Grand Lodge in accordance with our nsnal custom in snch matters.

It has been the oniversal doctrine that the only question submitted to the Lodge
in balloting opoo the petition of a candidate is, "Is he fit to be made a Ma•oo?"

The declarations by tho•e in authority, that any Mason, who allows personal feeling
of any kind to control his ballot, violates hie duty aud is guilty of uomasooic coo·
duct, are so numerous that it is unnecessary to quote them. This is couclosively
settled by the not Infrequent convictions of Masons for rejecting candidates for
personal and oomasooic reasons.
Bu\ It is said that good men are rejected from improper motive•. This is undoubtedly true, bat we believe not so frequently as those who ose this argnmeot would have
as believe. To admit that It is true is only to admit that Masons are hnmao, and Rome
of them guilty of onm1U1oolc condnct, as is •hown by the numerous convictions for
other offenses. But the coor,lusive answer i•, that when a law operates so uoj ostly
the\ any possible evasion of its effect becomes necessary or jostlllable, the law itself
shoo Id be modi fled or repealed. If the effect or the operation of the law of the secret
and unanimoos ballot is soch a• to justify an evasion of that effect, the law is faol\y.
The law necessarily assumes that every Mn.son, lo casting bis ballot, will do so In
good faith and lo accordance with Masonic duty. We repeat, that if the abuse is so
frequent as to justify a general provision to avoid its effect, a modiHcation of the law
ls imperatively demanded. While no one as yet has gone so far as that io his demand,
this argument is the entering wedge for the abrogation of the secret and unanimous
ballot, or for the entire evasion of its effect.
The rejection of a candidate, then, Is the decision of the Lodge--tbe tribunal to
which, lo behalf of the whole Fraternity, the law of Masonry entrusts the determina·
tion of that question without appeal-that the candidate is not, at the time, fit to
become a Mason.
" What is the effect of that decision?" Is the next qoestion: and while really bot
very few question the doctrine first stated, this question lies at the fonodatioo of the
differences now existing.
It is undoubtedly true that until recently the generally received law and Masonic
usage were that a rejected candidate oonld be thereafter legally accepted only by
the Lodge which rejected him, or by another Lodge with its consent, if io exi•tence.
If aov code of law (except in a single instance) provided otherwise, or any Mssonlc
writer held otherwise, anti! within Iese than fo.rty years, it ha• escaped the notice of
yoor committee after as careful and minute examination as we have had the time
and means to make.
But as this proposition baa been vehemently denied, with a confidence born appar·
eotly of iotnltioo rather than of an examination of the authorities, your committee

· This utterly ignores the idea that Masonry is an institution with laws binding upon

from the others in all respects, rather than a component part of one Institntion.

companion, Bro. WILLIAH C. BELCB&B, and he commenced hie notice of the Grand
Lodge of California with the following alfectionate and well-!leeerved tribnte. He
says:The Grand Lodge, and the Masonic Fraternity as a whole, have sulfered an
exceedingly great loss in the death of Past Grand Master WILLIAH CALDWELL
B&LCBER, for three years Grand Master and for twenty-eight years Chairman of the
Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence. He waR elected Grand Master in May, 1862,
almost the very day on which the writer was elected to his third term. His Annnal
Address, in 1864, was one of the first which we bad to review in onr first report for
this committee. We were struck by the unusual ability shown by his Address, and
as be was soon after appointed on the Committee on Jurisprudence, we have had
oocasitm to know him through his reports ever since.
At the Templar Reunion in Boston we met Past Grand Master WILLIAM A. DA vms,
and were greatly pleased to receive through him a special message from Bro.
BELCHER; we deemed it a sp.ecial honor. Little did we think that Bro. DAVIES would
be unable to deliver onr message in reply. But so it was; on the Sunday following
our interview Bro. BELCHER saw the last of earth, and Bro, DAVIES never looked on
his lace again.
Bro. BELCHED was born in Stockbridge, Vermont, December 12, 1820, and died in
San Franciscn, September 1, 1895, being nearly 75 years old.
He graduated at the Universi$y of Vermont in 1843 ; taught for some years, but
studied law, and was admitted to the bar In 1852. In 18;a be went to Marysville,
California, and went into practice with his brother; sn bsequently he removed to
San Francisco, and continued his practice there till bis death, dying with bis professional harness on. The committee say of him: " As a lawyer, be stood at the
bead of bis profession. He was honest and capable. No one who knew him ever
qnestioned bis integrity; and no one who ever practiced law with him doubted his
eminent ability. He possessed to a high degree the conrage of his convictions. In
debate he was strong and convincing. If in the wrong, he sought to be right; if
right, he was fearless, and asserted himself with all the vigor of his forceful man·
hood. The gentleness of his disposition, the simplicity of his manners, added to his
tall, commanding person made him at once a most conspicuous and most. lovable
man. Be combined in a high degree the opposite qualities of goodness and great·
ness."
To whicb Past Grand Master CURTIS adds :" He was wise in counsel, bold in action and fearless in debate. Conscious of the
rectitude of his own intentions, he was ever ready to grant to others the same
honesty of pnrpose that he claimed for himself. He was a profonnd jnribt, learned
in the science and ethics of the civil law, and by his scholarly attainments, his
unflinching integrity and unyielding fid~lity to every trust reposed in him, he left the
1alprees of his genius upon the jurisprndence of bis State."
He wa• an unceasing, tireless worker. He became Senior Grand Warden in 1860,
Deputy Grand Master and really ai:ting Grand Master in 1861, and Grand Master the
next yee.r. and for thirty· five sessions of the Grand Lodge was one of its main pillars
of support.
It has been our lot to discuss many of his reports, and, educated In ditlerent
schools of Masonic law, we did not always agree. He stated his own case as it
waB, e.nd bis adveraary's also; he never misrepresented his opponent's position.
He was not striving for victory, bot to discover and maintain the truth. He held tbat
a failure to meet his opponent's attack sqnarely was an admission that it could not
be done. We shall greatly miss his instructive reports and the rare privilege of dis·
cussing them.
T he Grand Master, JAMES BAUNTY STEVENS, was called npon to announce also
the death of Past Grand Master JOHN MILLS BROWNE, who died in Washington,
December 7, 1894. He was born in Hinsdale, N. B., :May 10, 1831. Re appeared
In Grmd Lodge in 1871, as Master of his Lodge. He was then a Surgeon in the U.S.
Navy. He distingnisbed himself so much at that session of Grand Lodge, in support
of an amendment to the constitution allowing Lodges to receive petitions·from oan·
~dates In the milit11ry and nave.I service who had not resided the required time in
ihejurisdictlon, and made so favorable an impres•ion that he was elected Junior
Grand Warden. He wa• elected Senior Grand Warden the next year, Deputy
Grand Me.ster the next, and then lonr times Grand Master. While he had not resided
.ID California for several years before his death, his able admlni-tration of' Masonic
alfalrs made an impress which is still felt. Moreover, be maintained his interest in
Xasonry to the time of his death. He was an oflicer and one of the ablest members
of $be Sonthern Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite.

A Special Communication was held in Framingham, June 13, for the purpose
of participating in the Centennial Celebration of Miitdlese:c Lodge, of which a full
report is given. The historical address is a paper of forty pages of much merit
and wit. Some of the characters described in the sketch of the Lodge history in
Revolutionary days .is both striking and amusing, and lead one to the conclusion
that "times ain't now as they used to be." For instance, the historian relates the
following anecdote in regard to the Teneral of bis great grandfather, the Selectman,
as characteristic of the customs and temper of the day :It bad been the estahlisbed rule in all families to provide liquors for the mourners, and, in the families of men in publi~ station, fo~ all who sh?ul~ attend the
services at the house of the deceased. Being an abstamer from pnnc1ple, _be gave
directions before his death, that no intoxicating liquors should. be fu~mshed to
relations or friends at bis funeral. Capt. JoE Wmon (the town wit and Joker, who
was on good terms with everybody), made it a rule to.be present on all such occa.
sions, and was always ready to do the honors. at the Bldebo~. He ~ad not heai;d
of the prohibition, and was taken by surpnse. After wa1tmg patiently, and m
vain for the usual invitation, be remarked, in his caustic way, as he slowlv
mou~ted bis old horse, "Queer funeral; no toddy! no tears ! " .
In describing the anti.Masonic excitement, and its effect upon the Lodge, the
historian says : "To Middlue:c Lodge belongs the credit of being one of the very
few Lodges that stood their ground, and held their meetings through the whole of
the reign of terror."
After the conclusion of the exercises, the quartette sang "Let Us Meet Upon
the Level." The benediction was pronounoed, and the brethren parted to reassem.
bleat the Town Hall, later, and enjoy a bounteous dinner, with the usual accompaniments of toasts and speeches.
At nine o'clock Grand Lodge returned from whence it came, and closed.

The Grand Lodge of Missouri has enrolled five hundred and sixty-three chartered Lodges, with a membership of 30, 728 Master Mnsons. Two hundred and

Another ruling of Grand Master OBME, excepted to by Bro. VINOIL, is that _one
who has lost an eye, and wears a glass eye in its place, or one who bas lost the s1ght
of one eye, cannot be lawfully initiated in this State." Undoubtedly th~ Grand
Master based his ruling upon a General Regulation reported by the Committee on
Jurisprudence and adopted by the Grand Lodge in 1864, which reads :-

=

Grand L0<lge of Oalifortcia.

1896.]

721

The person who desires to be made a Mason must he a man ; no woman nor
eunuch ; free born; neither a slave nor the son of a bond woman; a believer in
God and a future existence ; of moral conduct ; capable of reading and writing;
not deformed or "dismemhertxl," but hale and aound in his physical conformation ;
having his right limbs as a man ought to have, and be able to conform literally to
what the several degrees respectively require of him.
This regulation has been repeatedly reaffirmed by our Grand Lodl!'e. In 1892
the question was again asked of the Grand Master: "Can the petition of a man
who has lost one of his eyes, but is qualified in all other respects, be received in a
Lodge of Master Masons?" And was again referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, who made the following report :The same question was, during the year, several times proposed to the Grand.
Master, and was by him answered affirmatively. That portion of his address relating to this subject being referred to this committee, they have again carefully
considered the re~ulation which must control the answer. That regulation readsas quoted aforesaid. This regulation was adopted in 1864 upon the recommendation
of the Committee on Jurisprudence, of which Bro. HENBY H. RHEES was then
Chairman. If the last clause is to control, as some of our best informed brethren
seem to think was intended, then the only inquiry to be made is as to the ability
to conform to the requirements of the degrees, and if the candidate can do that
be may be deforme,d, or diamembertxl, and not be hale or sound in bis physical conformation. In the judgment of your committee, a fair construction of the regulation requires not only that the applicant shall not be deformed or dismembered
and shll.l.l be hale and sound ir. bis physical conformation, havinir his right limbs
as a man ought to have, but that he must a"8o be able to conform literally to what
the several degrees respectively req11ire of him. Such construction gives mt1aning
to every part of the reg11lation, as the rules of construction universally adopted
require, while the other construction gives effect to the last clause only. The law
fixes the standard. Can one who has lost an eye be said to come up to that
standard ? Your committee think that he cannot, and that his petition should not
be received.
Which report was concurred in.
We think there can be no doubt of the correctness of the Grand Master's ruling
under our law.
Bro. VINOIL closes his notice with good words for Calliornia. He says:It was the privilege of this writer during the summer of 1894 to visit, for the
first time, the land of "fair woman and brave men," as well as sunshine, fruits
and beautiful flowers in the Golden State. Thus the dream of years was realized.
Having traveled from ocean to cicean, and from the far north land to the "Sunny
South," in all my wanderings I never met with a country so d~sirable as "the
land of the setting sun." It was a revelation to me. I can not do it justice.
Therefore I shall not attempt to describe what to me is indescribable. It must
suffice to say that I would love to live in California, prlYlli,dtd I miirbt be allowed
to select my location according to fancy and taste. Let me dwell in beautiful
Oakland for a time, enjoyinl!' its rare chmate and flowers, then give me a season
for tarrying awhile at San Jose and Del Monte. Thence to Southern California,
taking in all places of beauty and delight. But please exempt me from the necessity of staying in San Francisco when the trade winds send up those cold mists
from the ocean, roouiring flannels and overcoats in June and ,July. Also deliver
me from the sirocco and scorching fires of the San Juan country about pretty
Fresno, when the mercury registered 110 and upwards, with the ice all exhausted
in July, and a "strike" on, cutting off supplies from everywhere. With twenty.
one days' detention in any one place, under the drawbacks incident to the worst
strike of the century, one wants ice and liberty. California is a good country
when one is free to go when and where he may list. But save me from another
California "strike," such as was walking about over that country during my stay
on the coast in 1894. There were many compensations, however, as the Fraternity
made it pleasant, and friends abounded in numbers.
