The first officers of the Lodge were John J • .Morgan, J obn Post and Micha.el Myers.
As these men took a leading pa.rt in the affairs of this portion of the State, It is fitting
for a moment to dwell upon the ma.in features of their lives.
John Jordan Morgan, the first Master of the Lodge, was born In the city of New
York November 7, 1768. He was the ilon of John Morgan and Mary DeLa.ncey, bis
wife. John Morgan wa.s a native of Wales and a sea captain. He intended bis ~on
for the British navy, bnt his intention was frustrated by the breaking out of the War
of the Revolution. John J. Morgan was a lifelong resident of New York. He was
twice married. His first wife was Catharine Warne of Jamaica, Long Island. Some
time after her death and the death of their child, be married Eliza Baldwin of Cork,
Ireland. After bis second marriage he adopted a niece of his first wife. She BS811med
the name of Morgan, and in 1826 Catharine Morgan was married to J oho Adams Dix,
then a yonng artillery officer and aid-de·camp to .Major·General Jacob Brown of the
United Sta.tee Army. In 1822 John J. Morgan was elected from New York City as
Representative in the Congress of the United States. He served in the Assembly of
the State, and also as Collector for the Port of New York.
In private life he was a scholar of rare accomplishments. He spoke and wrote
the French langna.ge with ease and fiuency. In domeslio and social life he had the
manners and courtesy of the gentleman or an age alto~ether pBSeed. He was an
ornament to the society in which he moved. Io his 1·elig1ous life he was a commnni·
cant of Trinity chnrch, New York, and served as vestryman for many years,
He was a large land holder in Oneida, Herkimer and other counties of New York.
He held them under patent of the State. It was a matter or pride with him to say
that he was the first white man who owned these lands after they bad been sold by
the Indians, and hie descendants are still in polll!es1ion of the original docnments
which note the transference of these lands to him.
He built a snmmer residence between the towns of Clarkville and New Berlin, and
gave it the name of ·" The Unadilla." For thirty or forty years he spent his snmmers
there. He died at Port Chester, while visiting his son·ln·law, General Dix, and .was
buried in the family vanlt, Trinity church yard, New York.
John Post, the first Senior Warden of the Lodge, son of Elias and .Maria Post, was
born December 28, 174.8. He was married Jannary 7, 1776, to .Ma.rgarietji Bellinger.
There were born to them eleven children: John, Jr. Maria, who died in infancy,
·Maria, Frederick, Catharine, Elias, Deborah, Cataline, Eliza.beth, Helen and Rebecca.
Elias Post, his father, after an eventful life, WAS found dead in his bed by bis son
John and Baron Stenben, who was an intimate friend of the family. His wife was the
da.nghter of Colonel Bellinger, who was an aid to General Nicholas Herkimer, and
fought at Oriskany.
John Post was a stalfofficer in the Revolutionary War. He took part in the snr·
render of General Burgoyne and in the expedition of Sullivan. He was present at
the Battle of Jilonmontb, and also at the surrender of General Cornwallis, which
virteally closed the war.
In 1790, in connection with a Mr. Martin of Schenectady, he engaged in trade with
the Six Nations. He pnrcba.sed large qna.ntltles of ginseng, which he exported to
China, it being snpposed at that time a remedy for the plague. After his removal to
Utica, later in that year, he still contlnned dealing with the Indians, and was the
first merchant in the place. About this time he established a line of stage boats on
the Mohawk River, to run between Albany and Utica. These boats were styled
" The Accommodation" and the "Diligence." For the times they were regarded as
comfortable and very useful oonveyanoes. They fnrnished room for twenty passen·
gers and were propelled by° means of poles, and though remarkable for their day,
thev furnish a marked contra.st to the splendid steamers of our modern commerce,
which show our national progress. He also established a line of freight boats,
which during the season of navigation were employed in carrying produce to Sche·
nectady and bringing back merchandise.
Previous to his settlement in Utica he had purchased near the Mohawk River,
land on which be caused a log honse to be bnilt. This was on the east side of what
is to-day Ueoesee street, and near the corner of Whitesboro street. At first he kept
his goods in his honse, but in 1791 he bnilt a store on the corner of Genesee and
Whitesboro streets. In this store he carried on for many years an extensive trade
with the Indians and white settlers. He extended his business to Floyd, .Manlins
and New York, and became a man of wealth. He served as first postmaster in the
village of Utica, and held the office for many years. On Joly 13, 1792, he purchased
from the representatives of General Bradstreet 89l acres of land-known as Lot

On Jnne 5, 1805, a petition from John Post and others, residing in Utica and
vicinity, County of Oneida, was received, recommended by Amicable Lodge, No. 23,
to- establish a Lodge of Master Masons in the village of Utica. The Grand Lodge of
New York granted the petition. Oneida Lodge was coustitnted and John Post became
its first Master, and held the office for several years.
In 1806 he took into partnership his son-in-law, Giles Hamlin, who pnrchased a
large stock of merchandise. A fire. broke out and destroyed his property, and in a
few moments swept away his wealth, leaving him a bankrnpt. Shortly after this he
removed to Maolins, where he re•ided until his death, which took place December 5,
1830. He was buried at Jamesville, near Manlius.
Michael Myers, theJnniorWarden of the Lodge, was born at Elizabeth, N. J.,
(formerly Anville,) February 1, 1753. He came to Herkimer with a company of
soldiers from New Jersey. At the battle of Johnstown, in 1781, be was seriously
wounded in the leg, crippling him for life. His brother Mathew, who was associated
with him, was killed in the battle.
In person General Myers was dignified and of aristocratic bearing, and a man of
marked ability. Aft.er the close or the war he remained at Herkimer-there be
married (Jatbarine, the eldest daughter of Captain Henry Harter. She was born in
Febrna.ry, 1758, at the village of Presoott, Canada, where her parents bad been
ta.lien as prisoners in the French and Indian wars. While residing at Herkimer there
were born five sons and three dangbters: Peter M., Henry, Nancy, Catharine,
Ma.thew, Michael, John and Margaret, the last of whom is still living at Little Falls
at the ripe age of eigbty·seveo.
He ver.v soon became largely Interested in the parchase of real estate in the
village of Herkimer and surrounding country, and became the owner of the homestead of his father-in-law. He was alRo the owner of a few slaves who lived on his
estate notil the time of his death. He was by far the most prominent man and
leading character in this pa.rt of the State. In 1790 he was a member of the AeRembly from Montgomery County, and in 1791 he was the first and only member from
the new county of Herkimer. In 1796 he was a member of the State Senate which
office he held for fonr years. In 1791 he was the first judge of Herkimer co'nnty, a
position which he also held in 1794.
March 5, 1794. the Grand Lodge of New York issued a warrant for holding Amica·
ble Lodge, No. 36, in the village or Herkimer, of which Michael Myers was the first
Master, and held the office for many years.
After a long and useful career in pnbllc and Masonic life, he died on Febrnary
17, 1814, at Herkimer, and was buried at that place. In the year 1887 bis remains
and those of bis family that were buried there were removed to Oak Hill Cemetery
which has lately been consecrated as the resting place of the dead of Herkimer.
'

Constitutions working in this Colony, the Board has heartily concurred in the proposal made by the It!.·. W.·. Grand Master that he should be authorized to remove
the last semblance of excuse for grievance on the part of the Mother Constitutions
against Grand Lodge, by returning the original charters unconditionally. The
Board feels that in making this concession in regard to what is considered are its
legal and Masonic rights, !10 loss of rugnity is involved, and no danger incurred.
Grand Lodge is nuw sufficiently strong to be under no afprehension of its interests
or those of any of its Lodges suffnring by the return o the charters, even if any
attempt Rhould be made to use any of them in an injurious manner. The Board
hopes, however, that no such attempt will be ma.de, but that the return of the
charters will be accepted by the Mother l; rand Lodges and their officers in the
same spirit as it is made. In each case a request has bePn preferred that the original charter may, after cancellation, be returned to the Lodge as a memento of the
source from which it sprung. As several Lodges have retained their own charters
in preference to leaving them in the custody of Grand Lodge, the Board would
earnestly request each such Lodge to now retnm its original charter to the Grand
Lodge which issued it, either directly_to the Representative of such Grand Lodge
or through the M. ·• W. ·• the Grand Master.

On motion, Grand Lodge appointed a committee to inquire into and report
upon the condition of Freemasonry in the Island of Cuba, and said committee
reported as follows :Y our committee appointed on the condition of Freemasonry upon the Island
of Cuba respectfully rep<>rt t hat from information furnished by the Committee on
F oreign Correspondence we find that the Spanish Government recently issued a
decree closing all the Masonic Lodges upon the I sland, and declaring the Masonic
Fraternity an unlawful organization; therefore he it
R&oWe.d, That the sympathies of this Grand Lodge be and they are hereby
cixtended to our Masonic brethren of the Island of Cuba in this their hour of
oppression, with the hope that they may soon see their Masonic homes re-opened
and re-established.
R&olved further, That the committee be continued with intructions to report

Past Grand Master ROBERT Cww, as Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence, presented that committee's report, an exceedingly able and inte~esting
paper, reviewing the doings of all the American Grand Lodges, except Rh.ode
Island, with the principal foreign Grand Bodies, making a complete record of the
sentiment and condition of the Masonic world. Bro. CLOW's notice of California
is for the administration of Grand Master STEVENS, from whose address he quotes
with commendation. He joins in the universal tribute to our Past Grand Masters
who have passed away, Brothers JOHN MILLS BROWNE an~ WILLIAM CALDWELL
BELOHEB, as exemplars of the Masonic virtues.
He gives his approval to the disaeminat_ion of Grand Lodge charities by Grimd
Lodge during the session as well as by its representative-the Masonic Board of
Relief-during the recess. His notice of California is kind and fraternal, and indicates the relations which we hope may continue forever and forever.
Under Kansas, we quote the following as evidencing Bro. CLOw's opinions upon
the question of the recognition of "the Gran Dieta Symbolica" of Mexico, an
issue being brought rapidly to the attention of our Grand Lodges, and the conditions of which we.have given in several parts of this report.
At the last Annual Communication the question of recognition of "the Gran
Dieta Symbolica of Mexico " was referred to the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, which now submits a special report recommending recognitifi of the
Mexican so called Grand Lodge, and their report was adopted. Witli all due
respect for the ability and penetration of this committee, we beg to dissent and
protest against snch recognition. The argument brought forward by the committee, in its behalf, is fallacious and misleading and ought not _to be accepted by
any regular Grand Lodge. 'fhe conclusions of the committee have confe•sedly
been largely influenced by the correspondence carried on between its Chairman
and our esteemed brother, T. S. PARVIN, the Grand Secretary of Iowa, who seems,
in this matter, to have ignored the very generally accepted tests of recognition and
become impressed with the idea that when he crossed the Rio Grande he might
lawfully do as Romans did and countenance "impostors and dissenters from the
original plan of Masonry."
Having treated the subject in another place, we only observe here that to
us Bro. Cww's comments seem not warranted, in view of the painstaking and
elaborate investigation of the subject of Mexican Masonry by the distinguished
committees of Kansas, Texas, Iowa and New York. The exhaustive report of
Bro. MATTHEWS of Texas, based upon personal investigation, would almost persuade us that the best interests of Freemasonry demanded recognition.

The proceedings of the Grand Lodge of l:'eunsylvania for the year 1895 appear

The first Quarterly was held in the city of Philadelphia, March 6, 1895,-the
M.·. W.·. MATTHIAS H. H:e:NnEBBON, Grand Master, presiding; R.·. W.·. MIOHAEL
NIBBET being Grand Secretary. One hundred and twelve Lodges were represented.
The business _of the session was almost entirely confined to the consideration of
the finances of Grand Lodge, its investments, etc.
The Committee on Printing and Publishing also reported.

A second Quarterly was held June 5th. the Grand Master presiding, at which
one hundred and six Lodges were represented.
Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form at 7:10 P. M.
An appropriation of five thou.sand dollars was made to complete certain altera·
tions being made on the first floor of the Temple.
The Grand Master then made the following announcement:The saddest duty which, as Grand Master, I have been called upon to perform
le to announce to you the death of Right Worshipful Past Grand Master Bro.
Richard Vaux, which occurred at his residence in this city on the 22d of March
last. When I received the telegram apprising me of the event it was a great shock
to me, as it was the first intimation I had of his illness. I had spent an hour with
him in his office about two weeks previously, and left him apparently in the best of
spirits, little thinking I would never see him again. Bro. Vaux was a member of
this Grand Lodge about fifty year1, and aside from the elective offices be filled,
served on many of its important committees. He was Chairman of the Committee
ou Correspondence about twen~y-five :1.7ears, and his fame as a M&J!onic jurist was not
bounded by the shores of this contment. He was also promwent in the social
political and business life of this city. Many of you knew him in these different
relations. I knew him only as a Mason, and as •uch am proud to feel that he was
!DY frie'!d. To me be was always cordial, kind and approachable. After my
mstallat10n he congratulated me on the event, and said, " If ever I can be of
service to you, command me." Had the occasion arisen I knew he would have
been as good as his word.
At the time of his death my business was of •uch a nature that it was impossible for me to leave ho~e. I. telegraphed the R!ght W?rshipf~l Deputy Grand
Master, Bro. Kelly, askmg him to act for me, which he kmdly did. I am satisfied
that all was done with proper solemnity and decorum, and feel under many obligations to Bro. Kelly for so efficiently representing me.
Soon after Bro. Vaux's death I requested Right Worshipful Past Grand Mas~r
Bro. ~ichael Arnold to prepare a memorial of him, which he has done, and which
he Wlll now present to you.

R.·. W.• Bro. MIOHAEL ARNOLD then delivered the eulogy upon the life and
character of RrnHARD VAUX, giving special attention to hie Masonic history. It
was an eloquent and affectionate tribute to a brother, companion and friend.
Grand Chaplain HENBY S. GETZ also added his testimony to the manliness of
the man. He said :This small tribute of my estimation of him as a man I pay with a full heart and
a grate.fa~ ac~owledgment of. those ~ndyinir.v.irtues wh!ch go to make up a manhood distingmshed as well for its sterhngqualities as for its practical bearing upon
those with whom he was associated.

"As Hiram slept, the widow's son,

following : It is not proper for the Wor:ihipful Master to receive the Tyler's avouchment

room and make bis avoucbment directly to the Worshipful Master There will
then be no danger of the identi~y of the visitor being lost. Any otb~r method is
not proper and cannot be permitted.

The Grand Lodge of Quebec held an Emergent Communication for the purpose
of laying the corner-stone of the Methodist Church in the village of Knowlton
May 22, 1895. Eleven Lodges were represented. The ceremonies were elaborate
and impressive. An Address was delivered by Past Grand Master Bro. J.P.
Nones, to a large audience of citizens and Masons.

The Grand Lodge held its twenty-sixth Annual Comruunication at the city of
Montreal the 29th and 30th of January, 1896,-M.·.
FR!l:DERIOK MAssu,
Grand Master, presiding, R.·. W.·. J. H. lBAAOBON being Grand Sec~etary. Fifty
Lodges were represented and Representatives of thirty sister Grand Lodges were
present. California's proxy did not appear. Quebec numbers fifty-six constituent
Lodges, with a membership of 3,530 Master Masons. The death roll for the year
bears the names of forty-two brethren. Worshipful Bro. JAOOB VooBBANGER
represents the Grand Lodge of Quebec near the Grand Lodge of California.
Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form and the Grand Master delivered his
Annual Address. He commenced his Address with a fervent acknowledgment of
the care and protection of the Almighty Father, and offered thanks for the privilege of meeting again for their annual deliberations. He said at no time in the
past history had Grand Lodge been so progressive and prosperous as at present.
The Grand Master reported his official acts for the year ; presented hill several
rulings on matters submitted to him, but which are of interest only to the Craft at
home, as the matters in question were governed in each case by the local law. He
announced the death of several eminent Masons of their own and sister Jurisdictions. As to their relations with other Grand Bodies, he says :-

w.·.

As far as our foreign relations are concerned they remain very much as heretofore, the Lodges ha»ing jurisdiction under the Grand Lodge of England baing
s~ill in existence in this city of Montreal. There are not wanting, in my opinion,
signs that these Lodges will possibly in the near future consider serionslv benelits
which would accrue to them from being in much closer contact to their Grand
Body than they are at present. Without going clo(le)y into this question, which
has been so fully discussed heretofore, I dismiss the subject with the remark that

762

Proceedings of the

[Oct'. 15,

1896.]

jt is to be hnped that ere long Lodges referred to will recognize it as their duty' to
relieve the Grand Lodge of England from the somewhat, no doqb!; to them, embarrassing position of still allowing Lodges to work under Englishctiii:rters in this
Province of Quebec; a position which, undoubtedly, no Grand Lodge cares' to
maintain, and one which has never become so solitary as to be marked among the
Grand Lodges of the Masonic world.
Reports were received from the six District Deputy Grand Masters, with full
reports of the condition of the Lodges in their respective Districts.
The Grand Chaplain delivered an eloquent discourse upon the subject of Masonry and Religion.
·
R.·. W.·. Bro. E.T. D. CHAMBERS submits the Report on Correspondence-an
unusually interesting paper, and especially so as Bro.CHAMBERS has passed through,
during the year, a long and severe illness. However, his report is his tenth annual
review of the Masonic doings of the world, with a most interesting disquisition of
fourteen pages preceding it, containing his comments upon the history, condition
and future of Freemasonry. In it he pays a merited and most eloquent tribute to
those eminent brethren with whom he had been associated as a Grand Lodge correspondent, who have rested from their labors and are at rest forevel'. His review
of California is of the administration of Grand Master STEVENS, whose Address
he pronounces "an admirable one." He notes the death of Past G~and Masters
BELCHER and BROWNE, and writes favorably of our proceedings.
Under the head of Missouri Bro. CHAMBERS, in discussing physical disqualification, declares himself in accord with Bro. VINOIL, whc. would require nothing
more than that the candidate should be able to conform literally to the requirements.of the several degrees.
And under Mississippi, he concurs in Bro. F&RDERIC SPEED'S observation that
if the Grand Master ever possessed the "inherent power" to make Masons at
sight, it ought never to be exercised.
Under Nevada, he says: "Grand Lodge very properly refused to subscribe to
the Mississippi heresy of perpetual jurisdiction.
Under Texas, in discussing the status of the Gran Dieta Simbolica of Mexico,
he says:We may mention as a matter of interest that there are under the jurisdiction
and warrant of the Gran Dieta Simbolica seventeen Grand Lodges and State
Lodges, with two hundred and twenty-Ii ve Blue Lodges, having a total membership
of 21,992. There are also in Mexico two so-called Grand Lodges which do not acknowledge the jurisdiction of the Gran Dieta, viz. : Vera Cruz, and in the City of
Mexico the Federal District, the two together having subordinate to them twenty
Lodges, with about five hundred members.

RHODE ISLAND.

The Grand Lodge &f Rhode Island and Providence Plantations held a Special
Communication in the city of Providence October 3, 1894, for the purpose of laying the corner-stone of the Ebenezer Primitive Methodist Church, which was performed with elaborate ceremonies, and were pa cipated in by his excellency the
Governor of the State as assistant to the Grand Master. Pleasing addresses were
made by the Grand Master and the Governor, and both were presented with
beautifully wrought silver trowels.
The ceremonies being concluded the dignitaries and brethren were entertained
at a banquet by the ladies of the church.

The Gra·nd Lodge held its one hundred and fifth Annual Communication in the
city of Providence May 20, 1895,-the M. ·. W. ·. ELISHA H. RHODES, Grand
Master, presiding. Thirty Lodges were represented.
The Grand J,odge was opened in Ample Form, with prayer by the Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master delivered his Annual Address. After a fraternal greeting
he offered praise and thanksgiving to Him who had preserved them to meet
again in Grand Lodge.
He read from the death roll the names of those brethren who had gone from
among them, in obedience to the divine summons, during the past year, and paid a
brief tribute to the memory of each.
The Grand Master reported the official acts of the year for their consideration.
He submitted his report of official visitation with his conclusions regarding the
condition of their Lodges and the standard of their work. He granted one dispensation for the formation of a new Lodge.
ReportR of the conditioa of the Lodges were presented hy the five District
Deputy Grand Masters and the Grand Lecturer.

Bro. RUGG, as Chairman of Committee on Correspondence, also reported on
"the Mississippi rules," which, for reasons given by the committee, they do not
recommend for passage by the Grand Lodge, but suggest that no action be taken
thereon and that the circular submitted be placed on file. Which action was had.
We note the presence of R. •. W. ·.GEO. M. CARPENTER, Representative of the
Grand Lodge of California near the Grand Lodge of Rhode Island, at this annual
session.
Under the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of Rhode Island the Grand Master
appoints the Deputy Grand Master, the five l>istrict Deputies, the Grand Chaplain,
Grand Deacons, Stewards, Marshal, Sword Bearer, Pursuivant, Lecturer, Musical
Director and Grand Tyler, the elective officers being only Grand Master, Wardens,
Treasurer and Secretary.
The Grand Lodge is now publishing a "Centennial Memorial Volume," a
volume of nine hundred pages, the same being a complete history of the origin
and establishment of Freemasonry in Rhode Island, with its one hundred years of
progress.

handRomely entertained by the new Lodire.

The M.·. W.·. F. C. GIRARD, Grand Master of Kentucky, was presented to the
Grand Master, received with the Grand Honors, and escorted to a seat in the
Grand 'East.
In his Address the Grand Master referred to the past history of the Grand
Lodge, paying fraten1al tribute to his distinguish ed predecessors, both living and
dead, and cordially greeting the brethren in attendance at their eighty-second
Annual Communication.
The Grand Master granted dispensations for unimportan t reasons, but refused
all applications for the same authorizing a re-ballot.
Among hi3 official rulings we note the following :The rejection of a candidate for Masonry does not give the Lodge rejecting him
perpetual jurisdiction over such candidate.
A brother was guilty of embezzlement in three cases. After the crime was
publicly known, before he could be disciplined, he committed suicide. The Lodge
correctly refused to accord him a Masonic bmial, not because of his suicide,
but
because of his crime.
It is not improper for a :Masonic Lodge to participate in the funeral ceremonies
of a brother entitled to Masonic burial with Knights of Pythias or other civic
societiPs or military body to which he may have belonged, the Maaonic ceremonies
to be separate from that of other bodies, and such as is prescribed the Text
Book. I take this view from what I conceive to be a proper constructioin
n of all the
law on the subject.
·
The Grand Master appointed PMt Grand Master HENRY H. INGERSOLL Chair·
man of Committee on Correspondence, to fill vac~ncy caused by the death of Bro.
WILLIAM H. MORROW.
The footprints of the dead messenger had been seen in their accustomed
walks and prominent brethren had been taken from among them, to return no
more forever. Bro. CHARI.Ell L. FuLI.ER, Grand Tyler; Bro. WM. H. MORROW,
Correspondent;· Bro. R. M. MASON and Bro. A. B. JXWl!.LL, Past Senior Grand
Wardens; Bro. GEORGE HARSH, Past Grand Sword Bearer, and Bro. Hl!.NRY R.
HOWARD, Past Senior Grand Deacon, with three hundred and ninety-one membere
of constituent Lodges, was surely a generous draft upon the Freemasons of Ten·
nessee for 1895.
The Grand Master announced the restoration of amicable relations with the
brethren on the other side of the river, and that so far as the Masons of Tennessee
were concerned "peace reigned from the rivers to the ends of the earth."
The Board of Custodians and Secretaries made an elaborate report of the con·
dition of the four hundred and twenty-six Lodges of the jurisdiction. One
Lecturer, Bro. CHARLES Coxsroox, adding that in the discharge of his duties be
had ridden one horse more than twenty-seven hundred miles.
The Committee on Jurispruden ce, in considering the Address of the Grand
Master, write their views of perpetual jurisdiction in the following forcible language:We recommend an approval of the official letter of the Grand Master to the
Grand Master of Illinois, that Tennessee does not believe in the dogma
· of per·
petual jurisdiction, and we trust that the near future may bring a satisfactory
aolution of this perplexing questi9n among the Grand Jurisdiction s of
America.
The proposition of the Grand Lodge of Colorado, referring to the Centennial
Anniversar y of the Death of G11.0RGE WASHINGTON, was heartily approved.

The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with prayer by the Grand Chap·
lain.
In his AddreBB the Grand Master gives the brethren fraternal greeting, and wel·
comes them to the pleasures and la.hors of tbe session. He predicts for the future
~ permanent prosperity and invokes from them renewed zeal and undiminished love
tor the great principles of Freemasonry.
Sixteen Lodges, chartered at the last Annnal Oomruunfcation, were constituted
upon the close of the session.
Fourteen corner-stones were placed with accompanying ceremonies during the
year, and the Grand :Master gave permiBBion to thirty Lodges to publicly install their
officers.
Under the bead of Foreign Relations the Grand Master gives mnch information of
great valne concerning :Masonry in Mexico; it is exceedingly desirable as being the
fullest "in detail" of any account we have heretofore beard of the :Masonic status
of the Gran Dicta Sim bolica of :Mexico.
From the Grand Secretary's statistical table we learn that of the 26,841 affiliated
:Master Masons in Texas ~igbt hundred and eighty-nine use profane language,
seventy-one are gamblers and four bnndred and nineteen drink too much whiskey.
They have 1,467 widows of Master Masons, of whom ninety.five are destitute, and
1,638 orphans, of whom one hundred and sixteen are destitute. Four hundred and
five Lodges own their own building; the valne of real estate and buildings is $428,·
480.00, on which property Insurance is maintained for $191,036.00.
M." W.·. Bro. N ATRJ.NIBL GaEBNR CURTIS represents the Grand Lodge of Texas
near the Grand Lo~ge of California.
One mourning page in the volume ia devoted to the memory of the four hundred
and eight Master Masons "whose bodies we have returned to mother earth and
whose spirits have penetrated the mvsterious future since last we met.''
California's representative, Past Grand Master and Chairman of Correspondence,
M.·. W.'. Bro. TBO>IAS M. MATTHEWS, again presents the report, in which be reviews the doings of fifty Grand Lodges, commenting upon their legislation in a con·
servative fraternal spirit and giving bis views upon the few questions of real interest
now engaging the attention of the Fraternity.
Bro. MATTBllWB' notice of California is for the administration of Grand Master
OBHE. He first notices the reported illneBB of Paet Grand Master CURTIS and ex·
presses a fervent desire for bis recovery. We are glad to assure Bro. M.t.TTHllWS
that their representative Is fully restored to health, and remains with us to advise
and guide the organization be has done so much to build up. He makes sympathetic allusion to the death of Po.st Grand :Masters STEVENSON and GBITlllAN. ·
Bro. MATTHEWS concurs in the action of the Grand Lodge on the Wisconsin
proposition relating to the dispensing of Masonic relief. He thinks the amendment
to the provision for restoration of members suspended for non-payment of dnes,
where delay has been made in such payment for the period of two years, that
subjects the applicant to ordeal of a ballot before restoration, to be a miatake. We
agree with Bro. MATTHEWS and think with him that the conditions heretofore imposed by him were quite as onerous as they should be ; we regret the action.
Bro. M.t.TTRBWS "now concurs" also in our action on the expenditure of Lodge
funds for social purposes. On that question we have no doubt but that the action
of the Grand Lodge will be fully sustained by an increased interest in Lodge association that will many times repay the cost of the experiment; and then, Bro. MATTHEWS,
It's a sort of 'Vindication of the right of a Mason so long as he pays bis debts and
keeps out of jail (which means "in good standing"), to the nee and enjoyment of
his own money. Thanks for kind words, Bro. M.

The good shi~ Free~ason has held to the course laid down by the fathers and upon
an even keel is beanng along, safely, we hope, the eternal principles and landmarks

There is great need of a. more general understanding among the family of Grand
Lodges in reference to the question of jurisdiction, the rights and privileges of
membership and consequent Masonic standing. Uniform action in these matters is
not only desirable, but is vitally necessary to the preservation of harmony among
the Craft.
In our examination of the proceedings we are impressed with the fact that the
P_resence of sociability among the Lodges indicates to a certainty a prosperous condi·
tion, and we are reminded that in the early days of Oalifornia sociability among
Lodge membership used to be the rule and the lack of it the exception.
Our Cuban brethren have had their Temples closed by order of a. tyrannical government and we have" no sign" from them this year, but as we are taught Magna
Bal 1leritas el prevalabu, we have faith that the right will triumph over the combined
efforts of Pope and King, and from rekindled fires on restored altars shall arise the
incense of a pure offering to the reasonable freedom of thought and action.

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oali/ornia:On entering upon the duties of Grand Lecturer one ye~r ago I was not

unmindful of the grave responsibilities I was then assuming. I knew that
much would be expected of me, and that on no other subject were the Craft
so punctilious and exacting as upon the accuracy of the secret work and
l ectures and the ma.oner of presenting the same by the G~d Lec~rer.
I recognized that I should be as perfect in the symbolism as m the mere
formula and language of the work, and should be able to give an intelligent

1896.]

Grand Lodge of Oaliforni,a.

787

reason for everything taught, to the end that the great moral truths therein
contained might be fully understood.
I also knew that I would be expected to make myself master of all the
ceremonies of our Order, and to give instruction in the manner of rendering
them the most striking and effective. I knew that I would be plied with
hundreds of questions on matters of jurisprudence, to which I ought to be able
to give an intelligent opinion, and thereby save the Grand Master a large
amount of needless correspondence . In a word, I knew that many eyes would
be upon me, and that much hard work was in store for me. Whether or not
I have discharged this trust I leave to the judgment of my brethren for
whom I have labored and their representatives in Grand Lodge assembled.
It is due me to say, however, that during the winter months I was not able to
do as much work as I had intended, owing to ill health which was brought on
by a severe attack of la grippe.
With the exception of informal visits to certain Lodges in San Francisco at
the close of our last Communication , my labor as Grand Lecturer began in the
southern division of the State.
On November 1, 1895, I visited Colton, Cal., in the Thirty-seventh District,
and gave instruction to the officers of A ghlar Lodge, No. 306. The Master,
Bro. CoNBTANTIN U'REN, has proven himself a most efficient officer, and the
Lodge has prospered under his care. He has since been appointed Inspector
of said Thirty-seventh District, an honor which he has well earned. On the
following evening (November 2d) in company with Bro. U'RE!i, I visited
Phaniz Lodge, No. 178, at San :Bernardino, and witnessed work in the
second degree, after which I gave instruction until a late hour. The attendance was good, and, as usual with this Lodge, a lively interest was taken.
On November 23d I again visited Ashlar Lodge, No. 306, and saw the third
degree conferred on two candidates. The officers and a large delegation of

this old Lodge, dedicated as it is to the memory of the great father of his
oountry, may yet survive and ag&i.n become prosperous. I arrived in Sonora

Orland Lodge is financially embarrassed. They have a good hall, but it is
very poorly furnished, and from what I could learn they had been paying very
extravagant hall rent. An examination of the books disclosed that the Lodge
had been scrupulously careful to appropriate every farthing (putting the case
mildly) of the percentage of Lodge funds allowed under the law for social
purposes, to the payment of refreshment bills. In fact the books would not
bear inspection on that point.
I could not refrain from the suggestion that it would be but justice to
themselves to foster their fonds, and make no appropriation whatever to
social purposes until they had put a carpet on the floor, and provided some
necessary furniture, of which the Lodge was almost entirely destitute. They
had but little of Lodge paraphernalia. by which a degree could be rendered intelligent. In this connection I would say that the opening of the way to the
use of Lodge funds for the cultivation of the much talked of social feature
has not proven _the boon to Lodges that was expected. Those brethren who
can only be induced to attend by i>ffering a premium to their appetites are
of but little value 't o the Lodge, and invariably leave the burden of the work
to those few brethren who prefer the interests of the Lodge to the banquet
table.

Grand Lecturer's work the coming year, and he should give himself sufficient
time in ea.ch district to put the Lodges, or at lea.et the Inspectors, in thorough
working condition. I think I have clearly demonstrated by my year's work
that a Grand Lecturer's visit is only beneficial when he remains long enough
to impress his work so that it will not be forgotten. The Inspectors, however, must of necessity be largely depended on to instruct the Lodges, and to
that end the Graild Lecturer should give his first attention to the Inspector,
and to the Lodges incidentally. He should make himself thoroughly acquainted with the condition of affairs in ea.ch district, the better to enable him
to select the most suitable a.nd best qualified brother for Inspector, for it is
needless to say that the Inspectors are not all a.a well qualified as they ought
to be. There is nothing so di~couraging and hurtful to Lodges as to give them

In pursuing my work a.a Lecturer, I often found it necessary to remain
longer in a district than I had calculated on, while a.t other times I had to

was to do the ~ea.test posmble amount of work with the lea.st po88ible expense, and to that end I traveled progressively from one district or Lodge to
the next nearest, so as to avoid the expense of long rune and the consequent
loss of time. I have also tried to confine my work to localities that have heretofore been somewhat neglected, and to that end I have assumed that the
districts Ml:jacent to and including Sa.n Francisco were in no particular need
of my services, and have, therefore, given them but little attention.
My labor has involved a nece88ary absence from home of 226 days up to

Our system of Masonic Districts and Inspectors is, in my opinion, one of
the best arrangements that can be devised for the purpose of securing uniformity of work, and ie attracting favorable comment in other jurisdictions.
To make the system most effective, however, it ie of the greatest importance
that the Inspectors should be selected from the bedt and most suitable material that can be found, and having been thus selected they should be given
every possible opportunity to qualify themselves for their duties. To that
end, they should be allowed transportation to and from the meetings of this
Grand Lodge, the same as the representatives of subordinate Lodges, not
only for the purpose of meeting the Grand Lecturer, but also that they may

w.·.

1896.J

Grand Lo<lge of California.

807

acquaint themselves with the legislation of this Grand Body ; for it will be
remembered that they are required to certify to the qualifications of each
Master-elect, not only in the ritual, but also in hie knowledge of the law. I
therefore earnestly recommend that transportation be allowed to these officers
'
under such restrictions, of course, ae will secure the beet service.
During my year's work among the Lodges I have been impressed with the
need of a better text-book. Our present Monitor ie deficient in many respects.
Our Grand Secretary hae improved it very much by inserting in the last
edition the explanation of the third degree emblems, known as the " eight
claeeee, " but still it ie unsatisfactory and not suited to our present wants. I
therefore recommend that the Grand Lodge take the necessary etepe to have
a new Monitor compiled which will be complete in every particular, and illus·
tratt>d with the emblems of the chart. It should contain the ceremonies
adopted by this Urand Lodge, such as the installation services funeral service, laying comer-stones, constituting Lodges, etc., but should ~ontain noth·
ing pertaining to the law, or any matter that ie subject to revision or change.
Such work can be compiled in a volume sufficiently large for convenient uee
in the Lodge·room, yet small enough to be carried in the pocket.
I desire to call the attention of the Grand Lodge to an evil which I have
found in all pa.rte of the State, and which ie working great injury to the cause of
true Masonic charity. It ie the existence of a large number of Masonic
tramps, "':ho tra~el from place to place imposing themselves on the Fraternity
for pecumary gam. The story of one is the story of all, with slight variation.
A stranger appears who claims to be a Ma.son in extreme want, and a member of
some Eastern Lodge. He is ta.ken to the Lodge-room and examined, and
found to possess the necessary information. He receives the amount he asks
as a. loan, and goes his way. The Lodge in which he claims membership ~
co'.°municated with and the reply comes that no such person ever belonged to
said Lodge. I have all the necessary proof that there ie an orga.nized band of
rognes- poseibly expelled Masone- who are traversh1.g the State and preying
on the credulity of our cliarita.bly disposed brethren. I believe the evil can
be stamped out in one year's time by a little legislation on the part of this
Grand Lodge. First, prohibit any Lodge from granting aid to a stranger on
Ma.sonic account, until authorized to do so hy the Lodge of which he claims
to be a member; a.nd secondly, prohibit any Lodge or member thereof from
ex.amining a ~trange~ on th.e ~ecret work of our Order, simply becanee he app~es for chanty. I know 1t 1.e argued that such measures might work a hard.
ship to true Masone who are. in want, but I believe that such would rarely if
ever happen. I do not believe that Masonry was ever intended to tum out
beggars broadcast over the country, and certainly the time has come when
every trne Ma.son should keep himself in touch with his own Lodge, nnlees
he is financially independent of ite assistance.
In conclusion, I desire to extend to the brethren my sincere thanks for the
many courtesies and expressions of appreciation th~y have been pleased to
extend to me, without which my year's work would have been tiresome indeed
whereas it has been one of both pleasure and profit to myself, as I trust it h~
·
been to those with whom I have labored,
Respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM ERSKINE SLOAN,

in the case of Ro:BERT CHRESTEBEN, sentenced to reprimand by Elk Grove.

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the trial record
Lodge, No. 173, on Septt.mber 28th, 1895, report as follows:-

812

Procee,dings of the

[Oct. 15,

This is the third time this case comes before this committee, the judgment
of suspension in the first trial having been reversed for error in the record.
The accused is charged with using the most vile, vulgar and violent language on the public highway in the presence of and towards the accuser and
his wife.
The charge is full and explicit, alleging the language, manner e.nd conduct
of the accused, with great care and particularity.
The record is fair and could be approved but for the fact that there is no
evidence given, nor was there any ta.ken.
The accuser and accnsed were both present during the trial ; the accused
entered an oral answer and made a statement admitting the use of the le.nguage.
The record states that the accuser was called upon to produce his witnesses,
and he stated that he had nothing further to offer than his written charges
and specifications. The accused was then called upon to produce his ~t­
nesses, e.nd he stated that he had nothing further to offer than his oral statement and admission, and upon this the case was concluded, submitted and
d.,cided.
The accused admits his guilt, admits the use of language too vile to ·
mention here, to a Master Mason and his wife, without any provocation.
His conduct and language, as admitted by himself, was unbecoming a man
and a Mason, and it should have met with severer punishment.
It seems useless to send this case back ; there must be an end to it as well
as to other good things, and your committee therefore offer the following resolution and recommend ita adoption;Resolved, That the judgment of Elk Grove Lodge, No. 175, given on Sep tember 28th, 1895, whereby ROBERT CRRll:STESEN was sentenced to reprimand,
be and the same is hereby reversed, and the said RoBERT CHRESTESEN be
and he hereby is, by this Grand Lodge, suspended from all the rights and
privileges of Masonry.

Your committee, to whom was referred the transcript of t he trial record
in the case. of WILLIA.II! HENRY MENTOR, expelled on April 25th, 1896, by
Janesville Lodge, No. 232, report as follows:The accused is charged with obtaining the sum of five hundred and fifty
dollars by means of a forgei promissory note, which he ma.de and passed.
This record also comes to us in fair condition, e.nd could be approved
with the single exception that the only evidence is an affidavit taken and
made before a Notary Public, in the town of Susanville, of which time and
place of taking the accused had been duly notified.
It wa.s undoubtedly the intention to take a deposition, notice was given to
the accnsed that an affidavit would be taken, and the document is e.n affidavit
e.nd contains no statement as to who wa.R present at t he time it was taken.
It is full e.nd complete, giving in detail an interview had by the deponent
with the aocnsed concerning the obtaining of the money and t he statements
and admissions of the accused to the deponent.
It shows clearly that the accused admitted the facts of the forgery and the
receipt of the money, the return of a greater portion of the money, the spending of a portion and an offer to give his personal note for the p_o rtion so spent.
The accused was not present at the trial, nor before the Notary, so far as
is shown by·the record, and no appeal bas been taken.
That the offense, a most serious one, meriting the enforcement of the extreme penalty, was committed by the accused, is conclu1ively shown by the
evidence, and though it may not have been taken and transcribed ent irely
r..ud completely in the manner provided by our Constitution, yet the time and
place of taking was designated, the accused had notice and ample opportunity
to avail himself of the privile11e of being present bad be desired.
While we cannot approve the procadure, a.nd must ~gain warn subordinate Lodges to exercise greater care in the trial of their cases, and particularly in the taking of evidence, this case is one that can properly be taken in
band by this Grand Lodge, and we therefore offer the following resolution and
recommend its adoption :Resolved, That the judgment of Janesville Lodge, No. 232, given on April
25th, 1896, whereby WILLIA.II! HENRY MENTOR was expelled from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby reversed, and the said
WILLIAM HENRY MENTOR be and be hereby is, by this Grand Lodge, expelled
from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Respectfully submitted.

reports a separate statement of the amounts expended for and owing by each

Grand Master F. & A. M. qf Oalifornia:The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home of
California herewith submits the fifth annual report of its work during the
year:The Board organized by the election of the following officers : CHARLES L.
PATTON, President; CHARLES F. CROOKER, Vice-President; GEORGE JOHNSON,
i&eoretary; EDWARD COLEMAN, Treasurer.
In accordance with the last report submitted by the Board, the springs
tnentioned therein, with sufficient ground around them, together with full

The :Board then selected a site for the building, and :Bro. W. W. :BRIER, of
Alameda Lodge, No. 167, surveyed and laid out a road to the same, and specifi.
cations were made for the necessary grading, road making and foundations for
.

the building.
At a regular meeting of the :Board bids were received for grading the site
and making the road, and this contract was let to :Bro. E. :B. STONB, of San
Leandro, he being the lowest bidder.
At a subsequent meeting bids were received for laying the necessary pipes
to carry the water from the springs to our property, and the contract was let
to Russ:e:LL & SMALLEY, of Haywards, they being the lowest bidders. The
necessary pipe for this purpose was purchased by the :BO&"d at a very low
price.
The contract for laying the concrete foundations was let to :Bros. WIIBON
~d PETERSEN, of MiaBion Lodge, No. 169, they beingthe lowest bidders.
:Bro. :BRIER, the engineer of the :Board, employed a number of men to
clean out and fence the springs, and we are pleased to report that we have
developed about 12,000 g&llons in the twenty-four hours, of ve~ _fine,_ pure
water for domestic purposes, and that it has been piped to the buildi~ s~te.
As these contracts have .not yet been entirely completed, and as it will be
impOBSible to estimate the exact cost of improvements until the amount ~f
grading done, pipe laid, and concrete laid, is definitely determined by the architect and engineers, it is impoasible to give the exa.ot cost of the work.
The Grand Lodge having attended the laying of the corner-stone of the
building, it will be unnecessary to make auy co~ents on. the character of
the work, the object having been to have everything done ID the most substantial manner.
All bills have been met as they beca.me due and there is more than
.
enough money subscribed to pa.y a.11 the a.mounts ~ontracted for: .
The :Board proposes to proceed with the erection of the bnildmg ea~ly ID
the spring, and trusts tha.t the Home will be dedica.ted a.t the next meeting of
the Grand Lodge.
The enthusiasm of the Craft in the matter of the Home has been ma.rked,
and there is no question that all funds necessary for the purpose will be forth·
•oming as the work progresses.
The :Board has not m&de any great attempt to collect funds or donations
during the past year, but it desires to call the attention of the brethren to the
fact that subscriptions to the fund should be made by all who have the success of this lasting monument of the charity of the Masons of California at

heart.

The Trustees would request that the Grand Lodge consider the ad visabili~
of establishing a special fund for the erection and maintenance of this Home.
In submitting the result of the :Board's labors of. the year for the approval
of the Ma.eons of California, it is but fitting to express its thanks to the hreth•
ren who have rendered it possible to make the progress indicated.

Bro. JoHN MABVIN MELENDY, from the specie.I committee on the
Report of the Grand Lecturer, presented the following report :-

1896.J

Grand Lodge of California.

825

First. We would in the outset commend the indefatigable energy and zeal
:manifested by the Grand Lecturer in his untiring and painstaking efforts to
;Secure uniformity of work, and heartily condemn the indifference of those
.Inspectors who failed to make any report to the Grand Lodge, believing that
no brother should accept a position, however onerous, unless with the determination and purpose to discharge the duties devolving upon it to the best of
.his ability.
Second. We heartily approve the recommendation of the Grand Lecturer,
touching the compilation of a new Monitor, and we recommend that that por·
tion of the Grand Lecturer's address be referred to the committee appointed
by the M. '. W. '. Grand Master on the revision of the Ritual

Bro. NATHANIEL GREENE CUB.TIS, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports :Relative to the centennial observance of memorial services of the dea.th of
W. '• GEORGE WASHINGTON.
Your committee, at the last session of this Grand Lodge, had this matter
under consideration. We then reported tha.t the memory of our deceased
brother wa.s enshrined in the hearts of the American people, a.nd we reverence
his memory with a devotion second only to that of the creature to the Crea.tor.
In our report of laat year we gave the proceedings of the Gra.nd Lodge of
Colorado in reference to this memorial observuce, which will be found in the
printed proceediilgs of our Grand Lodge, on pages 236-7. We believe a proper
observance of the centennial of the dea.th of that great and good Mason is desirable. We therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:-

Reaolved, That the Gra.ud Master be requested to appoint a committee of
one, with a.n alternate, whose duty it shall be to correspond with the committee appointed by the Grand Lodge of Colorado to arrange for the memorial
observance of the centennial anniversary of the death of Worshipful GEORGE
WASHINGTON, and that said committee be requested to report at the next
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge a.11 information that they a.re enabled to obtain in reference to the matter, that the Grand Lodge may deter~
mine whether it would be expedient for this Grand Lodge to participate in
said memorial observance.
Bro. R. H. LLOYD presented the following resolution :-

Reaolved, That any working tool of this Order presented to any Grand
Master, to be used by him in officiating at, or assisting in, performing any
ceremony which this Grand Lodge ma.y be invited to perform, shall be deposited with the Gra.nd Treasurer, to be held by the Grand Lodge in commemoration of the event.
Your committee are of the opinion tha.t a testimonial presented to a Grand
Master in recognition of some official public act, like the one in question, is
incidental to the honorable position which he holds, and should be regarded
as a peraonal souvenir of the occasion. Such testimonials, inscribed with the
recipient's name, the date and the occasion of such service, are treasured as
mementoes and are highly prized. They are evidences of the honor a.nd esteem
which you, a.s a Grand Lodge of Ma.sons, ha.ve conferred upon our brethren.
They a.re treasured with commendable pride during the lifetime of the individual, are bequeathed to loved ones when he has passed away, and your committee considers it unfair that the Grand Lodge should thus demand that
these testimonials be surrendered. We recommend that the resolution be not
adopted.

Relative to the recognition of the Grand Lodge of New Zealand.
At the annual session of this Grand Lodge of October, 1891, a communication was presented from the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodgl! of New Zealand asking for recognition from our Grand Lodge. At that time the request
was denied, it not appearing that recognition had been gra.nted by either of
the Grand Lodges under whom the constituent Lodges of New Zealand ha.d
heretofore held obedience.
From the documents received by the Grand Secretary and placed before
your committee, it appears that the Grand Lodge of England granted recognition to the Gra.nd Lodge of New Zealand a.ta. special communication called
for that purpose on the twenty-ninth day of July la.st, and the matter of our
recognition of that Grand Lodge has a.gain been submitted to your committee.
From the information furnished us, we are of the opinion that the Gra.nd Lodge
of New Zealand was regularly and legally organized, and is entitled to recognition. We therefore offer the following resolution :Reaolved, That the Gra.nd Lodge of California recognizes the Grand Lodge
of New Zealand a.a a. just and legs.Uy constituted Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Ma.sons, and we extend to the Grand Lodge of New Zealand a fra.·
terna.l welcome to the great family of Grand Lodges, a.nd respectfully ask from
that Grand Body a.n interchange of Representatives.
Relative to the recognition of the Grand Lodge of Victoria.
The Committee on Jurisprudence, at our la.st Annual Communication, reported to this Grand Lodge that they were not in possession of sufficient information in reference to the legality and regularity of the Grand Lodge of Victoria, and requested our Grand Secretary to correspond with the Grand Secretary of that Grand Body asking for further information.
Our Grand ·Secretary reports, as the result of his correspondence with that
Grand Lodge, as follows ;A copy of the above report and recommendation wa.s mailed to V. ·. W. '.
Bro. JoHN BRAIM, Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Victoria., on the
twenty-fourth da.y of December la.st, and, although all the information desired
by the committee has not come to hand, from a programme of the proceedings
at the installation of the Grand Officers of that llrand Body, held at Melbourne
on the fourth da.y of May la.at, it appears that Representatives have been exchanged with England, Scotland and Ireland, all the Grand Lodl(es of the Colonies and British America, and also by thirty-six of the Grand Lodges of the
United States of America.. The reque1t for recognition and an exchange of
Representatives has again been referred to the committee.
From the information furnished and the documents submitted to us, we
are of the opinion that the Grand Lodge of Victoria is a regularly and legally .
constituted Grand Lodge. We therefore offer the following resolution :ReBolved, That the Grand Lodge of California recognizes the Grand Lodge
of Victoria. a.a a. just and legally constituted Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons, a.nd we extend to the Grand Lodge of Victoria a fraternal welcome to
the great family of Grand Lodges, and respectfully ask from that Grand Body
an interchange of Representatives.

Grand Secretary.

We have given the foregoing communication careful and fraternal consideration. We have also read the able report of Bro. J. H. DRUMMOND, Chairman of the Committee of Jurisprudence of Maine, with great pleasure and
satisfaction. It is an able and forcible statement of Masonic law upon the
question involved. We earnestly recommend the perusal of the said report
to every member of the Fraternity in this Jurisdiction, as it contains information 11pon the Masonic law to be found nowhere else within the knowledge of your committee. The Grand Lodge of California, in 1883, made
rejection a bar for one year only, after which the Lodge which has territorial
jurisdiction can receive him. We believe that this regulation is well adapted
to our loca.l condition and has proved satisfactory, therefore we see no reason
why it should be changed.

Bro. WILLIAM SEWALL WELLS, from the Committee on Grievances,
presented the following reports : To the M. •. W. ·• Grand Lodge of California:

Yoiir committee, to whom wa.s referred the papers and records in the case
of Fresno Lodge, No. 247, against Corinthian Lodge No. 9, relative to the
claims of Freano Lodge for expenses incurred in the burial of a. deceased member of Corinthian Lodge, have ha.d the same under consideration and report as
follows:In July, 1894, Bro. S. C. HUTCHINGS, a. life member of Corinthian Lodge,
dropped dead in tb,e streets of Fresno. His Lodge wa.s notified, and instructed
.l!'rlJ8no Lodge to bnry the body a.t the expense of Corinthian Lodge.
Relatives had requested the shipment of the body East, but for ·this
expense Corinthian Lodge properly refused to become responsible, and the
remains were interred at Fresno.
Th~ bill, a.mounting to $130, was forwarded to Corinthian Lodge, but payment was refused a.t first upon the ground that the deceased had left a.n estate,
and that Fruno Lodge must look to it for payment before sending the bill to
Corinthian Lodge, a.nd in reply to a. communication to the Grand Master,
place their refusal on the ground that their By-Laws provide for the expenditure of but $75.00, and that the bill was unreasonable.
The estate of the deceased was insolvent, of which fa.ct Corinthian Lodge
was duly apprised, and still no payment was ma.de and no inclination shown
by the Lodge to arrive a.t a settlement.
The matter was finally submitted to the Grand Master, and his decision
that Corinthittn Lodge pay $75.00 a.t once, together with a.II the papers,
have been by the Grand Master referred to this committee. Corinthian
Lodge has since pa.id to firlJ8no Lodge the sum of $75.00, the balance of
$55.00 remaining unpaid.
From a. careful exa.minatiau we find that the expenditures were rea.sonable,
moderate a.nd just. The death occurred during the railroad strike and the
delay caused thereby necessitated a.n extra expense, which, under ordinary
conditions, would not have been incurred. Fresno Lodge, with due regard
for the rights of Corinthian Lodge, incurred no expense other than such as
was absolutely necessary.
No instruction wa.s received from Corinthian Lodge to limit the a.mount of
expenses to $75.00, and we find that even if there ha.d been, it could not have
been done in this case.
It is the duty of every Lodge to give to its deceased members decent
burial, and when such is done by a. sister Lodge the expense so incurred should
be at once remitted, and the necessities of the particular case and no By·La.w
of a. Lodge should govern as to the a.mount.

Grand .Lodge of California.

1896.]

No. 247, th~ ~urther sui:n of fifty-five dollars, ha.lance due for expenses
incurred by it 10 the burial of Bro. S. C. HUTCHINGS, a deceased member of"
Corinthian Lodge.

Bro. WILLIAM ABRAHAM DAVIES presented the following preamble
and resolution : -

Y onr committee to audit the bills of this Grand Lodge, have the honor
to submit the following report:The Auditing Committee have met the last Saturday of every month during the past Masonic year, when all bills and vouchers for expenditures of
money outside of the regular appropriations for this Grand Lodge have been
acted upon by your committee. Authority for expenditure and copies of
article8 purchased are presented to the committee in every case, and no bills
are approved until they have paBSed the scrutiny of this committee.
Every courtesy has beeu shown your committee by Bro. GEORGE JOHN·
soN, Grand Secretary.
Respectfully submitted.
EDWARD PEABODY,

Ohairman.

Which was concurred in.
Bro. WILLLUt: PRESTON JOHNSON presented a statement showing
the expenses of the Grand Lecturer in excess of tl).e amount appropriated.
Which was referred to the Committee on Finance.
The hour having arrived for the election of the Grand Officers for
the ensuing year, the Grand Master named as tellers Bros. EDWARD
PEABODY, FREDERICK ADAMS and FRANCIS CHUTE WooDBUBY, and the
election proceeded with the following result : -

The Grand Lodge having determined that a revision of the Work and
Ritual of the Jurisdiction is desirable for the purpose of restoring the text to
the work as the same was adopted and made obligatory upon the Lodges in
October, 1864;
Be it Re&olved, That the Committee on Revision appointed at the present
session be and they are hereby directed to ascertain, by such method as they
may de.em most reliable and expedient, the several expressions referred to in
the Address of the Grand Master 11 as at variance with the original authorized
text," to the end that the Work and Ritual of this Jurisdiction may be
restored to the system adopted in 1864 ; and they are hereby authorized to
make the necessary corrections for the accomplishment of that purpose and
to prepare for the exemplification of said revised and corrected work at the
next Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
In addition to said corrections said committee will further, in accordance
with the recommendation of the Grand Master in his address and affirmed by
the Grand Lodge, proceed to make the neceBBary changes in the ceremonial
of the second section of the Third Degree, to harmonize said ceremonial and
make it more "in conformity with the work of the principal Grand Jurisdictions east of the Rocky Mountains," and to suggest such changes in phraseology as shall make the revised Ritual "consistent with the traditions upon
which the scenes exemplified are founded."
When adopted and made obligatory upon the Lodges, such revised Ritual
shall be placed in charge of three custodians of the work to be hereafter
appointed by the Grand Master.
W~ich was concurred in, and the resolution accompanying it was

The surplus for 1896, as shown in the foregoing report, though large, does
not admit of a cha.nee at this time of any material reduction of the levy for
the Representati ve Fund for the ensuing year. But if the balances from year
to year were kept as a separate and distinct fund a reduction could in time be
made.
Your committee therefore offer the followins;: resolutione and recommend
their adoption : Jlllolved, That the surplus which may be shown to be on hand, after allowances shall have been pa.id from the Representati ve Fund, she.11 be kept in a
distinct fund by the Grand Treasurer and applied for no other purpose than
that for which it is collected, and it shall be shown from year to year as an
IOCUillUlated bal&nce to the credit of the Representati ve Fund, so that in time
the surplus thus accumulated may be applied to a reduction of the usual levy
. for that purpose ; also be it further
Resolved, That there ~e levied upon the subordinate Lodges of this jurisdiction for the current fiscal year, iu addition to the dues prescribed by the
Constitution , the sum of twenty-five cents for . each member borne upon the
Jfillective rolls at the date of the annual reports. Said levy shall be made for
the account of tlre Representati ve Fund, and shall be paid at the same time
and in the manner prescribed for the payment of the annual dues.
All which is most respectfully submitted.
ORRIN STAPLES HENDEBBON, Chamnan.
